PREFACE
The first part of this book (Chapters 1 through 5) has been derived from the class notes I had composed
formylecturesonselectedtheoreticalmethodologiesforcomputervision,signalprocessingandmachine
learning. These lectures and notes have evolved over several years during graduate courses I have taught
at the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering of the National Technical University of Athens
(NTUA) in the above areas. The emphasis of these lectures and notes is on the theoretical and algo-
rithmic aspects of the topics analyzed. The second part of the book (Chapters 6 through 9) deals with
somemodernapplicationsofcomputervisioninthedeeplearningeraandhasbeenco-authoredwithmy
research collaborators. Some of the topics or subtopics associated with these modern applications have
beeninspiredbyresearchonfundamentalcomputervisionproblemsperformedattheComputerVision,
Speech Communication and Signal Processing (CVSP) Lab and the Intelligent Robotics and Automa-
tionLab(IRAL)atNTUA.Theoverallpurposeofthisbookistoserveasagraduatetextbookforspecific
topics in computer vision and machine learning that combine theory and applications. It assumes that
students have already had prior exposure at an introductory undergraduate level to areas such as linear
algebra, computer vision or image processing, and machine learning.
The first three chapters present some foundational mathematical concepts and tools that are of im-
portance and which are frequently employed in several areas of computer vision and machine learning.
Chapter1explores linear operator theory from algebraic, topological-metric, and geometric perspectives
while covering Banach and Hilbert spaces. It includes examples from image and signal analysis, focusing
on Hilbert spaces and topics such as orthogonal projections, orthonormal bases, and generalized Fourier
series. It also discusses generalized inverses of linear operators and the representation of linear operators.
Chapter 2 summarizes key concepts from linear algebra, focusing on the geometry of solving linear
equationsusingleastsquares,generalizedinversesliketheMoore-Penrosepseudoinverse,andmatrixfac-
torizations-particularlySingularValueDecomposition(SVD).ItalsocoversPrincipalComponentAnal-
ysis and other SVD-based least-squares algorithms for computer vision and machine learning. Finally, it
providesrepresentativeexamplesofapplications-suchascompactimagerepresentations, regularization,
linear and ridge regression, multi-view geometry, shape recognition, and 3D reconstruction.
Chapter3 introduces basic concepts from abstract algebra that pertain to the application of computer
vision methods in the field of robotics. It mainly focuses on groups, as well as rings and vector spaces.
Symmetry groups and matrix-based representations of rigid motions are explored, particularly their ap-
xxiii

<!-- PDF_PAGE: 26 -->
### Σελίδα 26

xxiv PREFACE
plication in shape analysis and coordinate transformations, respectively.
Chapter4 covers the theory of the nonlinear operators of mathematical morphology, their generaliza-
tionusingtropicalalgebra,andsomeoftheirapplicationsinimageanalysis,computervisionandmachine
learning. After a concise theory of lattices and adjunctions of morphological operators, it focuses on lat-
tice projections and the morphological basis representation of both translation-invariant and adaptive
image operators. Then, it introduces nonlinear spaces, called weighted lattices or tropical spaces, whose
algebraic structure generalizes both mathematical morphology and max-plus algebra. The resulting trop-
ical vector operators are used to provide optimal solutions of nonlinear matrix equations in max-plus or
tropical algebra. The corresponding tropical signal convolutions are studied from the viewpoints of al-
gebraic representation and PDE-based multiscale analysis. Special cases include max-plus, max-min and
max-fuzzy-norm operators. Finally, it provides a survey of morphological neural networks (which are
networks with max-plus or max-min nodes) both from the era of traditional machine learning as well as
from the modern era of deep learning.
Chapter5 explores the theory of fractals and examines their applications within computer vision and
signal processing problems which involve the analyzing and synthesizing of the self-similar rough shape,
or texture, of fractal image objects and complex random time-series. It mainly covers methods for fractal
dimensionestimation, IteratedFunction Systems(IFS)for modelingfractalimages, fractalinterpolation,
and analysis of random fractal waveforms (fractional Brownian motions). Additionally, it includes an
application of IFS to fractal pre-training for visual recognition. It also provides an introduction to multi-
fractals and presents computational algorithms for fractal analysis and synthesis.
Therestofthebookismoreapplication-oriented,whilestillaimingtobeeducationalforcasualreaders
and students alike. Chapter6 introduces the basic concepts of deep learning, focusing on Convolutional
Neural Networks (CNNs) while also providing a summary of other significant Deep Neural Networks
(DNNs). These networks have evolved into large intricate architectures, which have shown great success
in almost every major computer vision problem. Their applications in object detection, image segmenta-
tion, and action recognition are explored by presenting the most foundational architectures that address
these problems.
Chapter7reviews visual gesture recognition, oriented towards the design of intuitive human-machine
interfaces for various applications. It delves into traditional machine learning methods based on hand-
crafted features, as well as deep learning approaches, and focuses on dynamic gestures while addressing
theoretical, practical, and data-related aspects.
Chapter8 covers some introductory concepts on emotion recognition in the context of affective com-
puting. Itpresentsthecomputationalmodelsofemotionandexaminesthevisualchannelsthroughwhich
emotions are expressed, exploring some deep learning algorithms that use these visual cues to recognize
emotions.
Chapter9exploresthe3DModelingofdeformableobjects,focusingon3DMorphableModels,which
aimatcapturingtheintricateshapeandappearanceofdeformableobjects. Themathematicalfoundations
and key methods of the field are covered, as well as many applications that 3DMMs have engendered.
Finally, some mathematical concepts and tools that are used throughout several chapters are reserved
for AppendicesA and B. These roughly cover several aspects of image set theory, topology, and metric
spaces, and they can be used for quick reference by the reader.

A Hamel basis of X is a setB ⊆ X that is linearly independent and its linear span makes up all the

1.1.2 Topological-Metric Structure, Banach spaces
A real-valued function‖ ⋅ ‖ defined on a linear spaceV over F is called anorm if for allx, y ∈ V and
a ∈ F :
(N1) ‖x‖ ≥ 0 and ‖0‖ = 0 (Positivity)
(N2) ‖x + y‖ ≤ ‖x‖ + ‖y‖ (Triangle inequality)
(N3) ‖ax‖ = |a| ‖x‖ (Homogeneity)
(N4) ‖x‖ = 0 ⟹ x = 0 (Strict Positivity).
If the function satisfies only (N1), (N2) and (N3), it is called aseminorm(orpseudonorm).
A linear space equipped with a norm becomes anormed linear space. Each normed space is ametric
spacewhere the given norm defines adistancefunction, such as:
d(x, y) ∶= ‖x − y‖ (1.1)
This in turn endows the space with a topology, called thenorm topology. This topology determines the
open and closed subsets of the normed linear space. In such spaces, the axioms for defining a linear space
determine its algebraic structure, whereas the norm endows it with topological and metrical properties.
Thus, normed spaces possess some weak geometric structure since, in addition to vector structure, they
have distances and lengths.
Twonorms ‖ ⋅ ‖a and ‖ ⋅ ‖b onalinearspace X arecalled equivalentiftheygenerateequivalentmetrics,
i.e. create the same topology onX. It can be shown that the two norms are equivalent iff there exist
positive constantsc1 and c2 such that for allx ∈ X
c1‖x‖a ≤ ‖x‖ b ≤ c 2‖x‖a (1.2)
On afinite-dimensionallinear space, two norms are always equivalent.
Proposition 1.1 A normed linear space(X, ‖ ⋅ ‖) is finite-dimensional iff the unit ball{x ∈ X ∶ ‖x‖ ≤ 1}
is a compact set.
Let X be a normed linear space. A sequence(xn) in X is calledconvergentif there isx ∈ X such that
‖xn − x‖ → 0 as n → ∞ ; we write limxn = x. If this sequence limit exists, it is unique. A sequence
(xn) is called aCauchy sequenceif ‖xn − x m‖ → 0 as n, m → ∞ . If each Cauchy sequence inX
converges to a point inX, thenX is calledcomplete. A complete normed linear space is called aBanach
space. Every finite-dimensional normed linear space is complete.

In the Euclidean geometry of the plane, two vectors are orthogonal if their in-between angle is90∘, or
equivalently if their inner product is zero. Similarly, in a general inner product spaceX, two elements
x, y are calledorthogonal, written asx ⟂ y , if⟨x, y⟩ = 0 . Two subsetsA, B of X are calledorthogonal,
written asA ⟂ B, if⟨x, y⟩ = 0 for all(x, y) ∈ A × B .

are orthogonal, then

The converse is true if the space is real.
A (complex or real)Hilbert space is a (complex or real) complete inner product linear space. Thus,
the inner product of a Hilbert space creates a norm (1.3), which in turn creates a distance function (1.1)
that makes it a complete metric space. Hilbert spaces generalize facts and geometrical intuition from
finite-dimensional Euclidean vector spaces to infinite-dimensional linear structures and provide a very
rich mathematical framework for the study of many linear problems that extend the linear algebra of ma-
trices to a combined algebraic and geometric study of linear operators.

1.2 Linear Operators
1.2.1 Algebraic Definitions for Linear Operators
A mappingΛ ∶ X → Y between two linear spaces over the same scalar field is called alinear operatorif
it preserves addition and scalar multiplication. This is equivalent to
Λ(a1x1 + ⋯ + anxn) = a 1Λ(x1) + ⋯ + a nΛ(xn)
for allx1, ..., xn ∈ X, all scalarsa1, ..., an and all finiten. An operator that does not satisfy the above is
called nonlinear. Thenull spaceand range(a.k.a. ‘image’) ofΛ are defined as
Nul(Λ) ∶= {x ∈ X ∶ Λ(x) = 0}, Ran(Λ) ∶= {Λ(x) ∶ x ∈ X}
Thenullspaceisalinearsubspaceof X,whereastherangeisalinearsubspaceof Y . Foranylinearoperator
Λ ∶ X → Y between two linear spaces, the dimensions of its null and range spaces are related as follows
to the dimension of the domain space:
dim{Nul(Λ)} + dim{Ran(Λ)} = dim{Dom(Λ)} (1.17)
Among other usages, the null space can help determine whetherΛ has aninverse.
Theorem 1.3 (a) A linear operatorΛ ∶ X → Y has an inverse onRan(Λ) ⊆ Y iff Λ is one-to-one, or
equivalently iffNul(Λ) = { 0}. (b) If it exists, the inverse mappingΛ−1 is also a linear operator.
Two linear spacesX and Y over the same scalar field are calledisomorphic if there exists an invertible
(i.e. bijective) linear operatorΛ ∶ X → Y . Such a mappingΛ is called anisomorphism between the
two linear spaces. All linear spaces over the same field are isomorphic iff they have the same dimension.
Hence, all real (resp. complex)finite-dimensionallinear spaces are isomorphic toRn (resp. Cn) for some
n. Thus, finite-dimensional linear spaces are essentially linearvector spaces, where by ‘vector’ we mean in
this case a finite tuple of scalars.

for each convergent sequencexn → x in X, or equivalently if lim‖f(x n) − f(x)‖ Y = 0 whenever
lim ‖xn − x‖X = 0. Continuous linear maps are the only ones that distribute with infinite series as the
following fundamental result implies.

tween two normed linear spaces. Then,Λ is a continuous linear operator if and only if

Space of Compact Operators:
A linear operatorK ∶ X → Y between two Banach spacesX, Y is called compact if it maps the
unit disk D = {x ∈ X ∶ ‖x‖ ≤ 1} of X onto a compact subsetK(D) of Y . (See also Prop.1.1.)
Equivalently, an operatorK is compact if it maps every bounded setS to a setK(S) that is relatively
compact (i.e. its closure is compact). Such operators are continuous (and hence bounded) and their col-
lection forms a closed linear subspace of BLT(X, Y ). Every linear operator on a finite-dimensional normed
linear space is compact. On infinite-dimensional normed linear spaces, if a linear operator has a finite-
dimensional range, then it is compact. In general, compact operators are not included in nor do they
include the class of normal (and self-adjoint) operators. However, an operator that is both compact and
normal creates a finite-dimensional structure on infinite-dimensional linear spaces and enjoys a simple
spectral analysis.

1.3 Linear Projections
1.3.1 Algebraic Decomposition
Assume we have two linear subspacesA and B of a linear spaceX. There are two ways to combine them
and form a new space. Theirsumis defined as the linear space
A ⊕ B ∶= {a + b ∶ a ∈ A, b ∈ B}
and theirproduct is defined as the linear space
A × B ∶= {(a, b) ∶ a ∈ A, b ∈ B}
where addition and scalar multiplication are defined componentwise.7 Thus, the sum of the subspacesA
and B equals the span(A ∪ B), whereas their product has as underlying set their Cartesian product.
Two subspacesA and B of X are calleddisjoint if A ∩ B = { 0}. If additionallyX = A ⊕ B , then
B is called thealgebraic complement of A. All algebraic complements of a subspaceA have the same
dimension,calledthe co-dimensionof A. Theconceptofthealgebraiccomplementoffersadecomposition
ofalinearspace Xintoasumofdisjointsubspaces A, Bwhereeachpointin Xadmitsauniqueexpression
as a sum of two points inA and B, respectively.
Lemma 1.2 Two linear subspacesA and B of a linear spaceX are algebraic complements of each other if and
only if for eachx ∈ X there is a unique pair(x1, x2) ∈ A × B with x = x 1 + x2.
A projection P ∶ X → X on a linear spaceX is a linear map that is idempotent, i.e.P P = P . A
projection enables the decomposition of a linear space as in Lemma1.2.
Theorem 1.7 (a) IfM and N are two disjoint linear subspaces of a linear spaceX such thatX = M ⊕ N ,
then there is a unique projectionP on X with M = Ran(P )and N = Nul(P ). (b) Conversely, ifP is a
projection, then its range and null space are algebraic complements of each other.

1.3.3 Convex Sets and Approximation
The projection theorem in Hilbert spaces is of fundamental importance for the best approximation and
general optimization theory. Its core idea is that a closed linear subspace and its orthogonal complement
decompose a Hilbert space into a Minkowski sum of of two orthogonal subspaces which correspond to
two orthogonal projections. Related to the projection theorem is the concept of aconvex set C, which is
defined by the propertypx + (1 − p)y ∈ C for allx, y ∈ C and allp ∈ [0, 1] . Note that any linear
subspace of a linear space is itself a convex set.
Proposition 1.5 A closed convex setC of a Hilbert space contains a unique vector of minimum norm.

1.4 Generalized Inverses of Linear Operators
1.4.1 Exact Inverse
The term “generalized inverses” is usually related to inverting matrices which are singular or rectangular,
either exactly or in the sense of least squares. This is a finite-dimensional problem and is discussed in
numerousbooksonlinearalgebraandinChapter2ofthisbook. Inaddition,thetheoryofgeneralizedin-
verseshasbeenextendedtooperatorson infinite-dimensionalspaces,especiallyinversesoflinearoperators,
and this is the subject of this section. References can be found in [1], [3], [5], [7].
In this section, whose exposition is based mainly on [3] and [5], we will attempt to solve a general
linear inverse problemwhere given are two linear normed spacesX and Y , a linear continuous operator
L ∶ X → Y between these two spaces and an input data vectory ∈ Y , and the goal is to find a solution
x ∈ X of the following equation
L(x) = y (1.36)
If L is invertible, which means both injective (i.e. one-to-one) and surjective (i.e. onto), then its inverse
L−1 ∶ Y → X exists and is unique; further,L−1 is linear (by Theorem1.3). In such cases, the unique
solution of the linear problem isx = L −1(y). However, in more realistic scenaria and depending on the
spaces and the operator, we may have difficulties to guarantee the existence or uniqueness of the solution
or (more importantly) to guarantee its continuity in the presence of some perturbation or noise on the
data. To address such issues it helps, as a first step, to endow our spaces with norms or even with inner
products and demand closure of the operator’s range and continuity of the operator. Before we proceed
with a generalized solution, let us summarize some facts about the closure of the operator’s range and its
bounded invertibility on normed spaces.
In general, the null space and range of any linear operatorL ∶ X → Y between two linear spaces are
linear subspaces ofX and Y respectively. Further, ifX and Y spaces are normed linear spaces andL is
bounded, the null space is a closed linear subspace ofX, where its closure is meant to occur in the norm
topology. There are additional relations between the null space and ranges ofL and its adjoint ifX and
Y are Hilbert spaces.
Proposition 1.6 Let X and Y be two Hilbert spaces. Consider a bounded linear operatorL ∶ X → Y
between two Hilbert spacesX and Y , and its adjoint operatorL∗ ∶ Y → X . Then, Nul(L)⟂ = Ran(L∗)
andRan(L)⟂ = Nul(L∗).
The following result, which is also known as theBanach-Schauder theorem, guarantees both the exis-
tence of and continuity for the inverse of a bijective linear bounded operator on Banach spaces.

Theorem 1.10 (Open Mapping Theorem).Consider Banach spacesX and Y and a surjective linear
bounded operatorL ∈ BLT(X, Y ). Then:
(a) L is open, i.e. the imageL(S) is an open set inY for any open subsetS of X.
(b) IfL is also injective, then its inverseL−1 is bounded.
For modeling physical phenomena, Hadamard in 1923 defined a mathematical problem to bewell-
posed if its solution 1) exists, 2) is unique, and 3) depends continuously on the initial data. For a linear
problem as in (1.36), these conditions mean:
1) Existence: the linear operatorL ∶ X → Y must be surjective; i.e., Ran(L) = Y .
2) Uniqueness: L must be injective; i.e., Nul(L) = { 0}.
3) Continuity: IfL(xn) → L(x) in Y , thenxn → x in X.
Conditions(1)and(2)make Linvertible. Condition(3)makesitsinversecontinuousandthusbounded.
Therefore, small perturbations in the data(yn) (due to errors or noise), which converge to or do not
deviatemuchfromacleanvalue y, causesmalldeviationsintheperturbedsolutions (xn)fromtheinitial
solution x. Indeed,
‖xn − x‖ = ‖L −1(yn) − L−1(y)‖ ≤ ‖L −1‖‖yn − y‖ (1.37)
Violation of any of the above conditions makes the problemill-posed. In relation to (1.36), note that
the correspondingdirect problemto computeL(x) = y ∈ Y for a givenx ∈ X is well-posed. While
most inverse problems in physics are well-posed, there are many interesting and important inverse prob-
lems in mathematics that are ill-posed, whereas their direct formulations are well-posed. Examples in-
cludeCauchy’sproblemfortheLaplaceequation, solvingbackwardstheheatequation, Sturm-Liouville’s
eigenvalue problem, inverse scattering, and the differentiation problem in the following example.
Existenceanduniquenessdependonlyonalgebraicaspectsofthespacesandtheoperator,i.e. whether
the latter is onto and one-to-one. Thus, conditions (1) and (2) are controlled by the invertibility of the
linear operator which can be remedied by properlyconstraining its domain andrange. However, the con-
tinuity depends on the topologies of the normed spaces, i.e. whether the inverse operator is bounded
(continuous); namely, continuity of the solution requires that small errors in the data induce small er-
rors in the solution. This continuity condition (3) is the most difficult issue to satisfy. Actually, in many
ill-posed problems, the linear operator involved is a compact operator whose inverse is unbounded.
Theorem 1.11 ([5]). Consider a linear compact operatorK ∶ X → Y on normed spaces and the inverse
problem of solving the linear equationK(x) = y . If the spaceX is infinite-dimensional and the operatorK is
injective, then its inverseK−1 is unbounded and hence the inverse problem is ill-posed.

1.6.2 Linear Functionals, Riesz Representation and Linear Convolution
Given a linear spaceV over a fieldF of scalars (sayR or C), alinear functionalon V is called any linear
transformation ofV into its field of scalars, i.e. any linear operatorφ ∶ V → F that maps points of the
space (e.g. vectors, signals) to scalar numbers. For example, ifV = R n and F = R , the inner product
⟨a, x⟩ = ∑ i aixi of any vectorx = [x i] ∈ R n with a fixed vectora = [a i] is a linear functional,
whereasthe lpvectornorms ‖x‖parenonlinearfunctionals. Bydefiningadditionandscalarmultiplication
of functionals in the obvious way, the set of all linear functionals onV becomes itself a linear space over
the same scalar fieldF; i.e. given two functionalsφ1, φ2 their linear combination is also a functional:
(a1φ1 + a2φ2)(x)) ∶= a 1φ1(x) + a2φ2(x), x ∈ V , a 1, a2 ∈ F ,
Assume now linear functionals on a normed linear space(V , ‖ ⋅ ‖). Such a functionalφ is calledbounded
if there exists a constantC > 0 such that
|φ(x)| ≤ C‖x‖ ∀x ∈ V
Itsnorm is defined (as in the bounded linear operator case) by

Thesetofcontinuous(inthenormtopology)linearfunctionalsformsanormedlinearspace V ∗,whichis
called thedual spaceof V . If the rangeF of the functionals isRor C, which are complete normed spaces,
thedualspace V ∗ isalwayscomplete,i.e. aBanachspace,independentlyofwhether V iscompleteornot.

1.6.3 Spectral Representation of Linear Operators

Summary: Linear algebra deals with the matrix-based algebra of linear operators on finite-
dimensional spaces. In this chapter we will summarize some ideas and results from linear
algebra which relate to (i) solving linear equations either exactly or approximately using
least squares, (ii) generalized inverses emphasizing the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, and
(iii) matrix factorizations emphasizing the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) both for
matrix representation of finite-dimensional linear transformations and for efficient numeri-
calsolutionsofleastsquaresproblems. Buildingonthis,wewillalsoanalyzePrincipalCom-
ponentAnalysis(PCA).Then,inourdiscussionofapplications,wewillproviderepresenta-
tiveexamplesofhowtoapplyleastsquaresandSVDmethodstosolvingclassicalproblemsin
computer vision and machine learning, including compact image representations via SVD,
regularizationofinverseproblems,linearandridgeregression,multi-viewgeometryand3D
reconstruction. We will also present PCA-based applications to 2D image and shape recog-
nition, such as of face and handshapes, as well as to 3D human shape reconstruction from
images. Inalltheabove,whereverpossiblewewillemphasizetheuseofgeometricinterpre-
tation.
Prerequisite Knowledge: Introductory course on calculus, linear algebra, computer vision,
and machine learning.

Before we analyze the above cases, it would greatly improve our understanding if we consider the four
fundamental spaces related to matrixA and their geometry, depicted in Fig.2.1(a). We have already seen
its range space and null space. The range space ofA is the linear span of its columns and is also called
its column space, whereas the linear span of its rows creates therow spacewhich coincides with the range
space Ran(AT ) of the matrix transpose. The fourth space is theleft null spaceNul(AT ), i.e. the null space
ofthematrixtranspose. Theabovefourspacesare linear subspacesofthesupportingEuclideanspaces Rm
or Rn:
Nul(A), Ran(AT ) ⊆ R n

The following theorem summarizes some of their algebraic and geometric properties.
Theorem 2.1 Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra (FTLA).
(a) The dimensions of the four fundamental spaces of a realm × n matrix A with rankr are:
column space ∶ dim Ran(A) = r
row space ∶ dim Ran(AT ) = r
null space ∶ dim Nul(A) = n − r
left null space ∶ dim Nul(AT ) = m − r
(2.5)
(b) InRn the null space ofA is the orthogonal complement of its row space. InRm the orthogonal complement
of the column space ofA is the null space of its transpose:
Nul(A) = (Ran(AT ))⟂ , Nul(AT ) = (Ran(A))⟂ (2.6)
Since the rankr equals the dimension of the column space (and of the row space)
rank(A) = dim(Ran(A)) (2.7)
and the dimension or the null space, called thenullity, equals n − r, an immediate consequence of the
FTLA theorem is therank-nullity theorem:
dimRan(A) + dimNul(A) = # columns ofA (2.8)
As Fig.2.1 shows, the mapping between the row and column spaces is always invertible. The existence and
uniqueness of the solution depend on the relationships amongr, m, n and on b. We distinguish two

2.1.3 Generalized Inverses and Pseudoinverse for Matrices
Inthissectionwewillformalizeandgeneralizetheexactandapproximatesolutionsoflinearmatrixequa-

generalized inverse for any complex matrix. In general, if anm × n complex matrixA does not possess

(ii) has some of the properties of the regular inverse; and
(iii) reduces to the regular inverse when A is non-singular.”

2Nashed [23] mentions the following historic note: Moore [22] defined the generalized inverse of anm × n matrix A

ABA = A, BAB = B, ( AB)H = AB, ( BA)H = BA
These conditions are equivalent to Moore’s conditions. The matrixB that satisfies the above relations is calledMoore-Penrose

Theorem 2.2 (Pseudoinverse [26].) For eachm × n matrix A ∈ C m×n there exists a uniquen × m
matrix A+, called itspseudoinverse, which satisfies all the four following equations:
AA+A = A (2.20)
A+AA+ = A+ (2.21)
(AA+)H = AA+ (2.22)
(A+A)H = A+A (2.23)
Now consider the following two matrix products ofA with its pseudoinverse:
P1 = AA+, P2 = A+A (2.24)
According to the fourPenrose conditionsof Theorem2.2, the first states thatP1 is a left identity andP2
a right identity ofA. Similarly, the second condition states that these two matrix products are identities
for A+. Finally, the third and fourth conditions state thatP1 and P2 are Hermitian matrices, i.e. equal to
their conjugate transpose. The first two conditions also imply that bothP1 and P2 are idempotent, i.e.
(Pi)2 = Pi. Hence,P1 and P2 are orthogonal projections3. Specifically,P1 is a projection on the image
of A (see (2.15) for an example), whereasP2 is a projection on the domain ofA.
If A has full rank, i.e. r = min{m, n}, then its pseudoinverse can be computed via a closed formula.
Namely, ifA has linearly independent rows (r = m ≤ n ), then the mapx ↦ Ax is surjective,AAH is
invertible andA+ becomes theright inverse:
A+ = AH(AAH)−1, AA+ = Im (2.25)
Similarly, ifA has linearly independent columns (r = n ≤ m ), then the mapx ↦ Ax is one-to-one,
AHA is invertible andA+ becomes theleft inverse:
A+ = (AHA)−1AH, A+A = In (2.26)
Obviously, ifA is square and nonsingular (r = m = n ), thenA+ becomes the regular inverseA−1.
In the general case (which often occurs in applications) whereA is not of full rank (r < min{m, n})
andhencebothitsrowsandcolumnsarelinearlydependent, itspseudoinversecanbecomputedusingits
singular value decomposition, something which will be explained later.

The pseudoinverse possesses several useful properties:
Lemma 2.1 ([26]). For any complex matrixA:
(a) (A+)+ = A.
(b) (zA)+ = z +A+ for any scalarz.
(c) Pseudoinversion commutes with conjugation and transposition:(AH)+ = (A+)H.
(d) (AHA)+ = A+(A+)H.
(e) If U and V are unitary,(UAV)+ = VHA+UH.
(f) A, AHA, A+, A+A all have rank equal to the trace ofA+A.
Furthermore, the null spaces and range spaces of a matrix and its pseudoinverse are related [4]:
Ran(A+) = (Nul(A))⟂ , Ran(A) = (Nul(A+))⟂ (2.30)
By combining this with (2.17), it follows that
Ran(A+) = Ran(AH) , Nul(A+) = Nul(AH) (2.31)
Some very useful applications of the pseudoinverse include finding the general solution of any matrix
system of linear equations if it exists, or an approximate solution that is optimum from a least-squares
perspective.
Theorem 2.3 ([4],[26]). Let A ∈ C m×n and b ∈ C m.
(a) (Exact solution): The linear matrix equationAx = b has a solution iffA+b is a solution; then, the set of all
its solutions consists of the following vectors
x = A+b + (In − A+A)y, y ∈ C n (2.32)
(b) (Least Squares approximation): If there is no exact solution, the set of all vectorsx ∈ C n that minimize the
Euclidean norm of the approximation error‖Ax − b‖ is (2.32).
Thetwopartsinther.h.s. ofthegeneral(exactorapproximate)solution( 2.32)areorthogonalvectors,
becausetheybelongtotwoorthogonalsubspacesof Cn. Asdiscussedbeforeinrelationto( 2.26),if Ahas
linearly independent columns (r = n ≤ m ), thenA+A = In and the second part in the r.h.s. of (2.32)
becomes zero, which makes the solution unique.

2.3 Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
The following is perhaps the most important matrix factorization in all modern applications of linear al-
gebra, according to several analytical, computational, and practical viewpoints [11], [30].
Theorem 2.4 (Singular Value Decomposition - SVD).
For any (real or complex)m × n matrix A ∈ C m×n there exist two unitary matrices
U = [u1| ⋯ |um] ∈ C m×m, V = [v1| ⋯ |vn] ∈ C n×n
and anm × n real diagonal matrix with nonnegative diagonal elementsσi (called singular values)
Σ = diag(σ1, ... , σp) ∈ R m×n, σ 1, ... , σq ≥ 0, q = min{m, n}
such thatA can be decomposed into the following matrix product:
A = UΣVH (2.40)
The SVD isnot unique. Specifically, the singular values are uniquely determined byAbut not their order.
Hence, the above factorization is unique4 up to making the same permutation of columns inU, V and
diagonal elements inΣ. By common convention, we shall assume, henceforth, that thesingular values are
sorted in decreasing order:
σ1 ≥ σ 2 ≥ ⋯ ≥ σ q ≥ 0 (2.41)
The number of nonzero singular values is equal to the matrix rankr ∶= rank(A) ≤ q .
The columns ofU (resp. V) are called theleft (resp.right) singular vectors. These provide orthonormal
bases for all four fundamental subspaces ofA:
Ran(A) = column space = span({u1, ..., ur})
Ran(AH) = row space = span({v1, ..., vr})
Nul(A) = null space = span({vr+1, ..., vn})
Nul(AH) = left null space = span({ur+1, ..., um})
(2.42)
Further, the left and right singular vectors are interrelated since (2.40) implies
AV = UΣ, AHU = VΣT (2.43)

determined: In the complex case, any multiplication of corresponding columns ofU and V with the same scalar factorsejθ is
also a valid SVD. In the real case,U and V are unique but up to a possible sign change of their corresponding columns.

SVD of Real Matrices:
In all the above, ifA has realelements, the only difference in its SVD (compared to the complex case)
is that U and V are real orthogonal matrices. In this real case, the SVD has several intuitivegeometric
interpretations. First, if we consider the semi-axes of the hyperellipsoid{Ax ∶ ‖ x‖ = 1} , their directions
are the singular vectorsui and their lengths are equal to the singular valuesσi. Second, if A is a square
n × nmatrix and we viewit as a linear transformation fromRn to itself, the orthogonalmatricesUand V
of its SVD perform rotations or reflections whereas the diagonal matrixΣ scales each coordinate by the
corresponding singular value.

Computational aspects of SVD:
The computation complexity of SVD isO(mn2) if m ≥ n . In general, the SVD performs excellently
for matrix computations [11],[30]. Its greatest advantage is thenumerical stabilityof the computations
involved. For instance, the unitary matricesUand Vpreserve a vector’s norm and hence preserve its scal-
ing. TheonlyfactorintheSVDthatcanaffectscalingisthematrix Σ. However,therelativemagnitudeof
the singular values provide easily accessible information on the importance of each component (singular
vector). For example, to define aneffective rankfor a matrix, we can keep only its singular values above a
thresholdthatdeterminesthenumericalprecision. Further,theSVDallowsustodeterminethe condition
numberof a matrixA which can be defined by
κ(A) = σmax(A)
σmin(A) ≥ 1 (2.50)
where σmax and σmin denote, respectively, the maximum and minimum of its singular values. The larger
(resp. smaller) its condition number, the more ill-conditioned (resp. well-conditioned) a matrix is. Ex-
treme cases include orthogonal matrices whereκ = 1 and singular matrices where, by convention,
κ = ∞ . To bypass the latter extreme case or to define aneffective condition number, we can apply the
definition (2.50) only for singular values that are nonzero or above another threshold.
2.3.1 Relationship of SVD with Other Matrix Factorizations and Special Cases

decomposition:
A = AH ⟺ A = QΛQH = UΣVH (2.51)
is identical to its SVD withU = V = Q and Σ = Λ.
If A is normal but not positive semi-definite, its spectral decomposition yieldsA = QΛQH, whereQ
is unitary and the diagonal matrixΛ has generally complex numbersλi = |λ i|ejθi along its diagonal. In
thiscasewemaymovethecomplexfactor ejθi toitscorrespondingsingularvector vi or ui andthusforce
Λ to become a symmetric positive semi-definite matrixΣ so that the singular values becomeσi = |λ i|.
Fornon-normalmatrices A we can consider their polar decomposition (2.39) and obtain it from SVD.
Indeed, starting from the SVDUΣVH of A, we can enable its polar decompositionQS as follows:
A = UΣVH = QS, Q = UVH, S = VΣVH (2.52)
where we can easily verify thatQ is unitary andS is Hermitian and positive semi-definite.

2.4.2 Ill-posed Problems in Vision, Tikhonov Regularization, and Pseudoinverse
According to Hadamard’s (1923) definition, a mathematical problem, modeling some physical process,
is said to bewell-posed if all three following conditions hold for its solution: i) existence, ii) unique-
ness, and iii) stability w.r.t. errors or noise in the data. If any of these conditions is not satisfied, then
the problem becomesill-posed. Several problems in image analysis and early vision are ill-posed [6, 28].
Examples include image restoration, edge detection, optical flow estimation, computer tomography, and
superresolution. In computer vision, as well as in many other sciences, a large class of interesting and im-
portant ill-posed problems are theinverse problems, whereas their direct formulations are well-posed. In
this section, we will focus onlinear inverse problems. In Sec.1.4 of Chapter1, there is an analysis of gen-
eralized solutions to linear inverse problems on infinite-dimensional spaces, including least squares and
regularized solutions. In this section we will briefly emphasize thefinite-dimensionalcase and relate it to
the pseudoinverse of a matrix.
Let us consider linear bounded operatorsA ∶ X → Y between Hilbert spacesX, Y and theinverse
problem of finding a vectorx ∈ X such thatA(x) = f for a given data vectorf ∈ Y . Then, existence
would be satisfied ifA is onto, i.e. if its range Ran(A) = Y . Foruniqueness A must be one-to-one, i.e. its
null space Nul(A) = { 0}. Finally,stability would need continuity, i.e. for any sequence(xn) in X with

lim A(xn) = A(x) in Y ,itshouldfollowthatlim xn = x in X. Whileexistenceanduniquenessdepend
only on algebraic aspects, i.e. whetherA is onto and one-to-one, the continuity depends on topological-
metric aspects, i.e. whether the inverse operatorA−1 ∶ Y → X is bounded (and hence continuous).
Thus, continuity of the solution requires that small errors in the data induce small errors in the solution.
Furthermore,continuityisanecessarybutnotsufficientconditionforstabilityorrobustnessagainstnoise
which requires the problem to also be ‘well-conditioned’. If the inverse operatorA−1 exists, thecondition
number of the problem is defined byκ(A) ∶= ‖A‖ ⋅ ‖A −1‖ ≥ 1 . If κ is close to 1, the problem iswell-
conditioned, whereas ifκ ≫ 1 then the problem is ill-conditioned. An ill-posed problem hasκ = ∞ .
Some well-posed problems can become ill-conditioned if they are not properly discretized for numerical
computations. If the inverse operator does not exist, we can define the condition number by employing
instead the generalized inverse operatorA+ (see Sec.1.4 of Chapter1):
κ(A) ∶= ‖A‖ ⋅ ‖A +‖ ≥ 1 (2.63)
In thefinite-dimensional case where the linear operator is represented by a matrixA and its generalized
inverse is the matrix pseudoinverseA+, the square root of the maximum eigenvalueλmax of the matrix
AHAyields the 2-norm‖A‖and the inverse of the square rootof the minimum eigenvalueλmin yields the
2-norm ‖A+‖. Thus, in this case the condition number becomesκ(A) = √λmax/λmin, which is equal to
its definition (2.50) via the ratio of the maximum to the minimum singular value.

2.5.3 Application of PCA to Image and Shape Representation and Recognition
The primary and widespread application area of PCA is for simultaneous dimensionality reduction and
componentdecorrelationinmachinelearningandpatternrecognition[ 7],[34]. Further,itenjoyssimilar
applications in computer vision, where it has also been used extensively for image and shape approxima-
tion and, subsequently, the recognition mainly of human faces, handshapes, and body shapes, both in 2D
and 3D. A few examples of such applications are summarized below.
Eigenfaces for 2D Face Detection and Recognition:

tection and recognition [37] by using as feature vector a small subset of the largest principal values from
projectinganincomingfaceimage(aftersubtractingtheaveragefacefromatrainingdataset)ontothe face

Figure 2.5: Active appearance modeling of faces using PCA: Top row: mean shape/texture and first two

In addition to their usage in computer vision, AAMs have also been used for modeling the face and/or
the mouth’s Region of Interest (ROI) in audio-visual speech recognition from videos [21] and [24].
Specifically, in [24] a cascade of two AAMs was used to accurately track the speaker’s face and extract
visual speech features from it. The first, full-face AAM spanned the whole face area and could reliably
trackthe speaker in long video sequences. Since visual speech-related information is mostly confined in
the lower-half part of the face, a second ROI-AAM covered the face area around the mouth and was used
to analyze the ROI’s shape and texture and produce at each new video frame a visual feature vector for
speech recognition, which was fused with a DCT-based acoustic feature vector extracted from speech
spectra and fed to a recognition system based on Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). The addition of the
PCA-based facial shape and texture features yielded a large increase in the combined audio-visual recog-
nition accuracy over audio-only speech recognition [24].

For training, first a semi-automatic alignment procedurewithout landmark points of a representative
setofSAhandimagesfromSLvideoframeswasdevelopedbasedontheinversecompositionalalgorithm
of [3], which substantially decreased the amount of manual annotation during training. Then, the eigen-
images Ai of the linear combination of the SA model were statistically learned using PCA on the aligned
training dataset of SA images. The numberNc of eigenimages kept is a basic parameter of the SA model.
Using a largerNc, the model can better discriminate different hand configurations. On the other hand,
if Nc gets too large, the model may not generalize well, since it will be consumed on explaining variation
due to noise or indifferent information. In the experiments of [31], the resolution of the aligned images
was 127×133 pixels, and the valueNc = 35 was found to be quite effective.

The overall result is a versatile a compact and descriptive representation of hand configurations as well
as regularized model-fitting, assisting hand tracking and extracting handshape features. These features
were employed in [31] to train statistical handshape models and were applied to handshape classifica-
tion (via Gaussian mixture models) and sign recognition (based on statistical data-driven subunits and
HMMs) in SL videos, yielding substantial improvements on known SL datasets over other competitive
methods with similar sign recognition technologies.
3D Humans (Body, Face, Hands):
Withtherecentsuccessesofdeepneuralnetworksasmachinelearningsystemsbasedontheavailability
of large training datasets and increased computing power, it has become feasible to reconstruct from 2D
images 3D human shapes with details of the body, facial expressions, and handshapes. At the heart of
building the initial 3D shape models is the application of PCA methods, e.g. on data from 3D laser scans
of humans. Next, we will summarize two such application areas.
1) Sign Language Recognition: Sign languages convey information and meaning via spatio-temporal vi-
sual patterns, which are formed by manual (handshapes) and non-manual cues (facial expressions and

upper body motion); both types of cues are important for sign recognition. Figure2.8 shows two exam-
ples from the 3D monocular visual reconstruction of upper body and handshapes from 2D images based
ontheSMPL-Xmodel[ 25]. SMPL-Xisbasedonatemplatemesh(with10475vertices)andakinematic
tree with a set of 54 jointsJ. The model is controlled by pose parametersθ, shape parametersβ and ex-
pressionparameters ψ. The162poseparameters θcorrespondtothe3Drotationofeachmodeljointwith
3 DoF. Bothshapeparameters andexpressionparameters correspond to 10 coefficients of a PCA of shape
and expression respectively that are trained on 3D scans to express the majority of body shapes and facial
expressions. With these parameters as the input, the model returns a mesh with the selected articulation,
body shape and expression. Then SMPLify-X [25] is applied to efficiently and effectively reconstruct 3D
human shapes from image data. This a two-stage method. In the first stage, a set of features is detected
on the image, typically 2D keypoints detected by OpenPose, which include body keypoints, hand key-
points and facial landmarks; see Fig.2.8. In the second stage, SMPL-X is fitted to these 2D landmarks, by
encouraging the projection of the 3D joints of the model to agree with the detected 2D locations.

3.1 Elements of Abstract Algebra
The branch of mathematics generally referred to as ‘algebra’ can be defined as the manipulation of sym-
bols. In classical algebra, these symbols are numbers and the main goal of the algebraic manipulation is
to solve polynomial equations or systems of linear equations. In ‘modern’ or abstract algebra the sym-
bols can be arbitrary and their manipulation can help with studying patterns and symmetries in nature
or mathematics, or extending common number systems to other useful systems, or decomposing an al-
gebraic system into simpler components and discovering isomorphic structures among various algebraic
systems.

In abstract algebra, the termalgebraic system(oralgebraic structure) or simplyalgebraformally means
a set S together with one or more operations defined on it that satisfy certain properties.S, called the
underlying setmay be finite or infinite. The number of operations may also be finite or infinite. However,
each operation must befinitary, i.e. a function fromSn to S; if n = 1, 2, 3, ... , the operation is called
unary, binary, ternary,..., respectively. Aunary operationon S is a map fromS to S. Some typical nota-
tions for the image ofc under a unary operation includec′, c, c∗, c−1, (−c). Abinary operationon S is
a function fromS2 into S, i.e. maps a pair(a, b) ∈ S × S to an element inS which is usually denoted
by anyof the following symbols:a + b, a − b, a ⋅ b, a ⋆ b, a ∘ b, a ∪ b, a ∩ b, a ∨ b, a ∧ b. IfS is the setof
complex numbers, examples of binary operations include addition and multiplication, whereas conjuga-
tionandnegationareunaryoperations. If S isthecollectionofsubsetsofsomeset E,examplesofbinary
operations include the set union and intersection, whereas set complementation is a unary operation.
Properties that a binary⋆ operation onS might satisfy include the following.
• Closure: The setS is calledclosed under⋆ if a ⋆ b ∈ S for alla, b ∈ S .
• Associativity: The operation⋆ is calledassociativeif (aηb)ηc = aη(bηc) for alla, b, c ∈ S .
• Commutativity: The operation⋆ is calledcommutativeif aηb = bηa for alla, b ∈ S .
• Idempotency: The operation⋆ is calledidempotent if aηa = a for alla ∈ S .
• ExistenceofIdentity: Thereexistsauniqueelement ein S,called identity,suchthat e⋆a = a⋆e = a
for alla ∈ S .
• Existence of Inverses:For eacha ∈ S there exists a unique elementa−1 in S, called theinverse1 of
a, such thata−1 ⋆ a = a ⋆ a −1 = e.
• Existence of Null:There exists a unique element0in S, callednull, such that0 ⋆ a = a ⋆ 0 = 0 for
all a ∈ S .
• Distributivity: If there are two binary operations⋆ and ∘ on S, we say that⋆ distributesover ∘ if
a ⋆ (b ∘ c) = (a ∘ b) ⋆ (a ∘ c)
for alla, b, c ∈ S .
The identity, null, and inverses are special elements of the set on which a binary operation is defined. It is
provable that if they exist, they are unique.
Therearethreebasicwaystocreatenewalgebraicstructuresfromolderones: (i)decomposeanalgebra
into its subalgebras, ii) find structure-preserving mappings between algebras, and (iii) form Cartesian
products of existing algebras. Next, we will briefly describe the first two.
An effective approach to understanding an algebraic system is to analyze itssubsystems. If S is the un-
derlying set of the original system, then the underlying set of the subsystem is a nonempty subsetX of
S, and the operations in both systems are the same. Formally, if the setS equipped with some binary
and/or unary operations is an algebra, thenX becomes an algebra by itself with the same operations,
calleda subalgebra, ifitisclosedundertheseoperationsrestrictedonit. Forexample, theset Cequipped
with the addition and multiplication of complex numbers is a specific type of algebra called afield, and its
subset R is asubfieldunder the same operations restricted to real numbers.
A fundamental concept in abstract algebra is a structure-preserving mapping between two algebraic
systems. Specifically, let(S, ⋆) and (T , ∘)be two algebraic systems consisting of the underlying setsX

3.2 Groups and Monoids
A group (G, ⋅)consistsofaset Gandabinaryoperation ⋅onitthatsatisfiesthefollowingfourproperties:
(G1). G is closed2 under the binary operation:a ⋅ b ∈ G for alla, b ∈ G.
(G2). The operation⋅ is associative:a ⋅ (b ⋅ c) = (a ⋅ b) ⋅ c for alla, b, c ∈ G.
(G3). There exists a unique identitye ∈ G such thata ⋅ e = e ⋅ a = a for alla ∈ G.
(G4). There exists a unique inversea−1 for eacha ∈ G such thata ⋅ a−1 = a −1 ⋅ a = e.
If the binary operation is also commutative, then the group is called acommutativeor Abelian group.
The order of a group is the cardinality of its underlying set. It is provable that any group whose order is
less than equal to five is commutative.
If (G, ⋅) is a group andH is a nonempty subset ofG, then (H, ⋅) is called asubgroup of (G⋅) if H
becomes a group under the same binary operation. This happens if and only if (abbreviated as ‘iff’) the
following two conditions are satisfied: (i)H is closed under the group binary operation and (ii) for each
element inH its inverse also belongs toH.
For example, the set of complex numbers forms a commutative group(C, +) under addition. Three
subsets of C are the realsR, the rationalsQ and the integersZ which form a chain of subgroups under
addition. Thus, if ‘A  B’ denotes ‘A is proper subgroup ofB’,
(Z, +)  (Q, +)  (R, +)  (C, +) (3.1)
In these groups the identity is 0 and the inverse of each elementr is its negative(−r). Now the set of
nonzero complex numbers forms a commutative group under multiplication whose identity equals 1;

for alla, b ∈ G . A group homomorphism preserves the group identity and inverses; i.e.,f(e G) = e H
and f(g −1) = −f(g) . A bijective group homomorphism is called agroup isomorphism. For example,

(r1, θ1) ⋆ (r2, θ2) = (r 1r2, θ1 + θ2)

3.2.2 Semigroups and Monoids
A monoid (M , ⋆)is a setM equippedwith a binary operation⋆ thatsatisfiesthe following threeproper-
ties:
(M1). Closure: a ⋆ b ∈ M for alla, b ∈ M .
(M2). Associativity: a ⋆ (b ⋆ c) = (a ⋆ b) ⋅ c for alla, b, c ∈ G.
(M3). Identity: ∃e ∈ M such thata ⋆ e = e ⋆ a = a for alla ∈ M .

Thus a monoid satisfies all the group axioms except for the existence of inverses. If from the three
monoid axioms we remove the existence of an identity, the remaining algebraic structure is called a semi-
group. Thus, asemigroupconsists only of a set and an associative binary operation defined on this set. A
monoid or a semigroup is calledcommutativeif the corresponding binary operation is commutative.
A mappingf ∶ M → N between two monoids(M , ⋆) (N , ∘)is called amonoid homomorphism if
(i) f(a ⋆ b) = f(a) ∘ f(b) for alla, b ∈ M and (ii)f(e M) = e M where eM and eN are the identities
of the two monoids. Iff is also a bijection, then it is called amonoid isomorphism.
Example 3.1 (Monoids). (a) The set of positive integers is a commutative semigroup under addition.

3.3 Rings and Fields
A ring is an algebraic structure(R, +, ⋅) consisting of a setR together with two binary operations, re-
ferredtosymbolicallyas‘ringaddition (+)’and‘ringmultiplication (⋅)’,thatsatisfythefollowingaxioms:
(R1). (R, +)is a commutative group under addition, whose identity0 ∈ R is called the ringzero.
(R2). (R, ⋅)is a monoid under multiplication, whose identity1 ∈ R is called the ringunit.
(R3). The ring multiplication distributes over the ring addition:a ⋅ (b + c) = a ⋅ b + a ⋅ c and
(b + c) ⋅ a = b ⋅ a + c ⋅ a for alla, b, c ∈ R.
Adding the axiom that the ring multiplication be commutative yields acommutative ring. The proto-
typical example of a commutative ring is(Z, +, ⋅), i.e. the integers under ordinary addition and multi-
plication. A ring whose zero and unit elements coincide is called thetrivial ringand consists of a single
element.
In a commutative ring(R, +, ⋅)if the equationx ⋅ y = 0 is satisfied for nonzero elementsx, y ∈ R ,
then these elements are calledzero divisors. An integral domainis any nontrivial commutative ring that
does not have zero divisors. Thus, in an integral domain we can use the cancelation law thata ⋅ c = b ⋅ c
implies a = b if c ≠ 0 . An archetypal example of an integral domain is(Z, +, ⋅). If onto the structure
of an integral domain we impose one additional axiom of having a multiplicative inversea−1 for each
nonzero ring elementa such thata ⋅ a −1 = 1 , then we form a richer algebraic structure called a field.
Thus, afield is a ring whose nonzero elements form a commutative group under multiplication.
If in a ring we weaken postulate (R1) by requiring(R, +) to be only on a commutative monoid, then
(R, +, ⋅)is called asemiring. The same weakening of addition in a field creates asemifield.
If (R, +, ⋅) is a ring (resp. field) andS is a nonempty subset ofR, then S is called asubring (resp.
subfield) ofR if it forms a ring (resp. field) under the same operations restricted to it. Equivalently,S is
a subring ofR iff it satisfies all the following: (i) it is closed under the ring addition and multiplication,
(ii) it contains the additive inverse of each element, and (iii) it contains the ring unit.
A mapping f ∶ R → S between two rings(R, +, ⋅) (S, ⊕, ∘) is called a ring homomorphism if
both the group ‘addition’ and the monoid ‘multiplication’ structures are preserved, i.e., if (i)f(a + b) =
f(a) ⊕ f(b) , (ii)f(a ⋅ b) = f(a) ∘ f(b) , and (iii)f(1 S) = 1 R where 1R and 1S are the units of the
two rings. Iff is also a bijection, then it is called aring isomorphism.
Wecanformnewringsfromoldringsinvariousways,e.g. bytakingtheCartesianproductoftworings
and defining the new operations pairwise. Three other possible ways begin from a commutative ringR
of scalars and create new rings by considering the sets of all 1) polynomials, 2) square matrices of certain
sizeand3)infinitesequenceswithcoefficientsfrom Randequippingthemwithappropriateringaddition
and multiplication operations. Examples will be presented below.

3.4 Vector Spaces and Modules
By using the previously defined algebraic structure of groups, rings and fields we can express below more
compactlythedefiningaxiomsofvectorspaces(a.k.a. linearspaces)andtheirgeneralizationscalledmod-
ules. In both cases we have a underlying set of elementsx, y, ..., which we may generally call ‘vectors’
and denote them as in matrix algebra (even if the space is infinite dimensional), a field of scalar num-
bers r, s, ..., and two operations: a binary operation on the set of vectors which we call ‘vector addition’,
and another operation called ‘scalar multiplication’ that combines a scalar with a vector and produces a
vector. By requiring that these two operations satisfy some properties we obtain the following algebraic
structures.
3.4.1 Vector Spaces
Let us consider a nonempty setV of general ‘vectors’ and a field(F , +, ⋅)of scalars. Let us define a
vector addition(x, y) ↦ x + yas a mapping fromV 2 to V and a scalar multiplication(r, x) ↦ r ⋅ xas a
mapping fromF × V to V . Then, the setV is called alinear spaceor vector spaceover the fieldF if for
every x, y ∈ V , r, s ∈ F all the following axioms are satisfied:
(V1). (V , +)is a commutative group under vector addition.
(V2). r ⋅ (x + y) = r ⋅ x + r ⋅ y.
(V3). (r + s) ⋅ x = r ⋅ x + s ⋅ x.
(V4). r ⋅ (s ⋅ x) = (r ⋅ s) ⋅ x.
(V5). 1 ⋅ x = x where 1 is the unit (i.e. multiplicative identity) ofF.
Note that we have used the same symbol+ for both vector addition and scalar addition, as well as the
same symbol⋅ for both scalar× vector multiplication and multiplication of two scalars. The differences
will be clear from the context. Axioms (V2)-(V4) endow the scalar multiplication of vectors by scalars
with properties of distributivity and associativity that are similar to the scalar arithmetic ofF.
3.4.2 Modules
Modules are a generalization of vector spaces where the scalars are restricted to lie in a ring instead of
a field. Consider a nonempty setM of general ‘vectors’ and aring (R, +, ⋅) of scalars. Let us define a
vector addition onM and a multiplication of vectors by scalars as done for vector spaces. Then, the set
M iscalleda moduleoverthering Rifforevery x, y ∈ M, r, s ∈ R allthefollowingaxiomsaresatisfied:
(M1). (M , +)is a commutative group under vector addition.
(M2). r ⋅ (x + y) = r ⋅ x + r ⋅ y.
(M3). (r + s) ⋅ x = r ⋅ x + s ⋅ x.
(M4). r ⋅ (s ⋅ x) = (r ⋅ s) ⋅ x.
(M5). 1 ⋅ x = x where 1 is the unit ofR.
Obviously, the above axioms are identical to those of a vector space and the only difference is that the
scalars lie in a ring. Since there is no division over a ring, some results on linear independence in vector
spaces over a field may not hold if we restrict the scalars to lie in a ring.

(b) Any commutative group(G, +) is a module over the ringZ of integers. If the group operation is
writtenasaddition +, thenforevery n ∈ Z, g ∈ G wecandefinethescalar ×vectormultiplication n ⋅ g

3.5 Shape Symmetries and Permutation Groups
Symmetries are important in nature and the arts [3], [16]. Two major application areas of group theory
aretodescribethesymmetriesofmathematicalshapesorstructuresandthesymmetriesofnaturalobjects
(e.g. crystalline lattices and elementary particles). In this section we will focus on shape symmetries. By
‘shape’ we mean any compact subset ofR2 or R3. A symmetry (a.k.a. isometry) of a shapeX is defined
as any bijection fromX to itself that preserves Euclidean distances. The set of all symmetries of shape
X forms a group (called itssymmetry group, a.k.a.isometry group) under function composition, since the
property of being a distance-preserving bijection is retained by function compositions and inverses.
We shall see that the symmetry groups of various Euclidean shapes inRn are finite subgroups of the
infinite group ofisometries3 of the Euclidean spaceRn. Examples of such isometries include rotations
and translations.
3.5.1 Cyclic and Dihedral Symmetry Groups in 2D
Figure3.1 below shows various symmetries of a rectangle and a regular polygon withn ≥ 2 sides. These
symmetries arerotations about various axes that permute the vertices of these polygons; all these rota-
tions fix the center of the polygon. A rotation of a planar shape is calledproper if it takes place in the
shape’s plane; otherwise, it is calledimproper. Improper rotations of planar shapes can also be viewed as
reflections w.r.t. an axis in the shape’s plane. Proper rotations preserve orientation, whereas reflections
reverse orientation. In Fig.3.1a, we can see that the rectangle has only three non-identity symmetries:
g is a proper rotation by 180o, whereas h and gh are improper rotations by 180o about the horizon-
tal and vertical axis, respectively. Thus, all the symmetries of a rectangle form a (commutative) group
K = {e, g, h, gh} , called theKlein 4-group. Regarding the regular polygon in Fig.3.1b, ifg represents
a proper counter-clockwise rotation around the center by360/n degrees, then all powers ofg form a
cyclic group Cn of ordern. Now, ifh represents an improper rotation by 180o about the horizontal axis,
by forming compositions ofh with all powers ofg we obtain the complete group of all symmetries of a
regular n-gon, called thedihedral group Dn. The elements of the cyclic and dihedral groups are
Cn ∶= {e, g, g 2, ..., gn−1}, D n ∶= {e, g, g 2, ..., gn−1, h, gh, ..., gn−1h}
where we writegh to mean the compositiong ∘ h . Thus, the order ofDn is 2n. For n = 2 , D2 is
commutative and isomorphic to the Klein 4-group. Forn ≥ 3 , however,gh ≠ hg and hence Dn is
non-commutative.

3.5.2 Permutations
A permutationof a setX is a bijection fromX to itself. LetS(X) denote the set of all permutations of a
nonemptyset X. Then(S(X), ∘)isagroupundercomposition,calledthe symmetricgrouporpermutation
group of X. The identity of this group is the identity map and the inverse of a permutation is its inverse
function. In general, this group is non-commutative.
If X is a finite set withn ≥ 1 elements, its permutation group is isomorphic to that of{1, 2, ..., n},
called the symmetric group on n elements and denoted bySn. If π is a permutation inSn we write its
action as a table, i.e. a list of points and their forward images:
π = (1 → π(1), 2 → π(2), ..., n → π(n)) (3.3)
A permutation is called ak-cycle if it cyclically movesk points {a1, ..., ak} ⊆ {1, ..., n} and leaves the
rest n − k points unchanged; i.e.,π(ai) = a i+1, i = 1, ..., k − 1 , π(ak) = a 1, and π(x) = x if
x ∉ {a 1, ..., ak}. We denote such a cycle by(a1a2 ⋯ ak). Every permutationπ in Sn can be expressed
as a composition of disjoint cycles. For example, ifn = 6 , consider the permutation that exchanges 1
with 3, moves cyclically the points 2,4,6 and leaves 5 unchanged:
π = (1 → 3, 2 → 4, 3 → 1, 4 → 6, 5 → 5, 6 → 2)

3.5.3 Group Action on Sets and Kleinian View of Geometry
A group(G, ⋅)acts on a setX if there is a functionψg ∶ X → X for eachg ∈ G such that the following
two conditions are satisfied:
(i) ψh⋅g(x) = ψ h(ψg(x)) for allg, h ∈ G, x ∈ X .
(ii) ψe(x) = x for allx ∈ X where e is the identity ofG.
It can be shown that every such functionψg is a bijection and hence a permutation ofX. Then, condi-
tion (i) essentially tells us that, the mappingφ ∶ G → S(X) , defined byφ(g) = ψ g, is homomorphism
from the groupG to the permutation group of the setX because
φ(g ⋅ h) = ψ h ∘ ψg (3.6)
The kernel of this homomorphism is Ker(φ) = {g ∈ G ∶ ψ g(x) = x, ∀x ∈ X} . The group action is
calledfaithfulifKer (φ) = {e},i.e. iftheidentity eistheonlygroupelementwhichfixeseveryelementof
X. In such a caseG is isomorphic toψ(G) which is a subgroup ofS(X). For example, the cyclic group
C4 = {e, g, g 2, g3} acts faithfully on the vertex setX = {1, 2, 3, 4} of the square of Fig.3.2 and is
isomorphic to the subgroup{(1), (1234), (13) ∘ (24), (1432)}of S4.
During the action of a groupGon a setX, the group elements that fix a pointx ∈ X form a subgroup
of G called thestabilizerof x:
Stab(x) ∶= {g ∈ G ∶ ψ g(x) = x} (3.7)
The set of all points reachable from the pointxvia the action of group elements onxis called theorbit of
x:
Orb(x) = {y ∈ X ∶ ψ g(x) = y, some g ∈ G} (3.8)
The stabilizer and orbit are useful for counting the elements of a group based on the following.
Proposition 3.2 If a finite groupG acts on a setX, then for eachx ∈ X
card(G) = card[Stab(x)] ⋅ card[Orb(x)] (3.9)

Felix Klein’s seminal view of geometry was “the study of the properties of a space that are invariant
under a given group of transformations”. Obviously, such transformations are permutations, and some
of them are symmetries (i.e. distance-preserving bijections). Thus, to study the geometry of an object
we need both to i) view it a set of points in a space, and ii) study transformations that leave it invariant.
These object transformations can be viewed as ‘movements’ of its points. Based on Klein’s vision, geom-
etry needs both objects and movements. It is interesting to observe that this view is consistent with the
aforementioned concept of group action on sets, since the object under study is represented by a setX
and its movements are permutations or symmetriesψg ∶ X → X that act on the object and are param-
eterized by elementsg of a groupG. Classical examples of objects are the Euclidean shapes as subsets of
the 2D or 3D Euclidean spaces and classical examples of movements are rigid motions, i.e. translations
and/or rotations. An illuminating exposition that expands Klein’s vision and offers numerous examples
of other non-classical objects and non-rigid motions together with inspiring visualizations is the book by
Mumford et al. [12], from which we provide the following example.

3.6 Euclidean Motions and Matrix Groups
When we describe something as a “rigid body” we understand this to mean a macroscopic body whose
distances between any two of its atoms or particles remain fixed. (This is a good approximation of many
real objects.)Euclidean motions(a.k.a. “rigid body motions”) of such bodies are displacements inRn that
areisometries. Recall that an isometry ofRn is a bijective transformation preserving Euclidean distances.
Thecompositionofrigidbodymotionsformsagroupandthisleadsustothegroupofallisometriesof Rn,
which is called theEuclidean groupin n dimensions and denoted by E(n). A fundamental geometrical
issue in Euclidean spacesRn is which properties remain invariant under its isometries. Thus, invariances
are described by corresponding symmetries. A similar effort in physics is the search to find (observed or
intrinsic)symmetriesofaphysicalsystem,i.e. physicalormathematicalfeaturesofthesystemthatremain

<!-- PDF_PAGE: 101 -->
### Σελίδα 101

TOPICS IN COMPUTER VISION AND MACHINE LEARNING 99
invariant under some transformation. For example, symmetry groups play a big role in crystallography
and elementary particle physics.
Euclidean isometries can be classified intodirect (a.k.a. orientation preserving) versusindirect (a.k.a.
orientation reversing). The direct isometries represent the rigid motions and comprise proper rotations
and translations. The set of direct isometries forms under composition a subgroup of E(n), called the
specialEuclideangroup anddenotedasSE (n). Theindirectisometriescomprisereflectionsandtheircom-
positions with rigid motions.
We shall show next that a rigid body motion (i.e. an isometry) onRn can always be expressed as the
composition of a rotation and a translation. A translation by a vectorb is a bijectionτb on Rn defined
by τb(x) = x + b. The set T(n) = {τ b ∶ b ∈ R n} of all translations forms a commutative group
under composition, called thetranslation group, which is isomorphic to the group(Rn, +). It will also be
shown that a rotation onRn is a linear transformation that preserves distances and inner products. Any
linear transformation onRn can be expressed via an × n real matrix. In particular, a rotation onRn
can be expressed via an × n real orthogonal matrix. Composition of such rotations corresponds to the
multiplication of their corresponding matrices, and this forms a non-commutative group, which is called
the orthogonal groupin n dimensions and is denoted by O(n). Both T(n) and O(n) are subgroups of
E(n), which enable the decomposition of Euclidean motions into rotations and translations.
3.6.1 Matrix Representations of Groups
Let us consider the set GL(n, F )of n × n non-singular matrices4 with elements from a scalars’ field
F, where F in our discussion will beR or C. This forms a group under matrix multiplication, called

elements fromF. To see this, let us consider a linear transformationLover F n which is equipped with a

The determinant mapping det∶ O(n) → {−1, +1} is a group homomorphism whose kernel is a
normal subgroup of O(n), called thespecial orthogonal group, which consists of all orthogonal matrices
with a unit determinant:
SO(n) ∶= { Q ∈ R n×n ∶ QT Q = I and det (Q) = 1}
This partitions O(n) into two cosets: SO(n) and its complement with respect to O(n) containing the
matrices with determinant−1. The operation laws of the quotient group O(n)/SO(n) simply express
that the composition of two proper or two improper rotations yields a proper rotation, whereas the com-
position of a proper with an improper rotation is an improper rotation. This operation is isomorphic to
the multiplication in the 2-element group({−1, 1}, ⋅).
Orthogonal matrices can represent rotations and linear transformations between frames of orthogo-
nal coordinate axes. Thus, some of their major applications areas include i) kinematics (of interest in
physics and robotics) and ii) camera calibration and multiview stereopsis (of interest in computer vision
and graphics). The property that makes orthogonal matrices suitable for all the above applications is that
they are equivalent tolinear isometries, as shown below.

Theorem 3.5 Let φ be an operator on the Euclidean spaceRn. Then, the following statements are equivalent:

(b) φ is a linear isometry.
(c) φ is unitary.
(d) φ can be represented by an orthogonal matrixQ ∈ O(n).
Proof: Assume (a), i.e. φ is an isometry withφ(0) = 0. Then, putting y = 0 in (3.14) yields norm
preservation: ‖φ(x)‖ = ‖ x‖. Observing that

and applying it to both sides of (3.14) yields thatφ preserves inner products:

{φ(e1), ... , φ(en)} is also an orthonormal basis ofRn. Then, for each linear combinationax + by and

3.6.2.1 Orthogonal Group in Two Dimensions: O(2)
In two dimensions,orthogonal matricesare only of the following two kinds, and each kind has only one
free parameter: The matrices in SO(2) represent proper planar rotations,
SO(2) = {[ cos θ − sin θ

origin, forming an angle ofθ/2 with the horizontal, and is left invariant by the above rotations. Their
eigenvalues areλi = ±1. The eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalueλ = 1 provides the direction
of the above axis of reflection.
IncomparisontoO (2),theunitarygroupU (2)ofcomplex unitarymatrices intwodimensionsconsists

3.6.2.2 Special Orthogonal Group in Three Dimensions: SO(3)
We shall explore the group of 3D proper rotations (henceforth named simply “rotations”) represented
by SO(3), i.e. the group of3 × 3 orthogonal matrices with unit determinant, calledspecial orthogonal
matrices. Such matrices have only three free parameters.
Theorem 3.6 (Euler[4]). Inthe3DEuclideanspace,anyrigidbodymotion[i.e. isometry]thatfixesapoint
on the body is equivalent to a single rotation about some axis that passes through the fixed point.
The axis of rotation is known as anEuler axis, typically represented by a unit vector̂e. Thus, each 3D
proper rotation can be represented by the unit vector̂e in the direction of the Euler axis and the rotation
angle α around this axis; see Fig.3.5. The required information is equivalent to three parameters, since
the unit vector has only two free parameters, and is called theangle-axis representation. Henceforth, we
shall assume that all 3D coordinate frames are a system of right-handed orthogonal axes. According to
Theorem3.5,any3Drigidbodymotionthatfixestheoriginofanorthogonalcoordinatesystemisalinear
isometry and can be represented by a3 × 3 special orthogonal matrixR. Such matrices always have at
least one real eigenvalue equal to 1. The axis vector̂ecan be found from the eigenvector that corresponds
to the unit eigenvalue, since thenR ̂e = ̂ e. Thus, a rigid body movement that leaves an axis invariant is a
rotation.
Another corollary of the above theorem is that the set of rotations forms a group under composition,
because the composition of two rotations is also a rotation since the product of two rotation matrices is
again a rotation matrix; further, each rotation has its inverse represented by the inverse of the rotation
matrix. Thus, any arbitrary composition of rotations (each of which leaves an axis invariant) is equivalent
to a single rotation around a new axis.

3.6.3 Quaternion Representation of 3D Rotations
Another representation of 3D rotations and their composition is based on Euler’s theorem but uses the
algebra of quaternions. Let us digress briefly by summarizing first a few elements from the algebra of
quaternions, introduced by Hamilton (1844) [8]. Quaternions are the elements of a 4D spaceH, whose
underlying set isR4 but its arithmetic is different. A Cartesian representation of aquaternion qis
q = s + x i + yj + zk = s + v, s ∈ R, v ∈ R 3 (3.34)
where i, j, kare3Dunitvectorsrepresentingthedirectionsofaright-handedCartesiancoordinatesystem
in3DEuclideanspace. Thescalar sisthe realpart,whereasthe3Dvector visthe imaginarypart. Ifs = 0,
we have apurequaternion. There are three arithmetic operations among quaternions: 1) quaternion ad-
dition,2)multiplicationbyscalar,and3)quaternionmultiplication. Operations(1)and(2)areidentical
with those inR4. However, operation (3) involves amultiplication of vectorsand Hamilton’s motivation
for introducing it was the extension of multiplication of complex numbers, represented by vectors in the
2D Euclidean space, to three dimensions. Thequaternion multiplicationis defined as follows:
q1 = s + v, q2 = t + u ⟹ q1q2 ∶= (st − v ⋅ u) + (su + tv + v × u) (3.35)
This multiplication isnot commutative and stems from the following four rules of multiplying the pure
quaternions i, j, k:
i2 = j2 = k2 = ijk = −1 (3.36)
Actually, the setQ = {±1, ± i, ±j, ±k} forms an 8-element group under quaternion multiplication,
called thequaternion group. Theconjugate q∗ of a quaternion is defined by
q = s + v ⟹ q∗ ∶= s − v (3.37)
its norm by
‖q‖ ∶= √qq∗ = √q∗q = √s2 + ‖v‖2 (3.38)
and itsinverse(for q ≠ 0) by
q−1 ∶= q∗
‖q‖2 (3.39)
Now, a 3D rotation can be represented by aunit quaternion(a.k.a. ‘versor’)
qα, ̂e = cos(α/2) + sin(α/2) ̂e, ̂ e ∈ R 3, ‖ ̂e‖ = 1 (3.40)
This representation is in one-to-one correspondence with the representation (3.32) via the four Euler
parameters (a, b, c, d); i.e. we can write the unit quaternion as
q = a + b i + cj + dk ⟹ ‖ q‖ = 1 (3.41)
These four Euler parameters are also the real and imaginary parts of the elements of an SU(2) matrix; see
(3.20) withφ = 0.
Considera3Dvector p ∈ R 3 whichisrotatedbyanangle αaroundanaxisrepresentedbyaunitvector
̂e and which yields the rotated vectorprot. We can obtain this rotation by using quaternion arithmetic, as
the following steps explain:
1. Embedp = (p x, py, pz) into a quaternion as its imaginary part:pquat = 0 + p xi + pyj + pzk.
2. Conjugatewith the unit quaternion corresponding to the desired rotation:
p′ = qα, ̂epquat(qα, ̂e)−1 = s + v (3.42)
3. The rotated 3D vectorprot is the imaginary partv of the resulting quaternionp′.
Representing3Drotationsviaquaternionsandrotatingvectorsviaquaternionmultiplicationhassome
numericaladvantagesovertherepresentationsviaEuler’sthreeanglesorEuler’sfourparametersoftheaxis
and angle information, because it avoids some non-uniqueness, degeneracy or singularity problems that
exist in the latter three representations.

3.6.4 Finite Symmetry Groups in 2D and 3D space
Let us recall the definition of a symmetry of a shapeX ⊆ R n as a distance-preserving bijection from
X to itself. Our previous discussion has established that any symmetry inR2 corresponds to a rotation
(proper or improper) around the origin, represented as a2 × 2 orthogonal matrix. Hence, any finite
group of symmetries of 2D shapes is isomorphic to a finite group of orthogonal matrices. For example,
the 6-element cyclic group of proper rotations of a regular hexagon is isomorphic to the group of the six
orthogonal matrices that represent planar rotations by quantized anglesθk = πk/3 , k = 0, 1, ..., 5 .
Further, according to Cayley’s Theorem, any such finite symmetry group is isomorphic to a subgroup of
permutationsofafinitesetofelements. Finally,wesawthatsubgroupsofpermutationsof nelementscan
represent the two types of symmetry groups of regular polygons, the cyclic groupsCn and the dihedral
groups Dn. The following is a synthesis of the main results.
Proposition 3.4 (a) IfG is a finite subgroup of proper symmetries inR2, thenG is isomorphic to a finite sub-
groupof SO(2),anyofwhichisisomorphicto Cn forsome n ≥ 1. (b)IfGisafinitesubgroupofanysymmetries
in R2, thenG is a finite subgroup ofO(2), any of which is isomorphic toCn or Dn for somen ≥ 1.

Figure3.7: ThefivePlatonicregularsolids. Source: KjellAndré,DTR,AquitaneHungerForce,Stannered,

Proper rotations of 3D shapes are elements of SO(3) and represent rotations that are physically real-
izable in 3D space. Improper rotations require a 4D space for physical realization; alternatively they can
be viewed as reflections of the 3D shape w.r.t. a plane, as shown in the example of Fig.3.3(b). Proper
rotations in 2D space fix a point (origin). Proper rotations in 3D space also fix an axis as shown in the ex-
ample of Fig.3.3(a) and Theorem3.6. As in the 2D case, important symmetry groups are discovered by
analyzingthesymmetriesofregularpolyhedra,calledregularsolids. Thesearedefinedbytwoconditions:
(i)theirfacesarecongruentregularpolygons,and(ii)alltheirverticesareincidentwiththesamenumber
of faces. In contrast to the 2D case where we have an infinite number of regular polygons, in 3D space we
have only fiveregular solids shown in Fig.3.7. The following results summarize their proper symmetry
groups. Their proofs can be found in [7].
Proposition 3.5 (a) The group of proper rotations of the regular tetrahedron is isomorphic toA4. (b) The
group of proper rotations of the cube and the regular tetrahedron is isomorphic toS4. (c) The group of proper
rotations of the regular dodecahedron and icosahedron is isomorphic toA5.
Proposition 3.6 Any finite subgroup ofSO(3) is isomorphic to one ofCn (n ≥ 1), Dn (n ≥ 1), A4, S4 or
A5.
Thus, to understand any finite group of proper symmetries of 3D shapes we need only to understand
the structure of the symmetry groups of regular polygons and of the symmetric groupSn for n ≤ 5.

3.6.5 Euclidean Motions are Affine Transformations
LetusconsidertheEuclideangroupE (n)ofisometriesof Rn. Next,wewillprovethateachsuchisometry
can be expressed as a composition of a rotation with a translation.
Theorem 3.7 (a)Thegroupofisometriesof Rnthatfixtheoriginisisomorphictotheorthogonalgroup
O(n).
(b)IntheEuclideanspace Rn,if μisanisometryand τ atranslationmappingvector xto y,then μ∘τ ∘μ −1
is a translation mappingμ(x) to μ(y).
(c) Defineφ ∶ E(n) → E(n) by
φ(μ) = τ ∘ μ, τ (μ( 0)) = 0. (3.43)
Then φ is a group homomorphism whose kernel is the translation group T(n). Its rangeφ(E(n)) is the
group in part (a).
Proof: Part (a) results from Theorem3.5. A proof of the results in parts (b) and (c) can be found in [7].
According to Theorem3.7, T(n) is a normal subgroup of E(n) that coincides with the kernel of the
group homomorphism φ in E(n) that maps each Euclidean isometryμ to an isometryτ ∘ μ that fixes
the origin. Thus, eachφ(μ) is a linear isometry. Further, the range ofφ is a group that is isomorphic to
the orthogonal group O(n). Thus, every Euclidean isometry (rigid body motion) can be decomposed into a
composition of a rotation and a translation:
μ = (τ −1) ∘ (τ ∘ μ)
Rigid Motion = ( Translation) ∘ ( Rotation) (3.44)
with τ (μ(0)) = 0 which makesτ ∘ μ representable by an orthogonal matrix. Note that every Euclidean
isometry is bijective.
The result of the above theorem is a special case of the following more general result.
Theorem 3.8 ([11]). If V and W are normed linear spaces overR and f ∶ V → W a bijective isometry,
then f is an affine transformation; i.e.f consists of a linear map and a translation.
Note that, as an element of E(n), any Euclidean isometryμ can be expressed as the composition of an
orthogonal linear operator and a translation. If the determinant of the orthogonal matrix is 1, then the
linear part of the isometry is a proper rotation andμ is adirect isometry(i.e. a physically realizable6 rigid
bodymotion). DirectisometriesformthespecialEuclideangroupSE (n),whichisadirectproductofthe
special orthogonal group and the translation group, and whose underlying set is the Cartesian product
SO(n) × Rn.
A corollary of the above affine decomposition of a Euclidean motion is that it hasn(n + 1)/2degrees
of freedom, of whichn is attributable to the translation, and the remainingn(n − 1)/2 to the rotation.
Thus, 2D Euclidean motions have three DoF, whereas 3D Euclidean motions have six DoF.
Theaboveresultisfundamentalanditsapplicationsspannumerousfields. Inadditiontophysics,other
notable examples include i) computer vision, where for image formation, motion analysis and 3D recon-
struction there is a need to relate camera coordinates to world coordinates, and ii) robotics, where in the
study of manipulators’ kinematics Euclidean motions represent an object’s configuration (pose) consist-
ing of position and orientation.
6Arigidbodymotioncanalsoberepresentedbyanimproperrotationandatranslation,butinstandardrigidbodydynamics
(e.g., in physics or robotics) only proper rotations are usually considered. Improper rotations (reflections) can be included
whenconsideringobjectsthatundergoreflection-likeoperationsthatreversethehandednessofanobject,suchasinsymmetry
operations in computer graphics or crystallography.
