Prerequisite Knowledge: Introductory course on calculus, linear algebra, computer vision,
and machine learning.
4.1 Introduction
In several scientific and technological areas related to computer vision, signal and image processing, ma-
chine learning, neural networks, and optimization, there is a need to studynonlinear operators for the
analysis and transformation of signals, images and data in general. Examples include:
• Computer Vision: Several problems such as the preservation of geometric features (e.g. edges, cor-
ners, motion directions) and shape analysis at multiple scales require nonlinear operators because
linear operators blur, distort and shift such geometric structures. Further, image segmentation can
be improved by nonlinear object-centric filtering and simplification.
• NeuralNetworks: Inbothclassic(i.e. multi-layerperceptrons)anddeepneuralnetstheinitiallinear
combination of inputs is followed by nonlinear activation functions (e.g. sigmoid, ReLU) which
convert the total input-output relation into nonlinear mappings. There are also classes of neural
nets where the combination of inputs is directly nonlinear, e.g. morphological neural nets.
• Signal Processing and Pattern Recognition: Several filtering tasks or data preparation and feature ex-
traction for pattern recognition require processing data in the presence of non-Gaussian noise for
which cases nonlinear filters are optimal or have better performance than linear filters.
• Control and Optimization: For the control of discrete event systems as well as in several optimiza-
tion problems (e.g. in convex analysis) the operations involved obey nonlinear laws or possess
algebraic structure of the max/min type, which requires nonlinear analysis.
In this chapter we will study two large classes of related nonlinear operators, which have applications
in several of the above areas and possess many algebraic properties that bear a close conceptual resem-
blance to those of linear operators. They are the advanced (lattice-theoretic) morphological operators
and their recent generalization to what we will start calling in this chapter ‘tropical operators’. These op-
erators act on nonlinear spaces that are either classic lattices or an extended richer version of lattices, the
weighted lattices, which we will start calling in this chapter ‘tropical spaces’. The material in this chapter
is roughly separated into four broad parts: 1) elements of lattices as nonlinear spaces and morphological
operators on completelattices; 2)weightedlatticesastropical spacesandthe tropical operatorsactingon
them; 3) max-plus algebra and related matrix-based operators; 4) morphological approaches to machine
learning systems such as neural networks with max-plus nodes.
We will begin by briefly surveying the main developments in morphological image operators, their
tropical generalizations, and applications to vision and learning, both chronologically and thematically.
4.1.1 Morphological Operators in Vision, Learning, and Optimization
The field of morphological operators is a relatively new scientific field. Its first theoretical developments
occurred in the highly influential and pioneering books by Matheron [173] and Serra [234, 235]. These
works focused more generally on nonlinear image analysis. The theory of morphological operators, pre-
sented from a purely functional analysis perspective, essentially started with Heijmans’ monograph [97]
which was a systematic effort to collect in a single book the definitions and properties of most known

morphological operators up until 1994, both the classic and the advanced ones, and present them using
the theoretical framework of operators on complete lattices
Beforeweoutlinethescopeofourdiscussiononmorphologicaloperatortheory,wewillprovideabrief
tour of the historical developments in the field of morphological image analysis.
Euclidean Morphology:
Mathematical morphology, as a field of nonlinear image analysis, was developed initially in the 1970s
and1980sbyMatheron[ 173],Serra[ 234]andtheircollaboratorsandwasappliedsuccessfullytogeolog-
icalandbiomedicalproblemsofimageanalysis. Inthisfirstperiod, i.e. thelate1960’sandthroughoutthe
1970’s,thebasicmorphologicaloperatorsweredevelopedfirstforbinaryimagesbasedonsettheory[ 173,
234] inspired by the work of [182] and [90], second for graylevel images based on local min/max opera-
tors and level sets [177, 234] or on fuzzy sets [194, 81], and third for graylevel images but with weighted
min/max operators using a geometric interpretation based on the umbra approach of [249, 248] which
is algebraically equivalent to max-plus convolutions. All these operators wereTranslation-Invariant (TI)
and their set generators were Minkowski set addition and subtraction; thus, we may occasionally refer to
them asMinkowski operatorsor asEuclidean morphological operatorssince their most common domain is
the Euclidean plane (R2) or its discretized version (Z2) and they commute with Euclidean translations.
Inthe1980sand1990s,extensionsofclassicmathematicalmorphologyandconnectionstootherfields
were developed by several research groups worldwide in image processing, computer vision, and pat-
tern recognition along various directions including: unified analysis and representation of large classes
of nonlinear filters, including morphological, rank and stack filters [159, 160, 139, 16]; multiscale image
processing, shape and texture analysis [41, 153, 31]; fractals [69, 145, 158, 163]; simple object detec-
tion [26, 151]; optimal design of morphological filters for denoising [229, 232, 240]; watershed-based
image segmentation [22, 268, 179]; color image analysis [10]; shape recognition [107, 206, 210, 278];
face recognition [124]. More accounts and references at varying degrees of detail can be found in books
[67, 92, 97, 173, 193, 234, 235, 246] or tutorial chapters and papers [84, 93, 161, 149, 148, 237, 248]
that deal with mathematical morphology or analyze the morphological operators and their applications
in the context of computer vision [146]. Overall, during the first two decades (1970’s until early 1990’s),
this methodology was essentially aEuclidean morphologywhere the basic operators could be understood
geometrically as TI Minkowski set operations:
Minkowski Addition (Dilation): X ⊕ B = { x + b ∶ x ∈ X, b ∈ B} = ⋃b∈B X+b
Minkowski Subtraction (Erosion): X ⊖ B = { z ∶ B +z ⊆ X} = ⋂b∈B X−b
Opening: X∘B = (X ⊖ B) ⊕ B , Closing: X•B = (X ⊕ B) ⊖ B
where X, B ⊆ R d represent sets (binary images),B is called the ‘structuring element’, andX+z =
{x + z ∶ x ∈ X} denotes the translation of setX by vectorz. These set operations were implemented
algebraically as binary signal filters via Boolean or min/max operations. They were extended to graylevel
images f ∶ R d → R = R ∪ {±∞} as nonlinear signal operations based on local max/min filters within
a moving windowB:
Flat Image Dilation: (f ⊕ B)( x) = max{f(x − b) ∶ b ∈ B}
Flat Image Erosion: (f ⊖ B)( x) = min{f(x + b) ∶ b ∈ B}
Flat Opening: f∘B = (f ⊖ B) ⊕ B , Flat Closing: f•B = (f ⊕ B) ⊖ B
In rare cases, the above local max/min operations were generalized to weighted sup/inf convolutions of
the max-plus or min-plus type:
Weighted Image Dilation: (f ⊕ g)( x) = max{f(x − b) + g(b) ∶ b ∈ B}
Weighted Image Erosion: (f ⊖ g)( x) = min{f(x + b) − g(b) ∶ b ∈ B}
where g is a weighting kernel with support on the setB.

Lattice Morphology:
In the late 1980’s and early 1990’s a new and more general formalization of morphological operators
was introduced:Lattice morphology. Specifically, the need to unify its analysis tools for both binary and
gray images as well as to use it for more abstract data types such as graphs led researchers in mathemat-
ical morphology to extend its theory by generalizing the image space to a complete lattice and viewing
all image transformations aslattice operators. The theoretical foundations of morphology on complete
lattices were developed by Serra and Matheron, presented as chapters in [235], and further extended by
Heijmans and Ronse [101, 221], [97], and [216]. Later, another algebraic approach to morphology was
developedbyKeshet[ 112]basednotoncompletelatticesbutonarelatedweakeralgebraicstructure: inf-
semilattices. The basic advance of lattice morphology was to develop more general operators that shared
with the standard dilation, erosion, opening and closing only a few algebraic properties. One such funda-
mental algebraic structure is a pair of erosion and dilation operators that form anadjunction. This guaran-
tees the formation of openings and closings via composition of the adjunction constituents. Other new
concepts and application areas include the group-invariant operators [101, 218]; connected operators
[236, 230, 257, 180, 142]; connectivity-based shape analysis [38, 257] and segmentation [233]; graph
morphology [265, 100]; the slope transform [66, 150] defined and studied in [150, 155, 143] and [99]
fromtheperspectiveoflatticemorphology;andtheprocessingofvector-valuedimages(e.g. colorimages
[9] or image sequences [85]) using lattice theory. Overall, the lattice framework allows us to unify the
conceptsandanalysisoflargeclassesofoperatorsthatshareafewfundamentalproperties,independently
of whether they are defined for sets (shapes), binary signals (binary images), multilevel signals (graylevel
images), or even more abstract image data types such as graphs. The generalization of Minkowski-type
morphological operators into lattice operators have influenced most previous applications of Euclidean
mathematical morphology and have found many applications in important image analysis and computer
vision tasks, such as multiscale geometrical smoothing, segmentation, shape analysis, motion analysis,
and object detection. Figure4.1 shows two morphological filters both of which can simplify an image
without the severe blurring caused by a linear (Gaussian) smoothing filter; from these two morpholog-
ical filters, one is based on cascades of morphological convolutions, whereas the reconstruction filter is
based on lattice-theoretic concepts.
Differential Morphology:
Duringthe1990’s,inparalleltothedevelopmentoflatticemorphology,anothernewdevelopmentwas
that ofdifferential morphology[143]. This term contains two subareas, both related to nonlinear dynami-
calsystems: (1)Thefirstsubareacombinedideasfromlinear(Gaussian)scale-spaceanalysisincomputer
vision based on the linear isotropic heat diffusion Partial Differential Equation (PDE) and from multi-
scale morphology [153] todevelop nonlinearPDEs that generatecontinuous-scale morphological filters
(mainly Minkowski-type dilation and erosion). The main three independent contributions in morpho-
logical PDEs are [7], [41] and [31]. For extensive overviews, interested readers should consider the two
tutorial chapters of [88] and [152]. Connections between the morphological PDEs and the slope trans-
form were developed in [66] and [99]. (2) The second subarea deals with 2D difference equations that
model distance transforms [32], and their analysis using slope transforms [143]. In this chapter we shall
not pursue the analysis of these aspects of morphological operators.
Convex Analysis and Optimization:
The scientific field ofconvex analysis and optimization[21, 215, 137], was initially unrelated to math-
ematical morphology, but it has been making extensive use of some of the main mathematical tools that
morphology has also been using, such as the max-plus (a.k.a. supremal) convolutionf ⊕ g and its dual

Image Algebra:
In the 1980’s an effort started to unify all digital image operations under a commonimage algebra
amenable to computation. The term ‘image algebra’ was first coined by [249] but it referred only to the
algebraic structure of mathematical morphology. Classic (Minkowski) erosions and dilations by finite
structuring elements are insufficient by themselves to represent all possible image operations via finite
combinations. In parallel to the development of mathematical morphology, there was another indepen-
dent effort in the 1980’s by Ritter and his collaborators [209, 214] to develop a more complete image
algebra that representsall digital finite-extentimage-to-image operations as a finite composition of a few
basic operations, which include Minkowski-type erosions and dilations; a subalgebra of their full image
algebra covers the classic part of mathematical morphology. The goal of the image algebra by Ritter and
his collaborators was to unify all digital image operations (linear and nonlinear) using traditional alge-
braic structures,2 e.g. groups, rings, fields, vector spaces, monoids, semirings. A fusion of image algebra
and lattice structures was done in [61]. The culmination of all these efforts can be found in [213].
Morphological Neural Networks:
Sincetheearly1990s,severalworldwideresearchgroups,inspiredbythecapabilitiesofnonlinearimage
analysissystemsusingmorphologicaloperators,havedevelopedandexperimentedwithNeuralNetworks
(NNs) whose nodes perform morphological operations on the input vectors, either flat or weighted; ex-
amples include [1, 2, 62, 204, 206, 211, 212, 251, 252, 273, 278]. Namely, these Morphological Neural
Networks (MNNs) have nodes with max-min or max-plus combinations of inputs. This activity since
the 1990s on using operations of mathematical morphology as models for neurons in single- or multi-
layer perceptrons was motivated by i) evidences that the max-min or max-plus operations may be part
of biologically plausible models of neuronal computation, ii) development of (mainly gradient descent)
algorithms to train these nonlinear networks, and iii) attractivepropertiessuch as faster training and sim-
ilar performance with linear perceptrons. In the modern era of deep learning, this effort is continuing
with alternative training algorithms [46, 87, 197, 196, 261], dense MNNs [186, 65], deep MNNs [73,
75, 176, 195] possibly combining morphological with linear layers, group equivariance [203], and the
unified morphological representation of the neuron input combination and its activations [263, 73].
4.1.2 Max-Plus Algebra, Weighted Lattices, and Tropical Geometry
Minimax Algebra:
For problems in fields traditionally separate from image processing, e.g. scheduling and operations
research, Cuninghame-Green [56, 57] has developed a nonlinear matrix algebra calledminimax algebra,
also known asmax-plus algebra, where he has exploited the interaction of the max/min idempotent al-
gebraic structure with the group structure of real addition+ and has developed analogies with the sum-
of-products structure of linear algebra. Minimax algebra wasnot originally developed for image analysis.
Its traditional applications areas were and still are in scheduling (e.g. material flow in automated manu-
facturing, traffic flow in transportation or communication networks), operations research [56], shortest
path problems in graphs [207], and algebraic modeling and control of Discrete Event Dynamical Sys-
tems (DEDS) [52]. The latter applications area (DEDS) shares some system theoretic aspects with the
operator representation issues discussed in this chapter. Minimax algebra is a nonlinear matrix-oriented
algebra,wheretheunderlyingarchetypalstructureforscalarsistheset R = R ∪ {±∞}ofextendedreals
equippedwithmaxorminoperationsandaddition. Itsbasicoperatorsaremax-plusordualmin-plusgen-
eralized products of matrices with vectors where the standard multiplication of a row vector (from left)
withacolumnvector(fromright)isdoneviaamax-of-additionsinsteadofthestandardsum-of-products

Max-plus Algebra and Nonlinear Dynamical Systems:
Ιn the 1980s and 1990s, several broad classes ofnonlinear systems were developed whose state-space
dynamics can be described by equations whose structure resembles linear state-space equations but has
nonlinear operations. These were motivated by a broad spectrum of applications, such as scheduling and
synchronization,operationsresearch,dynamicprogramming,shortestpathsongraphs,imageprocessing,
and non-Gaussian estimation, for which nonlinear systems were more appropriate. These nonlinearities
involve two major elements: i) a nonlinear superposition of vectors/matrices via pointwise maximum
(∨) or minimum (∧) which plays the role of a generalized ‘addition’, and ii) a binary operation⋆ among
scalars that plays the role of a generalized ‘multiplication’. Thus, with the above generalized ‘addition’ and
‘multiplication’, the set of scalars has a conceptually similar arithmetic structure as the field of reals with
standard addition and multiplication underlying the linear vector spaces over which linear systems act.
This alternative arithmetic structure (with operations∨, ⋆) is minimally an idempotent semiring. Exam-
ples of ‘multiplication’ include the sum and the product, but⋆ may also be only a semigroup operation.
The resulting algebras include: 1) themax-plus algebra(Rmax,max, +)with Rmax = R ∪ {−∞} used in
scheduling and operations research [56], DEDS [14, 43, 50, 103], automated manufacturing [50, 110],
synchronization and transportation networks [14, 42, 95, 30], max-plus control [42, 50, 95, 30], opti-
mization [14, 20, 42, 51, 82, 175], geometry [51, 78], morphological image analysis [97, 161, 235, 248],
and neural nets with max-plus or max-min combinations of inputs [211, 212, 46, 278]; 2) the min-plus
algebra or else known astropical semiring(Rmin,min, +)with Rmin = R ∪ {+∞} used in shortest paths
on networks [56] and in speech recognition and natural language processing [185],[104]; 3) themax-
timessemiring ([0, +∞), ∨, ×)used for inference with belief propagation in graphical models [24, 202,
254]; 4) thefuzzy logic or probability semiring([0, 1], ∨, T )with statisticalT-norms used in probabilis-
tic automata and fuzzy neural nets [117],[109], fuzzy image processing and dynamical systems [25, 147,
162], and fuzzy Markov chains [13].
Weighted Lattices:
Thus, in addition to mathematical morphology (i.e. its Euclidean and lattice-based versions), we have
mentioned so far two other related algebraic systems, image algebra and minimax algebra. All three sys-
tems have had some missing theoretical parts needed for them to be complete. Both the image algebra
and the minimax algebra use mainly min-max superpositions, max-plus arithmetic and some concepts
from lattice theory. A fusion of concepts from image algebra and minimax algebra was also done by [61].
However,theaboveeffortshavenotexploitedthecompletelatticestructuretothelevelthatmathematical
morphology has done, nor have they focused on the concept of lattice operators and, especially, the con-
cept of adjunctions (Galois connections). Further, both of them have emphasized the finite-dimensional
case. Minimax algebra [56] is mainly a matrix algebra over finite-dimensional vector spaces. Similarly,
imagealgebra[ 213]dealswithfinite-extentdigitalimageseitherbyprocessingthemwithfinitetemplates
in the spatial domain or via finite discrete transforms in the frequency domain. From both approaches
thereseemstobemissingcasesordetailsofworkingoverinfinite-dimensionalspaces;e.g. morphological
transformations with infinite-extent structuring functions either on a continuous or a discrete domain.
Missing also is the complete lattice structure which allows infinite signal superpositions based on supre-
mumorinfimum(oftenabbreviatedassup/inf)operations. Withregardstotheweightedlatticeoperators
discussed in this chapter, it is important to note that both Euclidean and lattice-based mathematical mor-
phologyhavefocusedonandmainlyexploitedthestandard(flat)latticestructure,i.e. superpositionsand
filteringsbasedonplainsupremumandinfimumwhichbecomemaximumandminimuminthefinitecase.
Although a few operations in mathematical morphology combine the sup/inf with max-plus arithmetic
(e.g.,sup/infconvolutionsoperationswithgraystructuringelements,chamferdistancetransforms),such
cases have always remained a small minority in mainstream morphological image analysis.

In Maragos [147] the above gaps were bridged and lattice-based mathematical morphology was fused
with minimax algebra, by allowing for both finite- as well as infinite-dimensional spaces and for sup/inf
superpositionsandotheroperationsoverinfinitesignalcollections. Whileachievingthisgoal,amoregen-
eral algebraic structure was introduced, called ‘clodum’ (complete lattice-ordered double monoid), that
combines the sup/inf lattice structure with a scalar semi-ring arithmetic that possesses generalized ‘addi-
tions’ and⋆-‘multiplications’. This clodum structure enables us to develop a unified analysis for: (i) rep-
resentations of translation-invariant operators compatible with these generalized algebraic structures as
nonlinear (sup/inf) convolutions, and (ii) representations of all increasing translation-invariant opera-
torsassupremaofsuchnonlinearconvolutionswithfunctionsfromaspecialcollectionthatcharacterizes
the operator. Special cases of this unification include generalized Minkowski operators and lattice fuzzy
image operators. Applications of this nonlinear signal algebra have appeared in [164, 162] for max-plus
nonlinear control and in [166, 165] for image analysis based on fuzzy logic.
The clodum structure was extended in [144] to spaces of vectors and signals creating nonlinear spaces
that we callComplete Weighted Lattices (CWLs). This enabled the unified representation of large classes
of nonlinear discrete-time dynamical systems obeying a weighted max/min superposition. Some of the
special cases include max-plus, max-times, and probabilistic dynamical systems. Applications include
DEDS and state-space modeling of nonlinear filtering; dynamic programming (the Viterbi algorithm)
and shortest paths; fuzzy Markov chains; and tracking salient events in multimodal information streams
using generalized hidden Markov models with control inputs.
From a geometrical viewpoint, the algebraic structure of CWLs, which henceforth will also be called
tropical spaces,createsapolygonalgeometrybecauseofthegeometricshapeofthecorner-formingpiecewise-
straight lines y = max(a + x, b) or y = max(ax, b) and their duals (by replacing max with min)
which express the basic algebraic superpositions in CWLs, in analogy to the geometry of the straight line
y = ax + b which expresses in a simplified way the basic superposition in linear spaces. See Fig.4.2 for
an example. Note: The adjective “tropical” was playfully coined by French mathematicians Dominique
Perrin and Jean-Eric Pin, to honor their Brazilian colleague Imre Simon, a pioneer of min-plus algebra as
applied to finite automata in computer science. To the word “tropical” we provide the following more
substantive interpretation: We take “tropical” from the Greek word “τ ρoπ ́η” which means “turning” or
“changing the way/direction”. Indeed, the plot in Fig.4.2 shows a tropical line that turns around corner
points forming a polygonal path.

Tropicalgeometryisarelativelyrecentfieldinmathematicsandcomputersciencecombiningelements
of algebraic geometry and polyhedral geometry. The scalar arithmetic of its analytic part pre-existed in

analyze and design NNs with PWL activation functions [39, 46, 45, 74, 121, 156, 184, 244, 282, 283].
4.1.3 Summary of Topics covered
Section 4.2 begins with a synopsis of partially ordered sets (posets) and various aspects of complete lat-
tices,includingsublattices,atoms,Booleanandfunctionlattices. Then,wewillprovideexamplesofimage
lattices. Afterwards, in Section4.3 we will summarize the definitions and properties of the main types of
lattice operators and talk about the monotone case, especially with regards to dilations as operators that
distributeoveranysupremaanderosionsasoperatorsthatdistributeoverinfima. Examplesaregivenfrom
the classic (Euclidean) morphological operators to show compatibility with their lattice generalizations.
This section will also focus on: (i) thelattice adjunctions, which are pairs of compatible lattice erosions
and dilations generating openings and closings, and (ii) thelattice projections, which are increasing and
idempotent filters that include the classic openings, closings, their lattice generalizations (e.g. area and
reconstruction filters), and their non-extensive combinations (e.g. levelings). Thelevelings are analyzed
using triphase operators. Finally, as an aside, we will mention issues of convergence and continuity for
lattice operators, mainly related to their order structure.
Section4.4presentsaunifiedrepresentationtheorytodecomposeoperatorsthatobeytwofundamen-
tal properties such as translation-invariance and increasingness into a parallel combination (sup/inf su-
perposition) of elementary morphological operators. It also extends the representation theory to two
important cases where one of these properties is missing: (i) the shift-varying lattice operations with
a structuring element map which create a variety of adaptive morphological operators; and (ii) object-
detection operators that are TI but non-increasing.
Sections4.6 and4.7 extend the lattice theory of morphological operators from the viewpoints of min-
imax algebra and max-plus dynamical systems by introducing a type of underlyingnonlinear signal space
that has both a complete lattice structure, i.e. partial order, and sup/inf superpositions of signals from
arbitrary (possibly infinite) collections, as well as two scalar ‘multiplication’-type operations (⋆ and its
dual ⋆′) that distribute over any suprema and infima, respectively. On the set of scalars, this generalized
algebraic structure is called a ‘clodum’. This is extended to arbitrary lattices of vectors or signals. Thus,
the linear superposition of signals over a linear spaces is replaced now by a max-⋆ combination case and
its dual min-⋆′ variant. The resulting nonlinear spaces areComplete Weighted Lattices (CWLs). The char-
acterization “weighted” contrasts with the structure of the regular lattices in Sec.4.2 which we may call
“flat lattices” since their max/min operations do not involve any scalar weights. We name the CWLstrop-
ical spacesforcompatibilitywiththedefinitionoftropicaloperatorsthatweintroduceinthischapter, and
summarizeasetofaxiomsfordefiningtheiralgebraicstructure. TheroleofCWLsforanalyzinglatticeop-
eratorsendowedwithmax- ⋆ arithmeticisconceptuallysimilartotheroleplayedbylinear(sum-product)

Section 4.7 provides a formal definition fortropical operatorsas operators obeying a (nonlinear) trop-
ical superposition of the max-⋆ or min-⋆′ type. We will focus on tropical operators acting on tropical
spaces of vectors and signals. In the infinite-dimensional (signal) case we obtain operations whose com-
putational structure is like that of linear convolutions but the linear sum-of-products has been replaced
by sup-of-⋆ or inf-of-⋆′ operations. In the finite-dimensional (vector) case, we will show that any opera-
tor that distributes over the main operations of a tropical space admits a matrix representation where the
outputvectoristhegeneralizedmax- ⋆ (oritsdualmin- ⋆′)‘product’oftheoperatormatrixwiththeinput
vector. This nonlinear signal and vector algebra unifies three main cases where we have CWLs: (1)Max-
Plus: classic morphological translation-invariant operators, which are based on nonlinear convolutions
of the max-plus type. (2)Max-Times: lattice extensions of morphological dilations and erosions that are
supremal and infimal convolutions with multiplicative structuring elements. (3) Fuzzy image operations
and convolutions, where⋆ (⋆′) becomes a fuzzy intersection (union). All the above representations as-
sumed either the framework of Euclidean or lattice morphology.
In Section4.9 we will summarize some results of minimax algebra, mainly from [56], on both exact
and approximate solutions of systems of max-plus equations using vector dilations and erosions based
on max-plus matrix algebra. We will also relate these ideas to lattice projections on CWLs. Then, we
will generalize the results of solving max-plus equations to solving arbitrary tropical equations, i.e. max-⋆
equations where the scalar operation⋆ distributes over any maxima.
Finally, Section4.10will present classic approaches to designing MNNs, i.e. networks where the com-
putingnodesperformoperationsofthemorphologicaltype,flatorweighted,withorwithoutactivations.
It also presents a brief overview of recent works on MNNs in the deep learning era. We will provide gen-
eral references, emphasize the main ideas, describe the training algorithms for some selected approaches,
and outline some applications to computer vision and machine learning.

4.2 Lattices and Nonlinear Image Spaces
4.2.1 Posets and Lattices: Order and Algebraic Structures
4.2.1.1 Lattices from Posets: Order Structure
A partially-ordered set, briefly poset (P, ≤), is a setP in which a binary relation≤ is defined that is a
partial ordering, i.e., satisfies the following three properties for allX, Y , Z ∈ P :
P1. X ≤ X (reflexive)
P2. X ≤ Y and Y ≤ X imply X = Y (antisymmetric)
P3. X ≤ Y and Y ≤ Z imply X ≤ Z (transitive)
If ≤ has the additional property that, for any two elements we have eitherX ≤ Y or Y ≤ X , thenP is
called atotally-ordered setor chain. The archetypal example of a poset is thepower set3 P(E) ∶= {X ∶
X ⊆ E} of an arbitrary setE (i.e. the collection of all subsets ofE) under set inclusion, whereas the
archetypal example of a chain is any nonempty subset of real numbers under their natural order.
Let S be a subset of a poset(P, ≤). Anupper boundof S is an elementB ∈ P such thatX ≤ B for
all X ∈ S . Theleastupperbound of Siscalledits supremumandisdenotedbysup Sor ⋁ S. Byapplying
the above definitions to theconverse ordering≥, we can define dual4 concepts such as alower boundand
the greatest lower boundof S; the latter is called itsinfimumand is denoted by infS or ⋀ S. By the anti-
symmetry of ≤, the supremum and infimum are unique if they exist. If the supremum (resp. infimum)
of S belongs toS, then it is called thegreatest elementor maximum(resp. least elementor minimum) ofS
and is denoted by maxS (resp. minS). An elementM of S is calledmaximal(resp. minimal) if there is
no other element inS that is greater (resp. smaller) thanM with respect to≤.
Asubsetofaposet Piscalled boundedifitpossessesbothanupperandalowerbound. If Ppossessesa
greatest elementI = sup P and a least elementO = inf P, these two extreme points are calleduniversal
bounds. Let us assume thatP is bounded and consider its empty subset∅. Then, all poset elements are
both upper and lower bounds of the empty set. Hence,
inf ∅ = sup P = I, sup ∅ = inf P = O (4.1)
Not all posets have the property that the supremum or infimum of any two of its elements exists. A
counterexampleisshowninFig. 4.3whereintheposetP6thesup {a, b}doesnotexistsince aand bhave
asupperboundstheelements c, d, I thesetofwhichhasnoleastelement. Ifanypairofposetelementshas
a supremum and infimum, then such posets possess the structure of an important algebra, called ‘lattice’,
which has far-reaching applications.
A lattice is a poset(L, ≤) whose any subset of two elements has a supremum and an infimum. If we
view the supremum and infimum of any two elementsX, Y as operations defined onL, then they are
actually binary operations, since they satisfy closure and uniqueness, and are denoted as
X ∨ Y ∶= sup{X, Y }, X ∧ Y ∶= inf{X, Y }
Several authors call∨ and ∧, respectively, the ‘join’ and ‘meet’ operations. We often denote the lattice
structure by(L, ∨, ∧).

a dual one inP′ which results from replacing≤ with ≤′.

4.2.1.2 Lattice Properties: Semigroup Structure
Consideralattice (L, ∨, ∧)andarbitraryelements X, Y ∈ L . Thelatticeoperationssatisfymanyprop-
erties; the five fundamentals are listed as (L1,L1′)–(L5,L5′) in Table4.1.
Table 4.1: Properties of Lattice Operations
Sup-Semilattice Inf-Semilattice Description
L1. X ∨ Y ∈ L L1′. X ∧ Y = X Closure
L2. X ∨ X = X L2′. X ∧ X = X Idempotence
L3. X ∨ Y = Y ∨ X L3′. X ∧ Y = Y ∧ X Commutativity
L4. X ∨ (Y ∨ Z) = (X ∨ Y ) ∨ Z L4′. X ∧ (Y ∧ Z) = (X ∧ Y ) ∧ Z Associativity
L5. X ∨ (X ∧ Y ) = X L5′. X ∧ (X ∨ Y ) = X Absorption
L6. X ≤ Y ⟺ Y = X ∨ Y L6′. X ≥ Y ⟺ Y = X ∧ Y Consistency
L7. O ∨ X = X L7.′ I ∧ X = X Identity
L8. I ∨ X = I L8.′ O ∧ X = O Absorbing Null

of each semilattice are reminiscent of a semigroup with some additional properties. These two views are
connected by the following.
Lemma 4.1 (a) Any set equipped with a binary operation∘ that is associative, commutative and idempotent
is a semilattice where the supremumX ∨ Y (resp. infimumX ∧ Y ) of any two elementsX, Y coincides with
the semigroup operationX ∘ Y and the partial ordering is given by L6 (resp. L6′).
(b) Conversely, any sup-semilattice(P , ∨)(resp. inf-semillatice (P , ∧)) is a commutative idempotent semi-
group (P , ∘)whose binary operationX ∘ Y among any two elements coincides with the supremumX ∨ Y
(resp. infimumX ∧ Y ).
Thus, we can define a semilattice not only via its ordering structure, i.e. as a poset where suprema or
infima exist, but also as an algebra of a commutative idempotent semigroup. The ordering and algebraic
structuresareequivalent,andthisconsistencyisexpressedviaL6. Itisnowevidentthatalattice (L, ∨, ∧)
contains a sup-semilattice(L, ∨) that satisfies properties L1-L4 of Table4.1, an inf-semilattice(L, ∧)
that satisfies properties L1′-L4′, and the two binary operations of supremum and infimum are related
via properties L5,L5′ that make themdual to each other. Thus, L1-L5 and L1′-L5′ can be taken as an
equivalent definition of lattices. Finally, L6 and L6′ make the supremum and infimum consistent with
the partial ordering. The additional properties (L7,L7′) and (L8,L8′) in Table4.1 hold only if the lattice
contains a least and a greatest element, respectively. Lemma4.1 and the previous discussion prove the
following.
Theorem 4.1 (Birkhoff [23]) Equivalence of Lattice Ordering and Algebraic Structure.
(a) Any lattice(L, ∨, ∧)satisfies properties L1-L5 and L1′-L5′.
(b)Conversely,aset Lequippedwithtwobinaryoperations ∨and ∧thatsatisfythesefirstfivepairsofproperties
is a lattice whose supremum is∨, infimum is∧, and the partial ordering≤ is given by L6.
As in posets, lattices also come in duality pairs.
Theorem 4.2 (Duality Principle in Lattices).In any latticeL = (L, ∨, ∧), by replacing the partial
ordering ≤with its converse≤′ and by interchanging the roles of the supremum and infinum, i.e., by considering
the dual operations∨′ = ∧ and ∧′ = ∨, we can form a new latticeL′ = (L, ∨′, ∧′), called theduallattice.
The duality principle dictates that for every definition and theorem that applies to the latticeL and involves its
partial ordering, supremum or infimum, there corresponds a dual one that applies to the dual latticeL′ and is
formed by interchanging the roles of≤ with ≤′ and ∨ with ∧.
In any lattice, if we have a finite collection of elementsK = {Χ 1, Χ2, ... , Χn}we can write its supre-
mum either in short form as⋁ K or in long form asΧ1 ∨ Χ 2 ∨ ⋯ ∨ Χ n; the last expression is well
defined due to the associativity and commutativity of supremum. Similarly, we can write the infimum
of K as ⋀ K = Χ 1 ∧ Χ 2 ∧ ⋯ ∧ Χ n. By induction, we can reason that the supremum and infimum
of any such lattice subset exist if it is finite. But what aboutinfinite subsets? To guarantee the existence
of the supremum and infimum of infinite subsets we need the concept of ‘completeness’. A latticeL is
called completeif any of its subsets (finite or infinite) has a supremum and an infimum inL. Obviously,
all finite lattices are complete. But there are many infinite lattices which are not complete. Any nonempty
completelatticeisuniversally boundedbecauseitcontainsitsgreatestelement I = ⋁ L,calledthelattice
‘unit’, and its least elementO = ⋀ L, called the lattice‘zero’. A bounded lattice is callednontrivial if
O ≠ I .

4.2.1.5 Sup-generators, Atoms
A subset A of a complete latticeL is calledsup-generating (resp. inf-generating) if each lattice element
can be expressed as a supremum (resp. infimum) of members ofA. Such generators can be found if the
lattice has atom-like elements. Specifically, an elementA ∈ L is called anatomif it is a minimal element
of L \ {O},i.e. if A ∈ L \ {O} and, foreach X ∈ L , X ≤ A implies X = O or X = A . Respectively,
a dual atomis called any maximal element ofL \ {I} . For example, the lattice of any power setP(E)
has, as atoms, all the singletons.

In a latticeL with universal boundsO and I, an elementX ∈ L is said to have acomplement X∗ ∈ L

A bounded lattice is calledcomplementedif each element has a complement.
A Boolean latticeisdefinedasanylatticethatiscomplementedanddistributive. InanyBooleanlattice
B, the complement of each element is unique and involutive:(X∗)∗ = X. Actually, the mappingX ↦
X∗ = ν(X) is a negation (i.e. an involutive dual automorphism) onB. Thus, any Boolean lattice is

The main examples of complete and infinitely distributive signal lattices used in image analysis are:
(a) The spaceG of all d-dimensional graylevel image signalsf ∶ E → R where the partial ordering≤,

tices by using several different partial orderings, as explained in [85]. The most common is the marginal

4.2.3.4 Lattices of Lipschitz Image Functions
A real-valued functionf on Rd is calledglobally Lipschitz continuous(or just Lipschitz) if there exists a
constant K such that for allx, y
|f(x) − f( y)| ≤ K‖ x − y‖
The infimum of such constantsK is called itsLipschitz coefficientand denoted by Lip(f). By restrict-
ing, for each point, the domain on which the Lipschitz condition holds to an open neighborhood around
thatpoint,wecanalsodefine locallyLipschitzfunctions. AnyLipschitzfunctionisuniformlycontinuous.
Given that Lipschitz functions are differentiable almost everywhere and the magnitude of their deriva-
tives is bounded by their constantK, they are the best choice (in terms of degree of regularity) between
continuous and differentiable functions. As observed in [235, ch.12], the pointwise infimum and supre-
mum of Lipschitz functions are still Lipschitz. Thus, the collection Funlip(Rd, R)of Lipschitz functions
is a complete sublattice of the lattice of continuous functions. Another interesting property of Lipschitz
functions is that they remain Lipschitz after their Minkowski dilation and erosion by another function, as
shown in [31].
4.2.3.5 Lattices of Convex and Concave Functions
A functionf is convexiff its epigraphU∨(f) is a convex set, i.e.
f(r x + (1 − r)y) ≤ rf( x) + (1 − r)f( y)
for anyx, y ∈ R d such thatf(x), f(y) < +∞ and 0 ≤ r ≤ 1 . Dually, a functionf is concave iff its
hypograph U∧(f) is a convex set, i.e.
f(r x + (1 − r)y) ≥ rf( x) + (1 − r)f( y)
for anyx, y ∈ R d such thatf(x), f(y) > −∞ and 0 ≤ r ≤ 1 . The collections of convex and concave
functions are denoted by Fun∨(Rd, R) and Fun∧(Rd, R), respectively, where the symbol∨ (resp. ∧) is
characteristic of the shape of a convex (resp. concave) function.

4.3.1 Monotone Lattice Operators
Of great interest are the monotone operators. They come in three basic kinds according to which of the
following three lattice structures they preserve (or map to its dual): (i) partial ordering, (ii) supremum,
(iii) infimum.
A lattice operatorψ is calledincreasing or isotoneif it is order-preserving, i.e.,∀X, Y ,
increasing ∶ X ≤ Y ⟹ ψ(X) ≤ ψ(Y )

It can be shown that an equivalent condition for an operatorψ to be increasing is the following:

If the lattice is complete, the supremum and infimum in (4.22) can be taken on infinite collections.
4.3.1.1 Increasing Operators
Examples of increasing operators are the homomorphisms. A sup-homomorphism is any operator that
preserves suprema over a finite collection, whereas an inf-homomorphism preserves infima. An operator
φ ∶ L → M between two latticesL and M that combines both properties is called alattice homo-
morphism. If the lattice homomorphism is a bijection, then it is called alattice isomorphism, or alattice
automorphism if L = M . From (4.6) it follows that, an operatorθ is a lattice isomorphism if it is a
bijection and bothθ and its inverseθ−1 are increasing; see (4.7).
Four important types of increasing operators, which are fundamental for unifying lattice-based image
analysis, are the following:
δ is dilation iff δ(⋁i∈J Xi) = ⋁i∈J δ(Xi)
ε is erosion iff ε(⋀i∈J Xi) = ⋀i∈J ε(Xi)
α is opening iff α is increasing, idempotent and anti-extensive
β is closing iff β is increasing, idempotent and extensive
The first two definitions require arbitrary,possibly infinite, collections{Xi ∶ i ∈ J } of lattice elements;
hence, the dilation and erosion operators need complete lattices. The special case of an empty input col-
lection equips each dilation and erosion with the following necessary properties:
δ(O) = O, ε(I) = I (4.23)

invariant Minkowski-type morphological image operators, whose definitions are given below.

Proposition 4.4 ([15, 101]). Let L be a complete lattice. Then:
(a) The classO+(L) of increasing operators onL is a complete sublattice ofO(L).
(b) The classO−(L) of decreasing operators onL is a complete sublattice ofO(L).
(c) The class of dilations onL is a sup-closed subset and hence a complete underlattice ofO+(L).
(d) The class of erosions onL is an inf-closed subset and hence a complete underlattice ofO+(L).
(e) The class of anti-dilations onL is an inf-closed subset and hence a complete underlattice ofO−(L).
(f) The class of anti-erosions onL is a sup-closed subset and hence a complete underlattice ofO−(L).
Both sublatticesO+ and O− contain the greatest operator (I) and least operator (O) ofO, as well as
the identity operatorid. Inthe lattice of dilations, the leastelementisOwhereasthe greatest elementis a
dilation that mapsO to itself and every inputX ≠ O to I. Dually, in the lattice of erosions, the greatest
element isI whereas the least element is an erosion that mapsI to itself and every inputX ≠ I to O.
4.3.2 Adjunctions and Residuations: Pairs of Dilations and Erosions
Dilations and erosions come in pairs as the following concept reveals. LetL and M be two complete
lattices, and consider two operatorsδ ∶ L → M and ε ∶ M → L . The operator pair(δ, ε) is called an
adjunctionbetween L and M if
δ(X) ≤ Y ⟺ X ≤ ε(Y ) ∀X ∈ L, Y ∈ M (4.30)
If L = M, then the above operator pair is called anadjunction onL. There is aone-to-one correspondence
between the two operators of an adjunction pair, as will be explained below. Note: In [97] and [235] the
adjunction pair is denoted by the two operators, though in reverse order to how we present them here.
Proposition 4.5 (Heijmans & Ronse [101], Serra [235]). Let L and M be two complete lattices. Then:
(a) Given a dilationδ ∶ L → M , there is a unique erosion

4.3.3.1 Convergence and Continuity on Topological Image Spaces
Let E be atopological spacethat is:
(1) locally compact (i.e. each point has a compact neighborhood),
(2) Hausdorff (i.e. two distinct points can be separated by two disjoint neighborhoods), and
(3) second countable, i.e. has a countable basis11 (i.e. every open set can be expressed as a countable
union of basis sets).
Examples of such topological spacesE are the continuous planeR2 with the Euclidean topology and the
discrete planeZ2 with the discrete topology. Consider now the collectionF(E) of the closed subsets
of E, which model binary image objects. Equipped with the hit-miss topology [173], F(E) becomes a
compact, Hausdorff space with a countable basis.

Consider now a set operatorψ on F(E). It is calledupper semi-continuous (u.s.c.)if limXn ⊆ ψ(X)
for each convergent set sequence(Xn) with limXn = X . Similarly, ψ is calledlower semi-continuous

4.3.4 Openings, Closings, Lattice Projections
A large variety of useful morphological operators share two properties:increasing and idempotent. Such
operators were called‘morphological filters’by Matheron and Serra. We shall call themlattice projections
(or ‘order projections’), since they preserve the lattice ordering and are idempotent in analogy with the
linear projections that preserve the algebraic structure of linear spaces and are idempotent. The most
well-studied special cases of lattice projections are the lattice openings and closings, each of which has an
additional property. Specifically, openings are lattice projections that are anti-extensive, whereas closings
are extensive lattice projections.
Combinations of such generalized filters have proven to be very useful for image enhancement, multi-
scale image simplification, segmentation, motion analysis, and object detection.
In this section we will focus on their lattice-theoretic properties and representations. To improve our
intuitive understanding of them, we will also mention some examples and show figures with image anal-
ysis experiments.
4.3.4.1 Lattice Theory of Openings and Closings
Several algebraic properties of lattice projections, and especially those of openings and closings, can be
analyzedbasedonthesetoffixedpointsofsuchanoperator ψ,calledthe invariance domainanddenoted
by
Inv(ψ) ∶= {X ∈ L ∶ ψ(X) = X}
The following summarizes some immediate properties of the invariance domain stemming from various
characteristics of its corresponding operator.

Proposition 4.11 ([97, 173]). Let ψ be an operator on a complete latticeL and letInv(ψ) be its invariance
domain. Then:
(a) (Tarski Fixpoint Theorem): Ifψ is increasing, thenInv(ψ) is nonempty.
(b) ψ is idempotent if and only ifInv(ψ) = Ran(ψ).
(c) Ifψ is increasing and anti-extensive, thenInv(ψ) is sup-closed.
(d) Ifψ is increasing and extensive, thenInv(ψ) is inf-closed.
Weseefromtheaboveproposition,part(c)and(d),thattheinvariancedomainsofincreasingextensive
and antiextensive operators are complete lattices. If we add the third property of idempotence, we get
openings and closings. The fixed points of an opening (resp. closing) contain sufficient information to
represent them via a supremum (resp. infimum), as the following important result explains.
Proposition 4.12 ([221, 235]). If α and β are opening and closing operators, respectively, on a complete
lattice L, then:
α(X) = ⋁{Y ∈ Inv(α) ∶ Y ≤ X}, X ∈ L (4.49)
β(X) = ⋀{Y ∈ Inv(β) ∶ Y ≥ X}, X ∈ L (4.50)
Thus, the invariance domain can uniquely represent an opening or closing. The following proposition
groups together some useful facts about openings and closings that are formed from adjunctions.
Proposition 4.13 ([97, 221, 235]). Let (δ, ε) be an adjunction. Then:
(a)δε is an opening, andεδ is a closing.
(b) δεδ = δ and εδε = ε.
(c)Inv(δε) = Ran(δ) andInv(εδ) = Ran(ε).
Thus,fromanyadjunction (ε, δ)wecanalwaysconstructanopeningandaclosingviathecomposition
of its erosion and dilation. The converse is also true: given an opening or closing, we can express it by
composing the erosion and dilation of some properly defined adjunction. This is explained next for the
case of an opening.
Proposition 4.14 ([97]). Any openingα on a complete latticeL can be can be expressed as the composition
δε of an erosion with a dilation, where(δ, ε) is an adjunction betweenL and the complete latticeM =
P(Inv(α)). The erosionε ∶ L → M is defined by
ε(X) = {A ∈ Inv(α) ∶ A ≤ X}, X ∈ L (4.51)
The dilationδ ∶ M → L is defined by
δ(K) = ⋁ K, K ⊆ Inv(α) (4.52)
The following result allows us to synthesize new openings (resp. closings) by taking the supremum
(resp. infimum) of a family of openings (resp. closings).
Proposition 4.15 [235, 221, 97]. Let {αi} and {βi} be indexed families of openings and closings on a
complete lattice. Then:
(a)α = ⋁i αi is an opening andβ = ⋀i βi is a closing.
(b)Inv(α) = ⋃i Inv(αi) andInv(β) = ⋂i Inv(βi).

Connected Filters:
The flat zonesof an image signalf ∶ E → R are defined as the connected components of the image
domain E on whichf assumes a constant value. A useful class of morphological filters was introduced in
[230] which operate by merging flat zones and hence exactly preserving the contours of the image parts
remaining in the filter’s output. These are calledconnected operators. They cannot create new image
structures or new boundaries if they did not exist in the input. Specifically, ifD is a partition of the im-
age domain, letD(x) denote the (partition member) region that contains the pixelx. Now, given two

is calledconnected if the flat zone partition of its inputf is finer than the flat zone partition of its output
ψ(f). Connected operators have found many applications in multimedia, biomedical and remote sens-
ing imagery for tasks suchas object-orientedfiltering, imagesimplification, segmentation, andmultiscale
shape analysis [231, 257, 267]. Next, we will discuss two types of connected operators: the area filters
and the reconstruction filters, which are lattice openings or closings.

The area filters can be generalized to other connected operators that operate by processing connected

of the largest (resp. smallest) circle that can be inscribed into (resp. circumscribed around) a connected
component, (ii) the area or perimeter of the convex hull of a connected component. Generalizations of
attribute filters based on second-order connectivity were studied in [199].

Levelings:
Despite their many applications, reconstruction openings and closings have, as a disadvantage, the
property that they arenot self-dual operators; hence, they treat the image and its background asymmet-
rically. A connected operator that unifies both of them and possesses self-duality is the leveling [178,
180]. Levelings are nonlinear ‘object-oriented’ filters that simplify areferencesignal or imager through a
simultaneous use of locally expanding and shrinking an initial seed image, called themarker f, and glob-
ally constraining of the marker evolution by the reference image. Specifically, iterations of the discrete
operator φ(f|r) = ( δB(f) ∧ r) ∨ εB(f), whereδB(⋅) (resp. εB(⋅)) is a dilation (resp. erosion) by
the unit-radius discrete diskB of the grid, yield in the limit the conditionalleveling of r w.r.t. f:

k→∞
gk, g k = (δB(gk−1) ∧ r) ∨ εB(gk−1), g 0 = f (4.64)
In contrast to the reconstruction opening (closing) where the marker is smaller (greater) than the ref-
erence, the marker for a general leveling may have an arbitrary ordering w.r.t. the reference signal. See
Fig. 4.10(c) for a 1D example and Fig.4.1(d) for a 2D example. The leveling reduces to being a recon-
struction opening (closing) over regions where the marker is smaller (greater) than the reference image.
Actually, as shown in Section4.3.5, the leveling can be obtained as a cascade of a reconstruction opening and
a reconstruction closing.

4.3.5.1 Multiscale Levelings and Level Sets
Consider a reference signalr and a levelingΛ. If we can produce various markersfi, i = 1, 2, 3, ... ,
that are related to some increasing scale parameteri, let us construct the levelingsgi = Λ(f i|gi−1),
i = 1, 2, 3, ... , with g0 = r . The signals gi constitute a hierarchy ofmultiscale levelingspossessing the
causality property thatgj is a leveling ofgi for j > i . One way to construct such multiscale levelings
is to use a sequence of multiscale markers obtained from sampling a Gaussian scale-space. As shown in
Fig.4.12,theimageedgesandboundarieswhichhavebeenblurredandshiftedbytheGaussianscale-space
are better preserved across scales by the multiscale levelings.
The main approach in mathematical morphology to extend set operators to image function operators
is using level sets and threshold superposition [234, 139, 97]. Specifically, ifXv(f) = { x ∶ f( x) ≥ v}
are the level sets of an extended real-valued image functionf, and we are given an increasing set operator
Ψ, then we can construct a so-calledflat operatorψ(f)( x) = sup{v ∶ x ∈ Ψ(X v(f))} via threshold
superpositionoftheoutputsofthesetoperatoractingonallinputlevelsets. Theflatoperator ψcanprocess
both binary and graylevel images. The levelings produced by the PDE (4.65) are flat operators and hence
they can be constructed by their set counterparts via threshold superposition. Thus,
Λ(f|r)( x) = sup{v ∶ x ∈ Λ(X v(f)|X v(r))} (4.66)
ThesetequivalentofthePDE( 4.65)isacurveevolutionthatpropagatesthelevelcurvesof uwithnormal
speed ±1 whose sign corresponds corresponds to sgn(r − u). Namely, whenu > r (u < r ), the level
curves are moved toward (opposite) the direction of the gradient ofu. In the limit, the curves will con-
verge to the level curves of the leveling. The level curves of the multiscale levelings are shown in Fig.4.12
to preserve the global boundaries of image regions much more accurately than the multiscale Gaussian
convolutions.

4.3.5.4 Multiscale Triphase Operators and Levelings
Triphase Operators:
Consider operators on the complete latticeL of images. To define levelings as in [178] and to gener-
alize them we shall begin by introducing the concept of triphase operators.
Definition 4.1 . Given two operatorsα and β from L2 to L that are increasing w.r.t. both arguments
and, ∀f, r,
f ∧ r ≤ β(f|r) ≤ r ≤ α(f|r) ≤ f ∨ r, (4.78)
a triphase operator λ is defined by
λ(f|r; α, β) ∶= α(f|β(f|r)) (4.79)
where r is the reference signal andf is a marker signal.
The triphase operators have four arguments: two signalsf and r and two operatorsα and β. The signal
arguments (f, r) are written as(f|r) to emphasize their asymmetric roles (marker vs. reference). If the
operators αand β areknownandfixed,wecanomitthemandwrite λ(f|r). Ifthereference risassumed,
we may writeλ(f), α(f), β(f); iff is also implied, we may express the operator outputs simply asλ, α,
β.
The inequality (4.78) and the assumption that they are increasing immediately implies the following
properties for the operatorsα, β.
Proposition 4.16 (a) f ≤ r ⟹ α(f|r) = r , andf ≥ r ⟹ β(f|r) = r .
(b) r ≤ α 2(f) ≤ α(f) ≤ α(f ∨ r) ≤ f ∨ r
(c) f ∧ r ≤ β(f ∧ r) ≤ β(f) ≤ β 2(f) ≤ r .
In the definition of the triphase operator, we shall, henceforth, assume that the operatorsαand β com-
mute13; i.e.,

The PDE (4.101) has a varying coefficient−sgn(u − r) with scale-space dependence which controls
the instantaneous growth and stops it wheneveru = r . Of course, there is no growth also at extrema

r(x) it acts as a dilation PDE and hence shifts parts of the graph ofu(x, t)with positive (negative) slope
to the left (right) but does not move the extrema points. Whereveru(x, t) > r(x) the PDE acts as an
erosion PDE and reverses the direction of propagation. The final resultu(x, ∞)is a leveling ofr w.r.t. f.

Experiments:
Someinsightsonthebehavioroflevelingsandmultiscalesemilatticeerosionscanbeobtainedfromthe
following image experiments. As shown in Figs.4.13, 4.14 and 4.15, the leveling limit is strongly domi-
nated by the structure of the reference image. Although the selection of markers suitable for producing
levelings with various designable properties is still an open issue, it appears that a smooth version of the

mixingormorphingthemarkerimageintothereference,evenifthetwoimagesarecompletelyunrelated.

Hence, the algebraic discrete algorithm yields a result that has a larger absolute deviation from the true
solutionthanthePDEnumericalalgorithm. (Recallthat f ⪯ r gimplies |f(x) − r(x)| ≤ |g(x) − r(x)|
∀x.) Further, the algebraic discrete algorithm is a special case of the PDE algorithm using the valueθ =
Δt/Δx = 1, which makes it marginallyunstable(resulting in small errors being amplified).
In the 2D case we have an additional comparison issue: In segmentation applications, as a triphase
operator evolves towards a leveling, the desired result is mainly produced by the final limit. However,
there may be other applications, for instance, such as mixing/morphing images, where we need to stop
the marker growth before convergence. For example, the mixing/morphing in Figs.4.14,4.15 indicates
that the multiscale TI semilattice operators may generate interesting intermediate results. In such cases,
as evolutions of 2D multiscale (geodesic or TI) semilattice erosions, the isotropy of the partially grown
marker offered by the PDE approach is an advantage over the discrete algebraic approach.
4.4 Morphological Representations for Lattice Operators
In general, it helps conceptually and practically to know that a particular system together with many oth-
ers sharing a few common properties result from the combination of a few simple generic systems. This
leads to the field ofrepresentation of operators. The representation theory of linear operator is already well
studied. Next, we will present the main ideas and a few examples of a representation theory for nonlinear
operators on lattices based on elementary morphological operators. This section follows Maragos [154]
which contains more details and discusses the usefulness of such representations from computational,
applications and nonlinear functional analysis viewpoints.
Let us consider d-dimensional binary images represented by subsets ofE, where E is equal to Rd

and dilations, which are essentially infimal and supremal convolutions.

Theorem 4.6 is theoretically interesting but has no direct practical importance, because it requires an

Thus,any increasingwindowoperator Ψ,canberepresentedeitherasafiniteunionofhit-missoperators
or as a finite union of erosions by patterns in its shape collectionT. However, the representation of any
such operator via erosions by the elements of its basis is more efficient because the basis contains fewer
elements than the shape collection. What follows below is a numerical example of this concept.
Example 4.8 (Morphological Basis of Window Operators).
Let W be the 5-pixel symmetric rhombus and consider the set medianΨ(X) = medW (X). Then, Ψ
is a window operator whose shape collection isT = {A ⊆ W ∶ 3 ≤ |wA| ≤ 5} . Thus, T consists
of 16 subsets ofW; these subsets are the shapes that the window transformation detects. The basis ofΨ
is B = {A ⊆ W ∶ |A| = 3} . Thus, B contains only 10 sets, and Theorem4.7 represents Ψ as the
union of 10 erosions by these basis sets. However, Theorem4.8 represents Ψ as the union of 16 hit-miss
operators by the elements ofT, and each hit-miss operator is the intersection of two erosions; hence, the
latterrepresentationiscomputationallylessefficientbecauseitrequiresalargernumberofmorecomplex
morphological operations. Similarly, Theorem4.9a representsΨ as a union of 16 erosions, which is less
efficient than the 10 erosions required by the basis representation. 2
The previous analysis gives us a very useful result:
Proposition 4.24 The basis of an increasing window operator is finite.
These representations are important because increasing finite-window operators encompass all rank
operators, stack filters, and increasing discrete morphological operators that use finite structuring ele-
ments.
The basis representation of window operators applies if they are increasing. The increasingness allows
us to easily extend these operators to graylevel image processing by building flat operators that process
all the level sets of the input graylevel image using a binary window operator. A lattice-theoretic study of
moregeneralbinarywindowoperatorsthatmaybenon-increasingwasdonein[ 19]wheretheywereused
as building blocks of computational morphological machines. Further, [17] investigated an extension
of binary window operators to graylevel image processing using weighted windows (i.e. windows with
graylevel weights), but the computational complexity is larger.
Concluding,thebasisrepresentationsofincreasingTIsetoperators(includingmorphological,median
and rank filters, and window-based feature/object detection operators) may be useful for alternative par-
allel implementations (hardware or software) of the corresponding binary image processing systems, as
explainedin[ 139]. Anotherapplicationareaistheoptimalrestorationofbinaryimages(e.g. documents)
in the presence of noise by using a union of erosions by a small number sets from a subcollection of the
basis [136]. They also apply to graylevel image processing in the case of flat operators defined based on a
finite window, which, as will be explained below, also accept a basis representation as a maximum of flat
erosions.
4.4.2 Basis Representations for TI Increasing Function Operators
For every TI, increasing, and u.s.c. signal operator there is a special collection of functions, called itsmor-
phologicalbasis,suchthattheoperatorcanberepresentedasasupremumoferosionsbyitsbasisfunctions.
As for the case of TI set operators, this basis is a subcollection of a suitably defined kernel. In this section
we will summarize this representation theory for signal and graylevel image operators and provide some
examples, e.g. its application to some nonlinear filters (openings, median and stack filters) and some lin-
ear digital filters.

4.4.2.3 Representations for Boolean Operators and Stack Filters
Boolean Functions:
The representation theory of discrete set operators as a union of erosions or as an intersection of dila-
tions has direct analogies with the representation ofBoolean functions. Any Boolean expression ofn vari-
ables v1, v2, ... , vn ∈ {0, 1} can be written as a Boolean Sum-Of-Products (SOP) terms or as Boolean
Product-Of-Sum (POS) terms [120,191]. Each product or sum term may contain eachliteral(a variable
or its complement) at most once and/or the Boolean constants 0 or 1. To each Boolean expression there
corresponds a unique Boolean functionb(v) ∈ {0, 1}, wherev = (v 1, v2, ... , vn). A Boolean function
is usually described via atruth table. Two Boolean expressions are calledequivalentif they correspond to
the same Boolean function. A Boolean functionb1 is said toimply b2 iff b2(v) = 1 for eachv such that
b1(v) = 1 ; this is the partial ordering (4.16). A prime implicantπ of b is a product term which implies
b, such that the deletion of any literal fromπ results in a new product which does not implyb. A prime
implicateof bisasumterm σ impliedby b,suchthatthedeletionofanyliteralfrom σ resultsinanewsum
term which is not implied byb. AnyminimalSOP (resp. POS) expression forb is a sum (resp. product)
of prime implicants (resp. prime implicates) such that the removal of any of them makes the remaining
expression no longer equivalent tob, and that the expression contains the minimum number of literals
and product (resp. sum) terms. This minimal expression is not necessarily unique. A functionb(v) is
called positiveif it can be represented by a SOP or POS expression in which no variable appears in an un-
complemented form. Each positive function has a unique minimal SOP expression that is positive and is
the sum of all its prime implicants; it also has a unique minimal POS expression that is positive and is the
product of all its prime implicates.
Consider now, from Example4.3, the latticeBVn = {0, 1} n of n-variable Boolean vectors and the
lattice BFn of Boolean functions defined onBVn. A Boolean function b is calledincreasing if v ≤ u
implies thatb(v) ≤ b( u). A Boolean function is increasing iff it is positive [80]. If b is positive, its dual
function bd(v) = b(v) is positive too.
In BVn, a vectorx is called aminimal true vectorof a Boolean functionb iff b(x) = 1 and x is not
preceded (with respect to the vector partial ordering) by any other vectorv with b(v) = 1 . Dually, a
vector y is called amaximal false vectorof b iff b(y) = 0 and y is not followed by any other vectoru with
b(u) = 0.

For aminimal representation, [16] have developed a different concept of a basis of the kernel of TI op-

collection of maximal closed intervals of the kernel. To guarantee the existence of this new basis they had

of sets that form intervals only inside the basis.
Let us compare the above minimal representation with the standard basis representation of Theo-
rem 4.7 for increasing TI operators. Since every hit-miss operation detects the locations of a template
(A, B), which has a positive part (A) hitting the foreground and a negative part (B) hitting the back-
ground, we see that the above representation acts like a Boolean function that can be expressed as a
Boolean SOP or as a Boolean POS. Considering only the expansion with sup-generating operations, i.e.
the SOP expression, we can see that each Boolean product corresponds to a single hit-miss operation
where the uncomplemented variables correspond to points ofA whereas the complemented variables
correspond to points ofB. If we compare this Boolean interpretation of the representation with hit-miss
operationsagainstthecorrespondingBooleaninterpretationofincreasingTIbinaryfilters,whichwasex-
plained in Section4.4.2.3, we observe that in the latter case the Boolean function is irreducible and has
only positive terms (i.e. no complementations). Thus, as also illustrated in Example4.8, if we use as basis
elementsofanincreasingTIsetoperatorthemaximalintervalsinitskernel,thentheseintervalsmayover-
lapwhichmaycreateredundanciesinthecorrespondingrepresentationasaunionofhit-missoperations.
Incontrast,thebasisusingtheminimalkernelelementshasnoredundanciesandsynthesizestheoperator
as union of simpler operations (erosions).

4.4.4 Representations for TI Openings and Closings
In previous sections we discussed representations of TI increasing operators. In this section we shall ex-
aminerepresentationsforTIoperatorsthatinadditiontobeingincreasingarealsoidempotentandexten-

4.5 Adaptive Morphological Operators
The adaptivity of a system or algorithm means its capability to automatically adjust its parameters to the
input data (by taking into account their spatio-temporal and range information) aiming at improving or
optimizing some criterion. The usefulness and necessity of adaptive algorithms are evident if one consid-
ers the variability of the signals or images that should commonly be processed by a unique algorithm, the
internal variability of the data in a single image or image sequence, the a priori knowledge (e.g. context or
noise) that needs to be incorporated in the processing, and the requirements of the processing in terms
of resulting signal properties (for instance, the preservation of certain image structures). Some practical
motivations include: adapting to the luminance, or the contrast, or the gradient norm or the gradient di-
rectionoftheimagefunctionateverypointinspaceisfundamentalifonewantstoencourageintra-region
smoothing while preserving edges; adapting to a possibly spatially-varying camera perspective is of cru-
cial importance in many surveillance situations; and the evolution of the image data throughout time is
also a precious information for video compression or action recognition.
There are two fundamental questions when dealing with adaptive algorithms or adaptive transforms.
First, how to mathematically define such operations? Second, how to practically design adaptive trans-
forms, i.e., how to define the link between the transformation parameters and the image data? These
questions have received an increasing level of interest in the image processing and computer vision com-
munity.
Inthissection,wewillfocusonadaptivemorphologicaloperatorsanddiscussthreemajorperspectives
and corresponding research directions: (i) adaptivity w.r.t. the operators’ spatial neighborhood, which
leadstotheconceptofa‘ structuringelementmap ’andshift-varyingmorphologicaloperators;(ii)algebraic
principles such as group and representation theory to unify important aspects of the adaptive operators;
and (iii) adaptivity w.r.t. how the operators process the image level sets at different levels, which leads to
viscous morphological operators.
Abriefoverviewofadaptivemorphologyhasbeenpresentedin[ 168]. Moreinformationcanbefound
inthepaperswecitebelowandthereferencestherein. Animportantissueiswhetherthepairsofadaptive
dilationsanderosionsproposedbyvariousresearchersareactuallylatticeadjunctions; thiswasexamined
by [217].

4.5.1.2 Specific Approaches for Spatially-Adaptive Morphology
Some additional approaches and applications of spatially-adaptive morphology include the following:
1) Distance-based:The SEM idea was explored by several researchers by developing morphological oper-

thanshift-invariantfiltersthatusedfixed-shapekernels. Anotherapproach[ 86]usedasimilaritymeasure

decreasing function of thegeodesic time, which is computed by integrating the image gradient magnitude
along paths. As in [129], the geodesic time is a weighted distance transform.
2)Connectivity-based: Adaptivity is omnipresent inconnectedmorphological operators [230,199], which
process connected components in images. For instance, area openings [266, 49] at scaleμare geometry-

of the image.

4.5.2 Viscous Morphology
Viscous morphological operators have shown very good performance in regularizing various image anal-
ysis tasks such as the detection of intensity-varying boundaries and segmentation [259, 258]. They are
special cases of a general class of intensity level-varying operators studied in [167], where their formula-
tion as solutions of nonlinear PDEs was also developed together with efficient numerical algorithms to
solve these PDEs and generate the viscous operations.
The dilation and erosion of a setX by a disk at scale (radius)t > 0 , i.e. the Minkowski addition
X ⊕ tB and subtractionX ⊖ tB, are denoted byδtB(X) and εtB(X) respectively, whereB is the unit
disk. Similarly, δtB(f) and εtB(f) denote the multiscale flat dilation and erosion of a graylevel imagef
by such a disk.

4.6 Weighted Lattices: Tropical Spaces
4.6.1 Lattice-Ordered Monoids and Clodum
A poset, lattice, or semilatticeLis often endowed with additionalstructure of the group type. Namely,L
may have an additional binary operation, called symbolically the ‘multiplication’ ⋆, under which(L, ⋆)is
any of the following:
• Semigroupif ⋆ is associative.
• Monoidif ⋆ is associative and has identity element.
• Groupif ⋆ is associative, has identity, and each element has an inverse.
In addition, if⋆ is alsocommutative, we obtain a commutative semigroup/monoid/group.
The lattice supremum together with the above generalized ‘multiplication’ ⋆ endow the lattice with a
structure reminiscent of a semiring. Let us briefly recall the definitions of ring-type structures(R, +, ×)
consisting of setR together with two binary operations, referred to symbolically as ‘ring addition(+)’
and ‘ring multiplication(×)’. This structure is any of the following:
• Semiring if (R, +) is a commutative monoid under addition, whose identity0 ∈ R is called the
ring zero, (R, ×) is a monoid under multiplication, whose identity1 ∈ R is called the ringunit,
and the ring multiplication distributes over the ring addition.
• Ring: a semiring where(R, +)is a commutative group.
• Semifield: a semiring where(R\{0}, ×)is a commutative group.
• Field: a semiring where both(R, +)and (R\{0}, ×)are commutative groups.
An algebra(M, ∨, ⋆)is called asemilattice-ordered monoidif M is a sup-semilattice under∨, monoid
under ⋆, and⋆ distributes over∨. If we assume for the rest of this section that⋆ is commutative17, this
can be written as:
A ⋆ (X ∨ Y ) = (A ⋆ X) ∨ (A ⋆ Y ) (4.206)
for all A, B, X, Y ∈ M . If M also has an infimum∧ that (together with∨) makes it a lattice, then
(M, ∨, ∧, ⋆)is called alattice-ordered monoid. Suppose now thatM is also a monoid under a ‘dual mul-
tiplication’ operation⋆′ that distributes over infimum:
A ⋆′ (X ∧ Y ) = (A ⋆ ′ X) ∧ (A ⋆ ′ Y ) (4.207)
Now M has four binary operations. We shall call the resulting algebra(M, ∨, ∧, ⋆, ⋆′) a lattice-ordered
double monoid. To the above definitions we will add the wordcomplete if M is a complete lattice and
the distributivities involved are infinite. We will call the resulting algebra acomplete lattice-ordered double
monoid, in short aclodum[147, 154].
In any lattice-ordered double monoid the distributivity of⋆ over ∨ and of⋆′ over ∧ imply that both
‘multiplications’ ⋆ and ⋆′ are increasing; i.e.,
X ≤ Y ⟹ A ⋆ X ≤ A ⋆ Y
X ≤ Y ⟹ A ⋆ ′ X ≤ A ⋆ ′ Y (4.208)
These properties imply in turn that

4.6.2 Complete Weighted Lattices
4.6.2.1 General Algebraic Structure
We are interested in creating nonlinear spaces whose algebraic structure will resemble that of traditional
linear spaces, like for example the spacesRn of vectors or the spaceslp(Zd, R)of d-dimensional signals
with finite norm, but whose vector/signal addition and scalar multiplication will be replaced by the lat-
tice supremum and infimum operations and the scalar addition and multiplication in the field of scalars
supporting a linear space will be replaced by the scalar arithmetic of a clodum.
Consideranonemptycollection Wofmathematicalobjects,whichwillbeourspace;examplesofsuch
objects include the vectors inR
n
or signals in Fun(E, R). We shall symbolically refer to the space ele-
mentsas “vectors”,althoughtheymaybesignalsorarbitraryobjects. Also,consideraclodum (K, ∨, ∧, ⋆, ⋆′)
of scalars. We define two operations among vectorsF , Gin W: their supremumF ∨ G ∶ W 2 → W
and infimum F ∧ G ∶ W 2 → W , which we will denote using the same supremum symbol (∨) and
infimum symbol (∧) as in the clodum, hoping that the differences will be clear to the reader from the
context. Further, we will define two operations among any vectorF in W and any scalarc in K: a scalar
‘multiplication’c ⋆ F ∶ (K, W) → W and a scalar dual multiplication’c ⋆ ′ F ∶ (K, W) → W ; again,
we will denote these scalar ‘multiplications’ of vectors by using the same symbols as in the clodum. Now,
we will defineW to be aWeighted Lattice (WL)space over a clodum(K, ∨, ∧, ⋆, ⋆′) of scalars if for all
F , G, H ∈ W and a, b ∈ K the following axioms hold:
(WL-A1). F ∨ G ∈ W and F ∧ G ∈ W , (Closure under sup/inf).
(WL-A2). F ∨ G = G ∨ F and F ∧ G = G ∧ F , (Commutativity of sup/inf).
(WL-A3). F ∨ (G ∨ H) = (F ∨ G) ∨ H and F ∧ (G ∧ H) = (F ∧ G) ∧ H , (Associativity of
sup/inf).
(WL-A4). F ∨ O = F and F ∧ I = F , (Existence of ‘addition’ identities).

We observe the following:
(1) The six axioms from (WL-A1) until (WL-A6) make(W, ∨, ∧)a (flat) lattice with a least element
(O) and a greatest element (I).
(2) Axiom (WL-A7) makes this lattice distributive.
(3)Theaboveaxiomsofaweightedlatticebearastrikingsimilaritytothoseofalinearspace. Forexample,

Onedifferenceisthatthevectoraddition( +)oflinearspacesisnowreplacedbytwodualsuperpositions,
the lattice supremum (∨) and infimum (∧); further, the scalar multiplication (×) of linear spaces is now
replaced by two operations⋆ and ⋆′ that are dual to each other. Only one major property of the linear
spaces is missing from the weighted lattices: the existence of ‘additive inverses’; i.e., the supremum and
infimum operations donot have inverses.
We define the weighted latticeW over the clodumK as aComplete Weighted Lattice (CWL)space,
or simply atropical space, if all the following hold:
(i) W is closed under any, possibly infinite, suprema and infima.
(ii) Its distributivities between supremum and infimum are of the infinite type.
(iii) The distributivities between the scalar operations⋆ or ⋆′ and the supremum or infimum are of the
infinite type.
Note that a scalar clodum is by itself a scalar CWL over itself.
A subsetX of a (complete) weighted latticeW over a scalar clodumK is called a(complete) weighted
sublatticeif it is, itself, a (complete) weighted lattice overK, or equivalently if it is (completely20) closed
under the original lattice supremum and infimum as well as by the two scalar multiplications.

An outcome of the previous discussion is the following result:
Theorem 4.20 ([147, 144]). (a) An operatorΔ on a CWLW of signals is a max-tropical shift-invariant
(max-TSI) system iff it can be represented as the max-tropical convolution of the input signal with the system’s
upper impulse responseH = Δ(q) . (b) An operator E on W is a min-tropical shift-invariant (min-TSI)
system iff it can be represented as the min-tropical convolution of the input signal with the system’s lower impulse
response H ′ = E(q ′).
The above theorem has a direct conceptual analogy with Riesz’s representation theorem forlinear op-
erators, which states that linear shift-invariant (in short, LSI) operators are uniquely represented as linear
(sum-product) convolutions of the inputF with their impulse responseH:

4.7.4.2 Generalized Shifts and Translation Invariance
Thepreviousshiftsof d-dimensionalsignals F (x)ontheirEuclideandomain E canbeextendedto d + 1
dimensions by consideringtranslation operatorsτ and their dualsτ ′
τ y,v(f)(x) = F (x − y) ⋆ v, τ ′
y,v(f)(x) = F (x − y) ⋆′ v (4.267)
where (y, v) ∈ E × K . A signal operator onW is called (dual) TI iff it commutes with any such (dual)
translation. The above translation-invariance contains both a vertical shift (via a clodum ‘multiplication’)
and a horizontal shift. Then, an alternative view of a max-TSI operator is that it is both a lattice dilation
and translation-invariant. According to this perspective, a max-TSI operator is adilation translation-
invariant (DTI) system. Dually, a min-TSI operator is both a lattice erosion and translation-invariant,
and hence may be called anerosion translation-invariant (ETI)system. The earlier analysis of tropical
operators in [154, 144] was based on this alternative view as either DTI or ETI systems.
So far, all signal shifts we have considered on the tropical spaceW were horizontal translations, which
can be viewed as a special case of Euclidean motions. These form a group of automorphisms of the
(continuous or discrete) signal domainE. Tropical operators are group-invariant w.r.t. to these shifts.
The signal domainE possesses various commutative group structures which allow us to define corre-
sponding signal shifts that form two major types ofhorizontal Euclidean motions. The most obvious
and practical choice is to consider thehorizontal shifts on the image plane where each such operator
σy(F )(x) = F ( x − y) performs a planar shift of an input signalF (x) along the vectory. The class
Ths = { σy ∶ y ∈ E} of all horizontal motions under composition is acommutative group of automor-
phisms both on the set latticeP(E) (the collection of all subsets ofE) as well as on the signal lattice
W; i.e. σxσy = σx+y. A second choice is to setE = R 2\{(0, 0)} and to considerpolar motions
σr,θ that transform the support of an input signal via a rotation byθ and a radial scaling byr. The class
Thr = {σr,θ ∶ r > 0, θ ∈ [0, 2π)} ofallpolarmotionsisalsoacommutativegroupofautomorphisms;
i.e. σr,θσρ,φ = σrρ,θ+φ. Both of these choices were studied in [96, 97]; the polar case was studied in
[219]. As a third possibility we can consider the group of all Euclidean planar motions, i.e. combined
translations and rotations; this is anon-commutativegroup of automorphisms studied in [216]. Another
example of a non-commutative group of automorphisms is the group of affine mappings on the plane,

4.7.5 Special Cases of Tropical Operators: Max-plus, Max-times, Max-min
By specifying the clodumK and its scalar ‘multiplication’ operations⋆ and its dual⋆′, we obtain a large
variety of classes of nonlinear image processing systems that are described by the previous unified repre-
sentations. Below, we will briefly describe three such choices.
4.7.5.1 Max-Plus Image Operators
Let us setK = R = R ∪ {−∞, +∞} . The scalar ‘multiplications’⋆ and ⋆′ are the regular extended
addition + and its dual+′ over R, respectively; i.e.,+ and +′ are identical for finite reals, but
a + (−∞) = −∞ and a +′ (+∞) = +∞ ∀a ∈ R.
Thus,theclodumofscalarsis ([−∞, +∞], ∨, ∧, +, +′). Inthiscase Kisa clogandcontainsanadditive
group (R, +)where each scalara has an inverse−a that coincides with its conjugatea∗. The adjunction

nel’, or in a minimal basis subcollection [139].
In addition to morphological image processing, there are many other scientific fields where the max-
plus algebraic system is often used. Examples include machine scheduling and operations research [56],
convexanalysisandoptimization[ 215],shortestpathproblemsongraphs[ 207],andmorphologicalneu-
ralnets[ 62,211,206,212]. Inshort,themax-pluscaseisthealgebraicallyrichestandmostwellexplored
case in mathematical morphology and image algebra as well as in minimax algebra, both in theory and in
applications.
