Classic fractal sets, including the Cantor set, the Koch curve, the Sierpinski triangle and carpet, and
the Menger sponge, can be modeled as attractors of some IFS whose contraction maps are affinities or
similarities. While this theory can model many fractal shapes as attractors of some IFS, it can also model
regular Euclidean shapes.

Random Point Iteration Algorithm (Probabilistic IFS):
A much faster (than the above deterministic) algorithm to synthesize an IFS attractor is the follow-
ing random algorithm:Start from an initial pointx0 on the plane and create a sequence of pointsxn by
randomly selecting one of the affine point mapswi with probabilitypi to create the next pointxn+1 =
wi(xn); i.e.
Pr{xn+1 = w i(xn)} = p i (5.150)
The shape of the generated attractor depends only on the mapswi, whereas the probabilitiespi control
the distribution of points over the attractor. In general, the probabilities can be chosen arbitrarily with
only two constraints:pi > 0 for eachi and ∑i pi = 1. In practice, if the 2D affine maps in (5.147) are
written aswi(x) = Mix + ti, where the2 × 2matrices Mi are responsible for rotations and scalings and
the ti are translation vectors, a usual good choice for the probabilities is
pi = |det(Mi)|

5.7.3 Fractal Pre-training for Visual Recognition
Nowadays, training computer vision systems via deep learning for specialized applications is often ac-
complished with better performance by firstpre-training on large generic datasets (e.g. ImageNet) and
then fine-tuning the models on specialized datasets. However, the requirement of large datasets actually
implies image and/or video datasets of enormous size, whose creation and curation is a huge effort for
multi-person groups (in academia or industry) with many resources. Some of the challenges include col-
lection and annotation of such huge image datasets, together with copyright and content bias or privacy
issues.
Tobypassthedifficultieswithlargedatasets,oneeffectiveapproachistocreate syntheticgenericdatasets
for pre-training. An interesting category of synthetic datasets has been proposed in [60] and [3] by gen-
erating random fractal images with IFS. Specifically, in [60] theN affine mapswi of an IFS as in (5.147)
were randomly created by samplingN uniformly from the discrete setU ({2, ... , 8}), where U (⋅)de-
notes uniform distribution, and the six parameters(ai, bi, ci, di, ei, fi) of each map by uniformly sam-
pling from U (−1, 1). In [60] this process was repeated thousands of times producing a dataset ofIFS
codes(i.e. parametervectors). Eachcodewasaugmentedbyscalingeachparameterseparately(exploiting

The approach of [3] for generating random fractal images was extended in [108, 109] toaction recog-
nition in videosby 1) automatically producing large-scale datasets of short synthetic video clips (100K -
400K videos of 20 frames each), utilized for pre-training neural models, 2) narrowing the domain gap by
emulating the properties of real videos during pre-training, and 3) identifying beneficial characteristics
of synthetic videos through ablations. The fractal video synthesis step was accomplished by creating the
first and last frames of each video clip via fractal image generation from randomly sampled IFS codes and
then interpolating the intermediate frames by exploiting properties of real videos. The generated fractals
at the first and last frame as well as at the intermediate interpolated frames utilized the matrix decom-

5.8 Fractal Interpolation Functions
The theory of IFS can also model graphs of functions as attractors. As explained in [55], this is done on
the complete metric spaceC of continuous functionsf ∶ [x 0, xN] → R equipped with thel∞ distance
‖f − g‖ ∞ = max{|f(x) − g(x)| ∶ x ∈ [x 0, xN]}, f, g ∈ C
A by-product of the synthesis of function graphs via IFS is theFractal Interpolation Functions (FIFs), ca-
pable of creating continuous fractal surfaces from discrete data [5]. In this section we will describe how
the contraction maps of an IFS can be designed so that the attractor function can interpolate given data

5.9 Multifractals
Fractal sets (e.g. curves, surfaces, graphs of functions) are characterized by roughness at multiple scales,
governed by self-similarity in a deterministic or statistical sense. Self-similarity (or self-affinity) implies
theyareinvariant,eitherexactlyorapproximately,tounionsofcontractivesimilitudes(oraffinities). This
usuallycreatesapower-lawscalingbehaviorofscale-dependentfunctionalswithglobalscalingexponents

geneous over the whole support of the object but vary locally. One large class of such multifractal objects
areself-similarmeasures. 13 Consideranonuniformmeasure μspreadoveraboundedset S ⊆ R m,which
mayormaynotbeitselfafractal. Themeasurecouldbeadistributionofmassorofelectricchargespread

The possible broadness of the support[αmin, αmax] of the singularity spectrumD(α) is closely related to
the possible existence of subsets ofS with different fractal dimensions and hence to the multi-fractality
of the measure. The idea of a ‘fractal measure’ first appeared in Mandelbrot [71, 72] to model the spatial
distribution of fully developed turbulence. Subsequently and towards the same application, the concepts
of ‘multifractal’, ‘singularity spectrum’ and its connection with Legendre transform were introduced by
FrischandParisi[ 38]. ThiswasfollowedbyHalseyetal. [ 45]witharicherformalismforstudyinginvari-
antprobabilitymeasuresonfractalsetsandstrangeattractorsofdynamicalsystems. Asstatedin[ 45],the
goal was “to model fractal measures by interwoven sets of singularities of strengthα, each characterized by its
own dimensionD(α).”
A broad class of multifractals areinvariant probability measures of nonlinear dynamical systems, i.e. mea-
sures created by counting the percentage of time that the points of an orbit of system’s iterations spend
in some subset of the system’s attractor. A rich and analytically tractable such class comprises the proba-
bility measures created by the probabilistic construction of IFS attractors. Namely, consider the random
iterationalgorithmforgeneratingtheattractorofaprobabilisticIFSwith N non-overlappingmaps wi by
iterating pointwise a mapψ that in each iteration is one of thewi randomly chosen with probabilitiespi,
i = 1, ... , N. This iteration is also called thechaos gamein [6, 7] because it exhibits chaotic dynamics. If
S is a subset of the attractor and we generate a sequencexk = ψ ∘k(x0), k = 1, ... , n, of points via the
chaos game starting from some initial pointx0 ∈ S, we can define a measure
μ(S) = lim

which equals the probability that the sequence of points will visitS. If the probabilities are all equal
(i.e. pi = 1/N ), then the measure will be homogeneous. Otherwise, if the IFS is run with unequal
probabilities, the measure will be multifractal.

Beyond the above two and other similar examples which can be solved analytically, it is difficult or
unknown how to analytically find the singularity spectrum of an arbitrary measure. If we resort to com-

5.9.4 Multifractal Functions and Analysis with Wavelets
We haveseenthatmultifractalmeasuresareheterogeneous in termsof their local fractal dimension, since
subsets of their support have a varying fractal dimension. Intuitively, we may use a similar idea to char-
acterize a fractal function (i.e. a function whose graph is a fractal set) as ‘multifractal’. Namely, from a
dimensionperspective,apracticalexamplecouldbethegraphofareal-worldnon-stationarysignalwhose
geometrical roughness (quantified by the fractal dimension) varies locally. For instance, Fig.5.37 shows
a speech waveform superimposed with the (Minkowski-Bouligand) fractal dimension of its graph com-
putedwiththemorphologicalfunctioncovermethodovermovingspeechsegmentsof10msecasashort-
time feature. There we see a temporal variation of the local fractal dimension of the signal. This is due to
the fact that, during the production of several classes of speech sounds there are some dynamic turbu-
lent phenomena in the human vocal tract that endow the sound waveforms with a fractal structure which
varies locally with time [81].

Intuitively, the local fractal dimension of a function is related to its local roughness, quantified via the
strength of its singularities. The main goal of the rest of this section is to link the singularities of a func-
tion whose strengths vary locally to a singularity spectrum, as we did for multifractal measures, which
quantifies the fractal dimensions of the subsets of the signal’s support that are characterized by different
singularity strengths. We shall limit our discussion to 1D functions and signalsf(x) where the indepen-
dent variablex may be a time or space variable.

Thus, in case (d), the valueγ is the most frequent Hölder exponent; actually the set of points in[a, b]

α0 = −(1/2) log2(p1p2) but there were many other values of local exponentsα whose points formed
sets with Hausdorff dimension in the interval(0, 1).
In [1] it is shown that, under very general assumptions on their parameters, there are large classes of

5.10 Notes and References
For a general and broad familiarization with fractals (main concepts and applications, historical aspects,
philosophical discussions) it is necessary to read the classic and very inspirational book by Mandelbrot
(1982). Details on mathematical aspects and inspiring applications of fractals, as well as impressive visu-
alizationsofthem,canbefoundintheclassicandnicebooksbyBarnsley(1988,1993),Falconer(2003),
PeitgenandSaupe(1988),Peitgen,JürgensandSaupe(1992,2004). Twootherniceandintuitivebooks,
rich in ideas and illustrations, are i) by Schroeder (1991) [104] on exploring links between fractals and
chaos with acoustics, language, physics, biology, and mathematics; ii) by Mumford, Series and Wright
(2002) [88] on symmetries and the links between geometry and groups, emphasizing complex-valued
functions of a complex variable and leading to visually beautiful pictures and fractals.
An historical account of the evolution of ideas toward the modern definitions of topological dimen-
sion can be found in Crilly with Johnson (1999). Caratheodory (1914) [15] introduced the methods of
defining measures using sets covers and arrived at the so-calledp-dimensional Hausdorff measure for in-
teger p. Hausdorff (1918) extended these methods for arbitrary positivep and developed the Hausdorff
dimension. The latter was analyzed and applied extensively by Besicovitch and his collaborators (1929 -
1937). A generalization of the Hausdorff dimension using Caratheodory measures and dimensions was
developed in Pesin (1997) [99] with applications to dynamical systems. The ideas on Minkowski con-
tent were extended by Bouligand (1928) to non-integer dimensions and more general shapes of covering
sets. The usual definition of box counting dimension was given by Pontrjagin and Schnirelman (1932)
[102]. KolmogorovandTihomirov(1959)definedtheentropydimension. Thesimilaritydimensionwas
introducedbyMandelbrot. Forageneraldiscussiononthe useofHölder-Lipschitzexponentsfortheap-
proximate estimation of fractal dimension see [74]. This technique is used extensively for approximately
estimating the box dimension of FBMs, Weierstrass functions and similar functions obeying power laws
[112]. For a theoretical analysis see [31].
All the fractal dimensions discussed in this chapter are related only to the geometry of a set and its
metric aspects. For fractals that are limit sets of nonlinear dynamical systems, there are also other types
of dimensions that depend on the probability mass of parts of the set; we have briefly mentioned some
of these generalized dimensions in Sec.5.9 on multifractals. Detailed analyses and applications of such
dimensionscanbefoundinGrassberger[ 43]andHentschelandProcaccia[ 50],aswellasintheliterature
related to chaotic systems; e.g. see more references and surveys in Peitgen, Jürgens and Saupe (1992,
2004) and in Alligood, Sauer and Yorke (1996).
Iterated function systems have been pioneered by Hutchinson (1981), Barnsley and his collaborators
(1986-1993), with applications to fractal image modeling and fractal interpolation. In Barnsley (1988)
more general FIFs are also discussed using hidden variables. Applications of the IFS theory to image
codinghavebeendevelopedbyBarnsleyandthiscolleagues[ 6,7],Jaquin(1992)andLundheim(1992);
see also the discussion on fractal image compression by Fisher in [92, Appendix A].
FBMsappearinKolmogorov(1940)[ 64]. TheyweredefinedusingstochasticintegralsbyMandelbrot
and Van Ness (1968), who studied many of their statistical and fractal properties. Voss (1988) popular-
ized their use in computer graphics. A rigorous study of the fractal dimensions of FBMs is done in [31].
AdifferentperspectivefordefiningFBMsbasedontheirself-similarityandsecond-orderstatisticscanbe
found in studies on self-similar processes, where FBMs are viewed as special cases ofα-stable processes;
concise treatments can be found in [29]. A nth-order generalization of the classical (first-order) FBMs
and FGNs has been proposed in [97] by extending their parameterH to lie in the interval(n − 1, n).
For the synthesis of FBMs, in addition to the methods discussed in Sec.5.5.4, there are also alternative
methods but they have not been widely explored. These include an improved Fourier synthesis [58],
linear recursive filtering [14], and wavelets [36],[115]. Extensions of 2D FBMs w.r.t. their analysis and
synthesis can be found in [59] and [100].
In 1872 Weierstrass published his famous function∑k=0 ak cos(bkπt) with 0 < a < 1 , b an odd

<!-- PDF_PAGE: 352 -->
### Σελίδα 352

350 FRACTALS: ROUGH SHAPES, TEXTURES, AND FRACTIONAL NOISES
integer, andab > 1 + 3π/2 , and he proved that it is continuous but nowhere differentiable. Its mathe-
maticalpropertieshavebeenstudiedbyHardy(1916)[ 47]. Mandelbrotobservedthatthefunctiondoes
not have a smallest scale but does have a largest scale. Thus, he proposed the extension (5.7) that has no
scale by including sines of frequenciesγk for all integerk, positive and negative. The properties of this
modified Weierstrass function have been studied in [9].
A topic in fractals that is not covered in this chapter is the theory of Julia sets and the Mandelbrot
set. Both are related to the complex dynamics on the plane generated by the simple iterationzn+1 =
(zn)2 + c, n = 0, 1, 2, ..., withz0, c ∈ C. For each complex numberc, we consider theescape setEc of
initialpoints zo whosegeneratedorbitdivergestoinfinity,i.e. |zn| → ∞ as n → ∞. Thecorresponding
Julia set Jc = ∂E c is the boundary of the escape set. The Mandelbrot setM is defined as the set of
complex numbersc such that the corresponding Julia setJc is connected. Thus,M creates a taxonomy
of all Julia sets. An equivalent definition that facilitates its numerical computation is
M = {c ∈ C ∶ c → c 2 + c → ⋯ remains bounded}
Its visualization on the complex plane creates stunning pictures at multiple scales. Both the Julia sets and
the Mandelbrot set are popular and rich sources of fractals characterized by great beauty and complexity.
For nice examples, see [92, 93, 94].
Fractals have found numerous applications in numerous areas related to computer vision, data science
and machine learning. Indicative examples include the following: FBMs as stochastic models in image
processing [100]; FBMs in computer vision for texture analysis and synthesis [59], [96]; FIFs in surface
interpolation [6, 7], [119]; fractals in speech processing and recognition [21], [63], [81], [101]; fractals
inmusicprocessingandrecognition[ 113],[120];multifractalsinoceanographicsatelliteimagery[ 118],
speech production analysis [61], and complex networks [117]; fractals in neural networks and machine
learning [27], [3], [60], [108]. More references can be found in the aforementioned books and the arti-
cles mentioned in this chapter.

CHAPTER 6
DEEP
LEARNING FOR COMPUTER VISION
APPLICATIONS
Pe
tros Koutras, George Retsinas, Petros Maragos
School of ECE, National Technical University of Athens
Summary: The resurgence of neural networks has been driven by the continuous advance-
mentofhardwarecomputationalcapabilitiesandtheavailabilityofextensivetrainingdatasets,
notably highlighted by ImageNet [138]. This resurgence has paved the way for the creation
of novel algorithms tailored to solve computer vision challenges, all rooted in deep learning
principles. Within this chapter, we will present a comprehensive overview of deep learn-
ing techniques and architectures, with a focus on their applications in computer vision. The
foundational concepts of deep neural networks are outlined, with special attention given
to Convolutional Neural Networks designed for visual tasks. Over time, these networks
haveevolvedintointricateandefficientarchitectures,initiallyconceptualizedtoaddressthe
fundamental task of object classification. Finally, we will investigate how these modern ar-
chitectures have been adapted to various computer vision objectives, considering selected
representative vision problems such as object detection, image segmentation, and action
recognition.
Prerequisite Knowledge: Introductory course on calculus, linear algebra, computer vision,
and machine learning.
6.1 Introduction
The history of neural networks spans over eight decades, and their evolution can be roughly outlined by
several notable breakthroughs, each marking significant advancements in our understanding of network
behavior. Among these breakthroughs are the development of the perceptron model in the 1950s, the
popularization of backpropagation in the 1980s, and the resurgence driven by deep learning techniques

358 DEEP LEARNING FOR COMPUTER VISION APPLICATIONS
in the 2010s. Notably, the pioneering LeNet ([92], 1998) laid the foundation for Convolutional Neural
Networks (CNNs), while AlexNet ([138], 2012) demonstrated the potential of deep architectures in
computervision. TheintroductionofResNet([ 60],2016)furtherrevolutionizedneuralnetworktraining
by mitigating vanishing gradient problems and enabling the training of unprecedentedly deep networks.
More recently, remarkable progress has been made in the broad category of attention-oriented trans-
former architectures [166]. Transformers, a neural architecture based on attention mechanisms, have
rapidlybecomethego-toapproachfornaturallanguageprocessing,settingnewbenchmarksintaskssuch
as machine translation and language understanding. Moreover, the attractive traits of transformers and
their notable performance led to their use being extended beyond language tasks, with them becoming a
prominent solution for computer vision tasks [36] and especially joint vision-language tasks [128].
Simultaneously, the field of neural networks has witnessed the emergence of groundbreaking develop-
ments in generative models, exemplified by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [51] and further
flourished by the introduction of diffusion models [65], have revolutionized the ability to create highly
realistic and diverse synthetic data, transforming applications in image synthesis, style transfer, and data
augmentation.
We will go through this evolution, while providing a brief summary of the most important advances
that led to the current most widely-used vision systems in use today. Emphasis will be placed on the
motivation and the functionality of modern deep learning components and neural network architectures
which have successfully addressed challenging computer vision tasks (e.g. image segmentation or action
recognition).
The impact of neural networks on modern computer vision applications, and in general to all machine
learning applications, is vast: the number of deep-learning publications has skyrocketed, while industries
haveinvestedindeeplearningtechnologiesandincorporatedthemintotheirproducts(e.g. facialrecogni-
tion in phones, autonomous driving). Moreover, hardware industry and specifically GPU-oriented tech-
nologies, themeansofefficientneuralnetworkimplementation, flourishedwiththeadventofneuralnet-
works. The mutual goal of developing more advanced neural networks has been a driving force behind
recent developments in the fields of design and implementation, where enormous architectures made up
of billions of parameters have been successfully developed [11]. As an indication of the enormous im-
pactofneuralnetworks,thepioneersofdeeplearning,YoshuaBengio,GeoffreyHintonandYannLeCun,
received the 2018 Turing award.
The focus of this chapter is the introduction of vision-oriented deep learning concepts and does not
substitute an in-depth analysis of neural networks and their optimization, as can be found in [160, 8].
6.1.1 The Early Days of Neural Networks
Theconceptofneuralnetworkswasinitiallyintroducedin1943byMcCullochandPitts. TheMcCulloch-
Pitts neuron, also known as a linear threshold gate, is comprised of a linear transformation followed by a
stepactivationfunction. Buildinguponthis,theperceptronwasproposedbyRosenblattin1958,enhanc-
ing the McCulloch-Pitts Neuron by introducing trainable weights and an associated training algorithm
for binary classification. To address the classification of non-linearly separable classes, the notion of ex-
tending the neuron concept led to the stacking of multiple neurons, forming a multi-layer feed-forward
network. This approach was notably applied to solve the XOR problem. Within these networks, layers
between input and output were referred to ashidden layers, introducing an intermediate processing stage.
Theperceptronandanexampleofamulti-layernetworkaredepictedatFigs. 6.1(a)and(b),respectively.
In the 1990s, Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), characterized by an input layer, multiple hidden lay-
ers (though not “deep”), and an output layer, became the prevailing neural network architecture. This
architectural trend was supported by the establishment of the backpropagation algorithm as the preva-
lent optimization scheme and the adoption of assisting regularization techniques. Consequently, MLPs

gained widespread popularity across diverse applications, including tasks like handwritten digit recog-
nition, speech recognition, and financial forecasting. However, the emergence of Support Vector Ma-

when neural networks resurged.

6.1.2 The Appeal of Neural Networks
First and foremost, one should understand the appeal of using neural networks. Broadly speaking, neural
networks are simply a way to define a functionf that maps the inputx to an outputy. This functionf,
fullydefinedbythearchitectureofthenetworkanditsweights,approximatestheunderlyingfunctionthat
models the pattern recognition problem at hand.
The major advantages of using such functions, formulated as neural networks, are briefly summarized
below:
• The Expressive Power of Neural Networks: In theory, neural networks are very expressive func-
tions,abletoapproximateanycontinuousfunctionforinputswithinaspecificrange. Thisconcept
is referred to as theUniversal Approximation Theorem[67] and has been explored and validated for
both arbitrary-width (how many neurons are used in a layer) and arbitrary-depth networks (how
many layers are stacked) [112].
• Computational Requirements: Neural networks are comprised of computationally cheap sub-
components with matrix multiplication being the core operator of the majority of such compo-
nents. Modern GPUs are optimized for executing these matrix/matrix and matrix/vector multi-
plications effectively, providing the ideal hardware implementation for neural networks.
• Robust Optimization: Training f effectively can be accomplished using first-order gradient de-
scent algorithms, as elaborated upon in Section6.1.5, even when dealing with extensive datasets
on a large scale.
6.1.3 Learning Spatial and Temporal Correlations with Neural Networks
Since the formulation of multi-layer feed forward networks, major progress has been made towards com-
plexstructuresofneurons,leadingtoseveralnotablevariations. Typicalmulti-layerfeedforwardnetworks
assumeinputsoffixed-sizedfeaturevectors. However,asreal-worlddataoftenexhibitintricatespatialand

<!-- PDF_PAGE: 362 -->
### Σελίδα 362

360 DEEP LEARNING FOR COMPUTER VISION APPLICATIONS
temporal relationships, the evolution of neural network architectures has naturally extended to accom-
modate these complexities. This expansion has given rise to the utilization of spatial and temporal neural
networks, which are uniquely equipped to capture the nuances of data that are distributed across dimen-
sions and sequences. More specifically, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) emerged as one of the
most notable examples for encoding spatial arrangements, while Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)
stand out as a prime example of a network capable of capturing dynamic information. These specialized
architectures have unlocked new avenues for tackling tasks that involve spatial arrangements, such as im-
age analysis and computer vision, as well as the dynamic temporal patterns seen in sequential data, such
as with audio, video, and time-series information.
6.1.3.1 Convolutional Neural Networks
An important aspect of neural networks which contributed to their resurgence was the introduction of
Convolution Neural Networks, which can effectively handle images. Problems relating to images had al-
ways been challenging, since spatial context had to be captured. Traditionally, spatial filtering was per-
formed by convolution with a handcrafted kernel, designed to capture specific patterns (e.g. edges).
Convolutional networks introduced trainable filters which can generate discriminative feature maps, op-
timizedwithrespecttothetaskathand. Thisapproachrevolutionizedthecomputervisiondomain,push-
ing aside suboptimal handcrafted features. CNNs are mostly comprised of stacked convolutional layers,
which perform the convolution operation:Y = X ∗ W, whereX and Y are the input and output 3D ten-
sors, respectively, whileW is the 4D weight tensor. Specifically,X ∈ R Cin×H×W and Y ∈ R Cout×H×W
are essentially feature maps of several dimensions, whereH × W are the spatial dimensions. The weight

6.1.4 Architecture Dictionary
At the heart of NNs lies a simple idea: alternate between linear transformations and non-linearities to
build complex functions. The expressive power of neural networks originates from these non-linearities
and the fact that we can build deep neural networks by stacking multiple blocks consisting of a linear
transformation and a non-linear activation1. In order to understand the existing architectures, or develop
a new one, we should be familiar with the “building materials”. In what follows, we will list the most
important and widely-used layers which comprise the majority of existing architectures.
6.1.4.1 Linear Transformations
The linear transformation can be one of the following:
1Applying sequentially linear filters without the intervening non-linearities can be expressed as a single linear filter.

Activationfunctions, typicallydenotedas σ(x), providetheneedednon-linearityafteralineartransform

• Hyperbolictangent (tanh): Thehyperbolictangentfunctionisdefinedas σ(x) = (e x−e−x)/(ex+
e−x). Its range is(−1, 1). The tanh function was widely used in early feed-forward neural net-

• Sigmoid: The sigmoid or logistic activation function is defined asσ(x) = 1/(1 + e −x), with
range (0, 1). Due to its range, it is usually used as an output function, when we have to predict a
probability-based value (e.g., binary classification or logistic regression). In the past, it was used as
an activation function in NNs, as an alternative to the most widely-used tanh function.

• Dropout: One possible problem of training a neural network is overfitting, i.e., learning exclusively
thetrainingdatasetwithouttheabilitytogeneralize. Thiswasaddressedbydataaugmentationand
the introduction of random noise into the network. A form of such noise is the random zeroing
of channels, dubbed “dropout” [150]. Dropout essentially assists the creation of multiple “paths”
of information through different channels and avoids correlating a neuron/channel with a specific
input sample, thus enhancing generalization.
• Upsample: A multitude of vision tasks demand predictions at pixel-level granularity (e.g., image
segmentation) or even sub-pixel precision (e.g., super-resolution). Yet, the standard process of
CNNs involves downsampling the feature map to accommodate an increasing number of features.

Finally, we should note that every task-related differentiable function can be used as a building block
for NNs, e.g. an interpolation function implementing affine transformations over images [75].
6.1.5 Optimization
We have already defined, architecture-wise, a variety of neural networks, but the main question remains:
how do we train such networks?Every NN realizes a nonlinear parametric function̂ y = fθ(x), whereθ is
the set of all the weights comprising the network. Training such a function, with respect to the weights of
the model, requires the following steps:
• Provide a training set of input samplesxi and output targetsyi.
• Define a loss functionL( ̂ yi, yi), which quantifies the proximity of the prediction ̂ yi to the re-
quested targetyi. The loss function is task-dependent and its minimization corresponds to having
perfect predictions, i.e. ̂ yi = y i. The overall loss function, denoted asJ, to be optimized is the
summation of the per-target losses, namely:J (θ) = ∑ i L(fθ(xi), yi).
• Selectanoptimizingalgorithmtoperform θ⋆ = argminθJ (θ). Duetothecomplexityoftheunder-
lyingfunction, thereisno analytic solution for the aforementionedoptimizingscheme. Therefore,
iterative gradient-based algorithms are employed in order to gradually minimize the overall loss
(e.g., gradient descent).

6.1.5.1 Loss Function
The selection of the loss function is critical for the effectiveness of the trained model. The formulation of
the lossfunction depends on the task athand and, thus, a vast variety of lossfunctions canbe considered.
Two main properties should be kept in mind:
• The loss function should reflect the task’s goal, e.g. Mean Squared Error (MSE) for regression or
CrossEntropy(CE)forclassification. Lossescouldbecomplexandconsistofmultipletermswhen
constraints are formulated as losses or a multi-task problem is considered.
• The function should be differentiable since a gradient-based optimization scheme is considered.
6.1.5.2 Backpropagation
The main problem with training neural networks is their complex structure of stacked layers. Computing
the gradient of each parameter with respect to the loss function relies on a simple yet powerful concept:
the chain rule. Iterative gradient-based optimizations schemes can be summarized by the following two
steps: 1) Compute Gradients and 2) Update Weights. These two steps are performed iteratively until
convergence is guaranteed3. Upon convergence the gradient would be close to zero, which translates to
detectinganoptima. Nonetheless,thisoptimizationschemecannotguaranteethattheoptima,discovered
by the iterative algorithm, can be applied globally.
Compute Gradients:Whentrainingdeeparchitectures,consistingofmanystackedlayers,thegradient
computation at each layer is not straightforward. The solution is to perform the gradients computation
layer-wise,startingfromthelossfunctionandmovingbackwardstowardstheinputlayer,hencetheback-
propagation term of this approach. Let’s consider the example of an intermediate fully-connected layer
describedby y = σ( wT x),where xisthe k-dimensionalinput, yisthesingledimensionaloutput, wisthe
layer’s weights andσ() is a non-linear activation. Bias is omitted and output is one-dimensional for sim-
plifying the analysis, but their extensions are straightforward. Given the gradient at the outputθJ /θy,
we want to compute the gradientsθJ /θw and θJ /θx in order to update the weights and propagate the
gradient error to previous layers, respectively. The first one, using the chain rule, can be expressed as:

Update Weights: “Vanilla” gradient descent computes the gradient score of the objective function
with respect to the parametersθ of the entire training dataset and uses the following update rule:θ ←
θ − η ⋅ ∇θJ (θ). Thehyper-parameter η controlstheconvergencerate. Smallvaluesmayleadtoslowcon-
vergence, while large values lead to overshooting and divergence. The above formulation is impractical,
since calculating the gradients over the entire dataset can introduce significant computational overhead.
To address this problem, the classical Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) optimization algorithm was
used. SGD performs a parameter update for each training sample. An entire iteration of every dataset
sample is referred to as anepoch. The pairs of inputs/targets are fed to the SGD in a different sequence at
each epoch (hence the Stochastic term in SGD). In practice, the mini-batch alternative of SGD is used,
where the gradients are computed over batches of samples. Additionally, SGD is usually accompanied by

a momentum strategy, where a “history” of previous gradients is used in order to avoid steep differences
in the gradient direction by the current batch. This way, extreme oscillation as well as the risk of getting
stuck in a local minimum are reduced. Note that both the learning rate and the momentum should be
empirically set by the user.
A widely adopted alternative to the SGD optimization algorithm is the Adaptive Moment Estimation,
known as “Adam”. Adam, introduced by Kingma and Ba in their work [82], is an optimization method
thatdynamicallycomputesindividualizedlearningratesforeachparameter,yieldingsuccessfuloutcomes
across a diverse spectrum of models and tasks. In its essence, Adam maintains an exponentially decaying
average of past gradients, akin to the concept of momentum. While momentum can be envisioned as a
ball rolling down a slope, Adam’s behavior can be likened to that of a heavy ball with friction, exhibiting
a preference for flat minima within the error surface. Notably, Adam’s formulation imparts robustness in
scenarios involving sparse targets, enhancing its performance and versatility.
6.1.6 Scheduling Tactics
The efficiency of gradient descent is further supported by recent theoretical developments concerning its
stability, as well as its convergence speed in the context of deep learning [58, 3]. As stated before, the
core rationale is to choose an improvement over current parameters along the path defined by the loss
(sub-)gradient. Other gradient-based methods such as Adam [82] or momentum-based methods [124,
126, 7, 120] share the logic of first choosing and then moving along a “good” search direction, which can
be understood as an improvement over the direction defined by the gradient.
The efficiency of such a training process greatly depends on the learning rateη, alternatively called the
step-size, which controls how “fast” the optimizer is moving along the gradient direction. In fact, for all
these gradient-based algorithms, the choice of the learning rate is arguably perhaps the weakest point of
these methods, and their performance is known to rely heavily on its choice. An inappropriate choice
of learning rate can easily lead to a suboptimal local minimum, leading in practice to inferior network
efficiency. An intuitive example of the importance of the learning rate can be seen in Fig.6.8, where a
small learning rate leads to slow convergence, while a large one could “skip” the optimum.

to more complex ones [147, 111], which typically require their behavior to be set by the user via a set
of hyper-parameters. The main idea of such scheduling tactics is simple: use a decreasing learning rate
to balance between “fast” convergence and accurate detection of the optimum. Such tactics may also in-
clude restarts or increasing the learning rate in a cyclic fashion in order to avoid cases when the optimizer

6.2 Computer Vision Architectures: An Evolution Overview
Having defined the fundamentals of neural networks, we will focus solely on computer vision tasks and
specifically neural network architectures that paved the path for recent advances in deep learning. In the
following, we will describe indicative families of such neural networks with emphasis placed on the mo-
tivation behind each “forward step”, while analyzing any novelties we introduce and their relative impor-
tance. Forthemajorityoftheforthcomingarchitectures,wewillassumeasimpleobjectclassificationtask.
A different vision task may require a different “head” for the network, as we will see in the next section,
but the network backbone remains the same, since it can be seen as a vision feature extractor.
6.2.1 Early Deep CNN Architectures
The first attempts at applying neural networks in computer vision tasks were focused on training “deep”
simplefeed-forwardnetworks,whichincludedconvolutionallayers. Severalconclusionsweredrawnfrom
theseattempts,bothfortrainingtacticsandnetworkcomponents,leadingtoapproaches/choicesthatare
considered now common practice. In what follows, we will briefly mention such notable contributions.
6.2.1.1 Architectural Structure
First, let us describe the architectural structure of typical CNNs that several architectures share. One can
distinguish three main parts:
• Convolutional Backboneconsisting of a cascade of convolutional layers, using a progressing num-
berofchannels,intervenedbynon-linearactivations,andpossiblybatch-normalizationanddropout
layers. Thedownsamplingoperationsofmax/average-poolingisperformedbetweenblocksofcon-
volutional layers to reduce spatial dimensionality. This backbone results in a 3D feature map (for
typical 2D vision problems) of sizeHr × Wr × C, where C is the number of output channels,
or equivalently the dimensionality of the feature space, andHr, Wr are the down-scaled spatial
dimensions, whereasH × W is the size of the input imageI.
• Flattening Operationis a necessary step to transform the arbitrary-sized feature map, that is gen-
erated in the output of the convolutional backbone, into a fixed-sized feature vector. This step is
typically performed by pooling operations (e.g. average- or max-pooling) with a predefined num-
ber of spatial segments (one can perform this pooling operation over the whole feature map). In
earlier architectures, this step was performed by a concatenation operation. Note that an adaptive
pooling operation, in the sense of having a fixed target grid of pooling regions rather than a strided
pooling approach, can be applied to arbitrary-sized feature maps.
• Fully Connected Head transforms the fixed-size feature vector of the previous step into the net-
work’s output. The output’s dimensionality depends on the task (e.g. for classification tasks, the
output has as many dimensions as the classes and is typically followed by a softmax activation). It
consistsof consecutive fully connected layers (in the simplest case, a single fully connected layer is
required), intervened by non-linearities.

6.2.1.2 LeNet
The LeNet architecture was one of the earliest convolutional architectures developed for image recogni-
tion tasks. It was introduced by Yann LeCun, Léon Bottou, Yoshua Bengio, and Patrick Haffner in 1998
andpavedthewayformodernCNNs. Itwasoriginallyappliedtohandwrittendigitsrecognition(MNIST
dataset [92]), a category of the Optical Character Recognition (OCR) field.
LeNet consisted of seven layers, including three sets of convolutional and pooling layers, followed by
twofullyconnectedlayersandanoutputlayer. TheinitiallayersinLeNetcontainconvolutionalfiltersthat
extract features from the input image. LeNet used a small kernel size (5x5) for the convolutions, which
helped capture local features and patterns. After each set of convolutional layers, LeNet employs average
pooling layers to downsample the feature maps. Pooling helps reduce the spatial dimensions of the rep-
resentationwhileretainingimportantinformation. Thefeaturemapsfromtheconvolutionalandpooling
layers are flattened and passed through two fully connected layers that provide the final predictions. The
overviewofLeNetarchitecturecanbefoundinFig. 6.3. Itshouldbenotedthatthesamehigh-levelratio-
nale for the motivation/functionality of the different layers lies behind every contemporary CNN-based
architecture, even though LeNet was not as deep as the modern CNNs. However, one notable differ-
enceistheusageofsigmoidnon-linearities, averycommonchoiceformulti-layerperceptrons, insteadof
ReLU that is the typical choice for modern CNNs.
6.2.1.3 Alexnet
The first notable resurgence of neural networks occurred with the Alexnet architecture, which shined by
outperformingeverycompetitorintheverydemandingobjectclassificationchallengeofImageNetLarge
ScaleVisualRecognitionChallenge(ILSVRC)[ 138]. Thissuccessofneuralnetworkshighlightedtheca-
pabilitiesofNNs,whenalargeamountofdataisavailableandshiftedthemajorityoftheresearchdirection
towards data-centric, deep learning based approaches. One more notable aspect of Alexnet was the use
of convolutional layers in an era when handcrafted features were dominating the literature.
Architecture-wise,AlexNetconsistsofeightlayers,includingfiveconvolutionallayersfollowedbythree
fullyconnectedlayers. Theuseofmultipleconvolutionallayershelpscapturehierarchicalrepresentations
of input images: the first layers learn low-level features such as edges and textures, while subsequent con-
volutional layers learn more complex and abstract features.
Moreover,AlexNetemploysmax-poolingtoreducethespatialdimensionsofintermediatefeaturemaps,
while Local Renspose Normalization (LRN)layers are used to enhance the generalization by applying a
spatial regularization step to the extracted feature maps of each layer, which takes into account the spatial
neighborhoods of these feature maps. These normalization layers have a similar motivation to the more
recent batch mormalization alternative.
Specifically, the first convolutional layer has a11 × 11spatial kernel and a stride of 4 to downscale the
initial image. The second convolutional layer has a5 × 5spatial kernel, while the remaining 3 layers have
3 × 3 kernels. Apart from the first strided convolution, downsampling is performed with a max-pooling
operation after the second and the third convolutional layer. The architecture is summarized in Fig.6.9.
More importantly, AlexNet popularized the use of Rectified Linear Units (ReLU) as the activation
function, as well as the use of dropout as a way to reduce overfitting. The ReLU choice is nowadays con-
sidered the default non-linear activation function for deep neural networks, since DNNs with ReLUs are
trained several times faster when compared with their tanh counterparts [138]. Similarly, using dropout,
namely randomly setting to zero the output of each hidden neuron with a predefined probability, has
become the norm for designing neural networks since it promotes the robustness of the network by be-
cominglessreliantonanyspecificneurons. Theuseofdropout,firstintroducedbyHintonetal.[ 64],was
further solidified in 2015 [150].

6.2.1.4 VGG
FollowingthesuccessofAlexnet,onewouldnaturallypursuedeeperarchitecturestoharnesstheirexpres-
sive power. Simonyan and Zisserman introduced a family of very deep convolutional networks, dubbed
VGG since it was developed by the Visual Geometry Group at the University of Oxford, designed for
large-scale image classification tasks [146].
VGG architecture consists of a convolution backbone with multiple stacked convolutional layers with
a 3 × 3 receptive field. Each such layer is followed by an ReLU non-linearity. Contrary to AlexNet,
VGGdoesnotuseLocalResponseNormalization(LRN)layerssincenoexperimentalgainwasreported.
Downsampling is performed with spatial max-pooling between group of convolutions. Specifically, five
max-pooling operations of kernel2 × 2 and stride2 are used. This convolutional backbone is followed
by three Fully-Connected (FC) layers, where the flattened output of the last convolutional layer is ap-
plied. Specifically, the first two FC layers have 4096 channels each, the third has as many channels as the
classes of (e.g., 1000 for ILSVRC classification) and is followed by a softmax operation. VGG is in fact a
family of architectures, where variations of different depth are considered, such as VGG-16 or VGG-19.
The number in the name denotes the overall depth of the network, including the fully connected layers,
but only the number of the convolutional layers changes in these variations. The VGG-16 architecture is
summarized in Fig.6.10.
Overall, the VGG architecture is characterized by its simplicity and uniformity, where multiple convo-
lutionallayerswiththeminimumreceptivefield(i.e., 3×3)arestackedsequentially. ContrarytoAlexNet
which consists of only five convolutional layers with various receptive fields, the gradual filtering of VGG
builds more intricate feature representations, simulating a high overall receptive field due to the network
depth. Moreover, the3 × 3 layers require fewer parameters, leading to more compact networks. Despite
its simplicity, its success in ILSVRC underscored the importance of deeper networks, while popularizing
the use of minimum receptive field building blocks. Notably, the VGG architectures paved the way for
a series of studies on transfer learning. More precisely, researchers leveraged pre-trained models on the
ILSVRC dataset, directing their efforts toward refining the VGG architecture for novel and demanding
tasks that had limited available data.

6.2.2 Training with Residuals: the ResNet Case
A significant limitation of the aforementioned feed-forward networks, where layers are stacked sequen-
tially, pertains to the optimization process. In particular, when training these deep models, the gradient
that propagates through them tends to diminish, resulting in a challenge known as the vanishing gradient
problem. This diminishing gradient issue leads to suboptimal model convergence, making it challeng-
ing for the network to effectively learn and harness the representation power of deeper models and thus
causing a decreased overall performance.
ResNets, short for Residual Networks, are a family of deep neural network architecture designed to
address the challenges of training very deep networks [60]. The key concept of Residual Networks was
the reformulation of typical layers as residual functions with reference to the layer input (see Fig.6.11).
Learningthroughthisinnovativeapproachovercamethevanishinggradientproblemandhadaprofound
impact on the field of deep learning, leading the way towards deeper architectures.
ResNet architecture falls into the typical architectural structure of a convolutional backbone, followed
by a fully connected head, as described in Section6.2.1.1. However, typical convolutional layers are re-
placed by residual blocks, the critical building blocks of ResNets. A residual block consists of multiple
convolutional layers, and its output is added to the original input, creating a “skip connection”, forming
a residual function. This process is depicted in Fig.6.11. Skip connections are in fact shortcuts that al-
low gradients to flow more easily through the network during backpropagation, assisting the training of
deeper networks and updating their weight more effectively.
Figure 6.11: Residual Block: an identity function acts as a skip connection and creates a shortcut on the
layer’s output. From [60].

The basic residual block comprises two3 × 3 convolutions, separated with a non-linearity, as shown

Overall, ResNet architectures are notably deeper than their predecessors, with ResNet-18, ResNet-50
and ResNet-101 being common variants, where the number in their name denotes the total number of
layers.
Furthermore, ResNet architectures included and showcased the effectiveness of batch normalization
layers [74]. Batch normalization was introduced the same year as ResNets (2015) and it plays a crucial
role in stabilizing and accelerating the training of deep neural networks by normalizing intermediate acti-
vations at each layer during training.
In essence, ResNets stand out as one of the most influential architectural innovations, serving as a pi-
oneering model that significantly advanced the construction and training of deeper neural networks with
increased efficacy. Indeed, its profound influence within the realm of deep learning remains evident, as
ResNetarchitecturespersistasthestandardbackbonefornumerouscomputervisiontasks,includingbut
not limited to image classification, object detection, and segmentation.
6.2.3 Compact Networks
Thecontinuousprogressofdeeplearningledtocomplexarchitecturesofmultiplebuildingblocks, which
(typically) share a common trait: increased computational requirements. A characteristic example is the
family of modern language models, that generate human-like responses, with several billion parameters
(e.g., GPT3 [11] has 175 billion parameters!).
Though training extremely large networks can help us better understand deep learning and unlock its
potential, it is impractical; one can use such models in a cluster of servers when everyday applications
are typically performed on embedded devices. Thus, creating compact networks has been an active re-
search direction. In this chapter, we will focus on compact architectures that serve as backbones to sev-
eraldeeplearningsolutions,whencomputationalrequirementsarelimited(e.g.,real-timeapplicationson
embedded devices). Many architectural improvements have been devised to improve the cost efficiency
of CNNs either by replacing a costly convolutional layer with a set of cheaper convolutions (e.g. point-

(e.g. multi-branched convolutional blocks) instead of sequentially convolving into a single flow [157, 60,
90, 71, 135]. Here, we will focus on two widely-used compact architectures, namely MobliNet [69] and
EfficientNet [159].
A common practise is thereduce-transform-expandstrategy, where reduction and re-expansion of a fea-
ture map is performed with pointwise convolutions while the transformation is a regular convolution on
the reduced feature maps. Grouped convolutions are used as an alternative, or even complement, to the
reduce-transform-expandstrategy, since they drastically reduce the required parameters by applying filters
only on distinct groups of the input tensor [73, 179, 188]. A special case of grouped convolutions is
channel-wiseconvolutionsinwhichthenumberofgroupsisequaltothenumberofchannels,commonly

depth scaling, which changes the number of layers; or even resolution scaling, which controls the size of
theintermediatefeaturemaps,theauthorsof [ 159]proposedanewscalingmethod: ”compoundscaling”,
which uniformly scales all dimensions to depth, width, and resolution. The different scaling options are
visualized in Fig.6.13. Relying on this compound scaling idea and a neural architecture search approach,
anewfamily of modelswascreated, dubbedEfficientNets, alsobasedinMobileNetbuildingblocks [ 68].
These models achieved state-of-the-art performance with fewer parameters, since appropriate scaling as-
sists better, more balanced distribution of weights per block.

Other approaches towards compressing DNNs include:network pruning, pioneered in the early de-
velopment of neural networks [93], seeks to induce sparsity in a neural network by removing unimpor-
tant connections. Different approaches vary in terms of the granularity at which they prune the network
and the criteria used to determine connection importance. Researchers have proposed pruning individ-
ual weights [54, 2, 117, 16, 134, 47] or channels/filters [177, 61, 195, 189, 94, 34, 62, 118]. Quantiza-
tion, which dates back to the 1990s [46], uses low-precision fixed-point formats instead of high-precision
floating-point formats to represent the weights and/or activations of a model in order to reduce its mem-
ory footprint both in terms of storage and working memory during inference [29, 129, 72, 12]. Other
approaches includetensor decompositionmethods [31,32,101] which derive low-rank approximations of
the weight tensors. Delving into such approaches is outside the scope of this book; details can be found
into the respective references.

6.2.4 Recurrent Architectures
Recurrent architectures, as seen in Section6.1.3.2, are ideal for data of a sequential nature. Such cases
include tasks such natural language processing, audio recognition, or video processing and recognition.
To this end, recurrent architectures are not often met in image processing literature, but have been cru-
cial for tasks of temporal dependency, such as action recognition. Of course, there are cases of recurrent
architectures in image processing, such as handwritten text recognition - a task with an innate sequential
formulation, or by breaking an image into patches and assuming these patches to form a sequence.
As we have seen in Section6.1.3.2, vanilla RNNs have the following recurrent formulation:ht =
σ(Whht−1 + Wxxt + b), where {xt} is the input sequence,{ht} the hidden state,σ() a non-linear
activation function andWh, Wx shared weight matrices and a biasb. Apart from vanilla RNNs (see Sec-
tion 6.1.3.2), there exist several variants. Specifically, we will distinguish the following cases:
• Multi-layerRNN: Inpractice,RNNshaveseverallayers,wheretheoutputsequenceofthefirstRNN
is fed as an input sequence to the second RNN, etc. Each layer is described by the aforementioned
recurrent relation and uses a pair of shared parameter tensors(Wx
k, Wh
k), where k is the layer’s
identifier. This way we can build deeper RNN architectures.
• Bi-directional RNN:A major issue with typical RNNs is that they learn representations from pre-
vious time steps: rt = f r(rt−1, xt) (here r is the hidden state in a right-oriented formulation).
However, it may be helpful to incorporate information from “future” time steps:lt−1 = f l(lt, xt).
Bi-directional RNNs combine both information flows, rightwardrt and leftward lt, at each time
step t: ht = f c(rt, lt). Including future time steps to extract intermediate representationsht as-
sists the network to better understand the context and eliminate ambiguity.
• Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) Networks:RNNs are notori-
ously difficult to train due to the vanishing gradient issue, where the quality of information dete-
riorates as it flows backward through the system and, in the case of RNNs, through multiple time
steps. To address this issue, LSTM networks have been proposed [27], where this information
flow is controlled via so-called gates. A gated recurrent unit has an update gate, which decides on
how much of information from the hidden state should be let through, and a reset gate, which de-
cides on how much of information from the hidden state should be discarded. GRUs have been
proposedascost-efficientalternativestoLSTMs[ 66]andbothnetworksaimtoretaininformation
from distant time steps, without vanishing it through time. LSTMs and GRUs are preferred in the
majority of recent sequence-related applications.
6.2.5 From Attention Modules to Transformers
Stemmingfromtheattempttoformulatethenaturallyoccurringsub-problemofre-directingtheattention
ofthenetworktoareasofinterests,attentionmodulesandthefamilyofnetworksthatrelyonthem,namely
transformers, have been a focal point in state-of-the-art approaches.
Originally,attentionmoduleshavebeendevelopedfortext-to-texttranslationtasks,aproblemofnatu-
ral language processing. Specifically, an attention mechanism [6] was originally introduced to the widely
used sequence-to-sequence approaches [156], which focus on explicitly correlating a word in the trans-
lated output to a word (or set of words) in the original input. These sequence-to-sequence approaches
consisted of an RNN-based encoder-decoder scheme.
Theattentionmechanismmetnotablesuccess,leadingtoamore“extreme”viewpoint,whereattention
modulesreplacedeverymoduleofthearchitecture(bothencoderanddecoder),asproposedinthesemi-
nalwork“AttentionIsAllYouNeed”[ 166]. Thisattention-onlyarchitectureisreferredtoasa Transformer
and its design can be seen in Fig.6.14. The core component of a Transformer is theMulti-Head Attention
module, which consists of multiple basic attention modules, as shown in Fig.6.15.

First, letusdescribethefunctionalityoftheseattentionmodules. Theirinputisasetofvectors: Query
(Q), Key (K), and Value (V). The high-level concept behind the attention mechanism is to identify Keys
within a set of data that are most similar to a given Query and then use these similarities to determine
how to weight the associated Values. This process allows the attention mechanism to focus on specific
parts of the data that are most relevant to the Query. In more detail, Query-Key similarity is calculated
by a scaled dot product and then passed through a softmax function, which scales the scores to produce
attention weights. These weights represent the importance of each Key with respect to the Query and are
finallyusedtocomputeaweightedsumovertheValues,whichistheoutputoftheattentionmodule. This
whole process can be formalized as:
Attention(Q, K, V) = Softmax( QK⊺
√dk
)V, (6.7)
where Q, K, V are the Query, Key, Value matrices anddk is the shared feature dimensionality of these
matrices( K, Varebothofsize S×d k,where S isthesourcesequencelength,and Qisofsize L×dk,where
L is the target sequence length). The scaling1/√dk has been proven effective in practice to counter the
case of extremely large gradients through the softmax where dot products grow large in magnitude for
high dimensional data [166].
Multi-headAttentionisthenconstructedwithmultiplesuchattentionmodulesinparallel. Specifically,
the initial set of Query, Key, and Value is augmented by multiple different sets of Query, Key, and Value
projections through a set of linear transformations, each one with different parameters. This allows the
attentionmechanismtocapturedifferentpatternsandrelationshipsintheinputdataandfocusondifferent
parts of the input. The outputs from multiple heads are typically concatenated or linearly combined to
producethefinalattentionoutput. Itshouldbenoted, thatmulti-headattentionistypicallyusedasaself-
attention mechanism, simply transforming the input sequence into a transformed context-aware output
sequence. In such a case, Query, Key, and Value are given as linear projections of the input.
Overall, the Transformer architecture employs several stackedMulti-Head Attention modules to build
both the encoder and the decoder. Multi-Head Attention is used in a self-attention manner, except for
a cross-attention step between the encoder and the decoder, where the Query and the Key are attained
fromtheoutputoftheencoderandcontroltheinformationflowinthedecoder. Aftereachself-attention,
the resulting representation passes through a feedforward network of a fully connected layer. Residual
Connections and Layer Normalization are applied over the Multi-Head Attention and the feedforward
modules. Since Transformers don’t inherently possess information about the order or position of ele-
ments in the input, one important extra step is the use of positional encodings. Positional encodings are
typically generated using sinusoidal functions, ensuring that the input tokens at different positions have
uniqueencodings. Thepositionalencodingsarethenaddedtotheinputembeddings,toexplicitlyencode
tokens’ position and order. This whole process is visualized in Fig.6.14.
A transformer’s ability to model complex relationships and dependencies across input sequences has
proven to be extremely effective and addresses the issue of recurrent networks that struggle to capture
long-term dependencies. Their notable success led to their extension to vision tasks, where Vision Trans-
formers (ViTs)[36]haveemergedas apowerfulalternativetotraditionalconvolutionalneuralnetworks.
Vision Transformers segment the input image into patches and treat them as the input sequence, effec-
tively using the same architectural structure. The spatial structure is retained through 2D positional en-
codings. The outline of a ViT architecture is depicted in Fig.6.16. Just as with NLP Transformers, Vision
Transformers have excelled in a range of challenging visual tasks, ushering in a surge of research and in-
novation focused on transformer-based architectures for vision tasks (e.g., [106]). Furthermore, as they
tend to have greater computational complexity compared to convolutional neural networks, researchers
have introduced several hybrid architectures, where self-attention layers alternate with convolutional lay-
ers, aiming to harness the strengths of both paradigms (e.g., [113]).

6.3 Selected Computer Vision Tasks
6.3.1 Two- and Single-stage Systems for Object Detection
Within the field of Deep Learning, the sub-discipline called “object detection” involves processes such
as identifying the objects through a picture, video or a web-camera feed. The challenge of detecting all
objects existing in an image is a counterpart of action localization in videos and thus several object detec-
tion techniques are used in action localization architectures. Object detection methods are used almost
everywhere these days. The use cases are endless such as tracking objects, video surveillance, pedestrian
detectionetc. Anobjectdetectionmodelistrainedtodetectthepresenceandlocationofmultipleclasses
of objects. For example, a model might be trained with images that contain various pieces of fruit, along
with a label that specifies the class of fruit they represent (e.g. an apple, a banana, or a strawberry), and
data specifying where each object appears in the image. There are several main approaches for object
detection using CNNs [79, 103] that can be organized into two main categories:
1. Two-stagedetectionframeworks: Theseapproachestypicallyinvolveapre-processingsteptogen-
erate object proposals, followed by a separate CNN to classify the proposed regions.
2. One-stage detection frameworks: These approaches, also known as region proposal-free frame-
works, use a single CNN to directly predict object locations and class probabilities in an image.
These approaches are widely used and have achieved good performance on benchmark datasets such as
MS COCO [100] and PASCAL VOC [40]. However, new and improved object detection methods are
constantlybeingdevelopedandtherearemanyotherobjectdetectionmodelsavailable,eachwithitsown
strengths and weaknesses.

378 DEEP LEARNING FOR COMPUTER VISION APPLICATIONS
6.3.1.1 Region-based (Two Stage) Frameworks
R-CNN
R-CNN(RegionswithCNN)isatwo-stageobjectdetectionapproachthatwasproposedin2014[ 50].
It is one of the first successful methods for object detection using CNNs. The main idea behind R-CNN,
as shown in Fig.6.17, is to use a pre-processing step to generate object proposals, which are then passed
through a CNN for classification and bounding box regression.
Figure 6.17: Object detection using the R-CNN system. From [50].
The first stage of R-CNN is to generate object proposals. This is typically done using a selective search
algorithm [164], which generates a set of regions that are likely to contain an object. These regions are
called region proposals and are usually generated by using a sliding window approach to scan the entire
image at multiple scales and aspect ratios. A selective search algorithm is used to extract regions that are
morelikelytocontainanobjectbycombiningseverallow-levelcuessuchascolor,texture,andshape. The
regions are then passed through a CNN for feature extraction.
The second stage of R-CNN is to classify the object proposals and refine their bounding boxes. This is
done by training a separate linear SVM for each class and using the CNN features to train it. A classifier
is then used to predict the class and the bounding box coordinates of the object. The bounding box coor-
dinates are refined by training a linear regressor which takes the CNN features as inputs and predicts the
bounding box coordinates. It uses the offset values predicted by the regressor to adjust the bounding box
of a region proposal when its prediction of an object presence is correct, but its exact position within the
proposal is partially cut off.
OneofthemainlimitationsofR-CNNisthatitiscomputationallyexpensive,asitrequiresrunningthe
CNNforeachobjectproposal. Thismeansthatforanimagewiththousandsofregionproposals,theCNN
needs to be run thousands of times. Moreover, the selective search algorithm is a fixed algorithm, since
nolearningishappeningatthatstage. Thiscouldaffectthequalityofthecandidateregionproposals. This
was later addressed in its successors such as Fast R-CNN and Faster R-CNN which improved the speed
of the detection pipeline.
Despite this, R-CNN was an important step in the development of object detection, it was able to
achieve state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets such as PASCAL VOC and MS COCO.
R-CNN, and its variants, have been widely used in many applications, such as image search, self-driving
cars, and surveillance systems. It introduced an important concept of region proposal and this idea has
been used in many subsequent object detection methods.
Fast R-CNN
Fast R-CNN is an object detection algorithm that was proposed in [49] to overcome the limitations
of R-CNN. The main advantage of Fast R-CNN over R-CNN is its speed and efficiency, with a typical

<!-- PDF_PAGE: 381 -->

From [49].
improvement of three times faster in training and 10 times faster in testing.
The algorithm works by, first, feeding the input image into a CNN to generate a convolutional feature
map. The feature map is then processed by a Region of Interest (RoI) pooling layer to identify region
proposals and reshape them into a fixed-length feature for each proposal. The RoI feature is fed into a
sequence of fully connected layers that predict the class of the proposed region and the offset values for
the bounding box (see Fig.6.18).
The training process in Fast R-CNN is streamlined compared to R-CNN, as it simultaneously learns
thesoftmaxclassifierandboundingboxregression,whereasR-CNNtrainsthesesubpartsseparately. The
RoIpoolinglayerhelpstoapproximatewarpingattheimagelevel, bywarpingatthefeaturelevel. This, in
turn, helps to improve the efficiency of the algorithm.
It is important to note that while the use of region proposals can improve the detection quality, it can
also slow down the algorithm during testing. Thus, region proposals can become a bottleneck in the Fast
R-CNN algorithm, affecting its performance. Overall, Fast R-CNN is a fast and efficient object detection
algorithmthathasimproveduponthelimitationsofR-CNN.Itssingletrainingprocess,RoIpoolinglayer,
and shared computation of convolutions across region proposals make it a better alternative for object
detection tasks.
Faster R-CNN
FasterR-CNN[ 133]isatwo-stageobjectdetectionalgorithmthatusesadeepCNNforfeatureextrac-
tion and object detection. Unlike its predecessor, R-CNN, which uses the selective search algorithm to
identifyregionproposals,FasterR-CNNgeneratestheregionproposalsusingaRegionProposalNetwork
(RPN) within the network itself (Fig.6.19a).
At the first stage of Faster R-CNN, as shown in Fig.6.19b, the RPN generates region proposals by
mapping some predefined boxes (also known as anchors) of different scales and aspect ratios at each
convolutional feature map location to a lower dimensional vector. The reference boxes are then fed into
two fully connected sibling layers for object category classification and box regression. The RPN shares
the convolutional features with the Fast R-CNN, which helps to make the region proposal computation
efficient.
Atthesecondstage,FastR-CNNperformsregionclassificationbyusingtheregionproposalsgenerated
by the RPN. The convolutional feature map is reshaped using a RoI pooling layer, which is then used to
classify the image within the proposed region and predict the offset values for the bounding boxes.
The Faster R-CNN framework is designed to be fast and accurate, and it has been shown to perform
wellinobjectdetectiontasks. Forexample,usingtheVGG-16backbonemodel[ 146]forFasterR-CNN,

Region-based Fully Convolutional Network (R-FCN)
TheR-FCN(Region-basedFullyConvolutionalNetwork)[ 30]wasintroducedasamodificationofthe
Faster R-CNN architecture, with the goal of making it more efficient and accurate. The main difference
between Faster R-CNN and R-FCN is the design of the RoI (Region of Interest) sub-network. In Faster
R-CNN, the RoI sub-network cannot be shared, but in R-FCN, all the convolutional layers are used to
construct a shared RoI sub-network (Fig.6.20).
However, this original design of using all convolutional layers in the RoI sub-network was found to

be less accurate due to the deeper convolutional layers being more sensitive to category semantics and
less sensitive to translation, which is important for object detection. To improve the accuracy of object
detection, R-FCN introduced the concept of position-sensitive score maps. This involves using a bank
of specialized convolutional layers as the FCN output and adding a position-sensitive RoI pooling layer.
Thisallowsthenetworktocapturethespatialrelationshipsbetweenobjectsandtheirpartsandtoproduce
more accurate representations of the localization of objects.
The R-FCN architecture with ResNet101 was shown to have comparable accuracy to Faster R-CNN,
often with faster running times. The fully convolutional nature of the region-wise sub-network and the
introduction of position-sensitive score maps are key factors in the improved performance of the R-FCN
model.
Mask R-CNN
Mask R-CNN [59] is an instance segmentation model that is built on top of the Faster R-CNN archi-
tecture. Instancesegmentationinvolvesbothobjectdetectionandsemanticsegmentation,i.e. identifying
the objects in an image and also segmenting their individual pixels.
In Mask R-CNN, the first stage of the pipeline is the same as Faster R-CNN, where a RPN is used to
generate potential regions of interest. At the second stage, in addition to predicting the class and box
offset, a binary mask is also predicted for each RoI (see Fig.6.21). The mask branch is implemented as a
FCN on top of the feature map generated by the CNN.
To ensure that the masks align correctly with the image, Mask R-CNN uses a RoI-Align layer instead
of the RoI-Pooling layer used in Faster R-CNN. Using the RoI-Pooling layer the wrapping is digitalized
because the cell boundaries of the target feature map are forced to realign with the boundary of the input
featuremapsasshowninFig. 6.22a(thetopleftdiagram). Asaresult,eachtargetcellsmaynotbethesame
size (Fig.6.22c). On the other hand, the RoIAlign layer preserves the pixel-level spatial correspondence
betweentheimageandthemask. RoI-Alignavoidsdigitalizingtheboundaryofthecells, asshowninFig.
6.22b, and manages to make every target cell the same size, according to Fig.6.22d. In order to calculate
the values of feature maps, RoI-Align uses bi-linear interpolation as shown in Fig.6.23. This means that
we can calculate the value of the desired bins according to their neighbors’.
With a ResNeXt101-FPN backbone network, Mask R-CNN has achieved state-of-the-art results for
the COCO instance segmentation and object detection tasks. It is simple to train and generalizes well,
and adds only a small overhead to Faster R-CNN, with a frame rate of five FPS.

6.3.1.2 One Stage Frameworks
Single-stage models for object detection employ a unified pipeline that directly predicts class probabil-
ities and bounding box offsets from an entire image in a single feed-forward pass through a CNN. They
differfromregion-basedpipelinestrategies,whichinvolvemultiplestepsincludingRPNandfeaturepool-
ing, making them computationally expensive. Single-stage models simplify the detection process and are
more suitable for mobile or wearable devices with limited storage and computational capabilities. The
first methods [158, 141] for designing single-stage approaches for object detection opened the path to
the later and popular frameworks of YOLO [130] and SSD [104].
You Only Look Once (YOLO)
YOLO is a family of object detectors that operate by treating object detection as a regression problem.
It predicts detections directly from image pixels to bounding boxes and class probabilities, eliminating
the region proposal generation stage. YOLO uses features from the entire image to make predictions,
meaning that it implicitly encodes contextual information about object classes and is less likely to predict
false positives in the background. On the other hand, it can make more localization errors than other
methodsduetoitscoarsegriddivisionandlimitationsinlocalizingsmallobjects. YOLOdividesanimage
intoan S ×S gridandpredicts C classprobabilities, Bboundingboxlocations,andconfidencescoresfor
each grid cell (see Fig.6.24). The region proposal generation step is completely dropped, making YOLO
faster by design.
The YOLOv2 [131] version introduced improvements such as replacing the custom GoogLeNet net-
work with the simpler DarkNet19, using batch normalization, removing the fully connected layers, and
using good anchor boxes learned via K-means and multi-scale training. YOLO9000 extends YOLOv2 by
jointly optimizing on ImageNet classification and COCO detection datasets, allowing weakly supervised
detection of over 9000 object categories. YOLOv3 [132] is another updated version of YOLO that uti-
lizesanewarchitecturewithalargerneuralnetworkandthusitisabletodetectobjectsofdifferentshapes
and sizes. These improvements have led to YOLOv3 achieving state-of-the-art performance on various

The YOLO detector models described above (as well as their more recent updates) offers a fast and
effective solution for object detection tasks, but on the other hand they have difficulties on localizing
small objects or objects in dense scenes due to the limitations of the grid cell approach.
Single Shot MultiBox Detector (SSD)
The Single Shot MultiBox Detector (SSD) is a single-stage object detector that has become one of the
most popular object detection models for real-time applications. The core idea behind SSD, unlike the
two-stage approaches, is to use a single CNN to predict both the class probabilities and the bounding
boxes for objects in an image.
ThearchitectureofSSDconsistsofaFCN,wheretheearlylayersofthenetworkarebasedontheVGG
architecture. There are also several additional auxiliary convolutional layers that are used to extract fea-
turesfromtheinputimageatmultiplescales(Fig. 6.25). InSSD,anchorboxesareusedatdifferentaspect
ratios todetect objectsof differentscales. The anchorboxes areused topredict the classprobabilities and
bounding for objects of a certain size. This allows SSD to perform detection at multiple scales, making
it more effective at detecting small objects. Like most object detection algorithms, SSD applies a Non-
Maximum Suppression (NMS) step to remove overlapping bounding boxes and keep only the one with
the highest class score.
OneofthemajoradvantagesofSSDoverotherobjectdetectionalgorithmsisthegoodbalancebetween
speed and accuracy. As shown in Fig.6.25, it is faster than YOLO [130] and has a mAP (mean Average
Precision) comparable to Faster R-CNN [133]. However, compared to two-stage models, SSD may have
a lower accuracy for detecting small and occluded objects.
Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN) and RetinaNet
FPN (Feature Pyramid Network) [98] is a deep learning architecture commonly used in many com-
puter vision tasks such as object detection and segmentation. In traditional object detection networks,
the feature maps from the last few layers of the network are used for object detection. However, these
feature maps may not provide enough information to detect objects of various sizes effectively. More-
over, SSD only uses upper layers for detection, which results in poor performance for small objects. FPN

More recently, [14] proposed an object detection approach based on the transformer architecture,
called“DEtectionTRansformer”orDETR,whichhasachievedbreakthroughresultsinmanynaturallan-
guage processing tasks. In DETR a single transformer network is employed to directly predict object

TheDETRmodelistrainedend-to-endontheCOCOdataset,whereitoutperformsthepreviousstate-
of-the-art object detection approaches. The DETR model is a groundbreaking and promising approach
for object detection in images, utilizing the transformer architecture, which has great potential for future
progress in this field.
6.3.2 Image segmentation
Image segmentation is the partition of an image into meaningful regions that correspond to real-world
objects or structures and it is a central step in a wide range of applications, including medical image anal-
ysis, autonomous vehicles, video surveillance, and augmented reality. For example, in the construction
of an autonomous driving automobile, the driving system would first collect photos of the environment
and would then be able to understand the scene quickly and segment or recognize pedestrians and other
objects. Over the years, many image segmentation algorithms have been developed, but deep learning
models have proven to be a game-changer in the field, yielding significant performance improvements
[116].
Image segmentation can be formulated as either a semantic segmentation or an instance segmentation
problem. Insemantic segmentationthe taskis toassign a semantic labelto eachpixelin an image, suchthat
pixels with the samelabelbelong tothe sameobjector backgroundregion. The goalof semantic segmen-
tation is to provide a detailed and dense pixel-level annotation of the objects present in an image. On the
other hand,instance segmentationis an extension of semantic segmentation which aims to separate each
