6.3.2.1 Fully Convolutional Netwroks (FCN)
The Fully Convolutional Network (FCN), that was first proposed by [110] is a pioneer work in the field
of deep learning for semantic image segmentation. The main innovation introduced by the FCN was to
modify existing CNN architectures, like VGG16 and GoogLeNet, to handle non-fixed sized inputs and
outputsbyreplacingallfully-connectedlayerswithfully-convolutionallayers. Thesemodelsareconverted
from typical classifiers to dense FCN by replacing fully connected layers with1 × 1 convolutional layers
and thustrainthemtotakean imageof anysizeandproduce a segmentation mapof the same sizeinstead
of classification scores (Fig.6.29a).
While FCN may be fine-tuned to deal with the semantic segmentation problem and produce dense
masks,theiroutputistoocoarse. The 32pixelstrideatthefinalpredictionlayerrestrictsthescaleofthede-
tailintheoutput. Inordertoaddressthisissue,semanticinformationfromthehigh-level(low-resolution)
layers is upsampled and fused with appearance information from the low-level (high-resolution) layers
through the use of skip connections (Fig.6.29b). These connections allow the model to combine feature
mapsfromthefinallayersofthemodelwithfeaturemapsfromearlierlayers,leadingtomoreaccurateand
detailed segmentations.
The introduction of FCN is considered a game-changer as it shows that CNNs can be trained for se-
mantic segmentation via an all-in-one approach on images of different sizes. However, the conventional
FCN model has used only local information for semantic segmentation and does not effectively incor-
porate global or scene-level semantic context. To overcome these limitations, the ParseNet [105] model
enhances the FCN model by adding global context, expressed as the normalized average of a layer’s fea-
tures over the entire image. This context vector is unpooled to produce new feature maps and then fused
with the original features at each location. In addition, in order to incorporate more scene-level semantic
context, various approaches employ probabilistic graphical models such as Conditional Random Fields
(CRFs) and Markov Random Fields (MRFs) into the FCN architectures [19, 191, 108].
6.3.2.2 Encoder-Decoder Models
One very popular category of deep-learning models for image segmentation is based on the convolu-
tional encoder-decoder architecture. Typically, a pre-trained network for image classification, like VGG
or ResNet, is utilized as the encoder. The decoder part is responsible for semantically projecting the en-
coder’s discriminative features onto the pixel space in order to get a dense classification of each pixel in
the input image.
DeconvNet
The work of [123] introduced a semantic segmentation architecture based on deconvolution, also
known as transposed convolution. As we can see in Fig.6.30, the proposed architecture consists of two
main parts: a convolutional encoder and a deconvolutional decoder. The encoder uses convolutional lay-
ers adapted from the VGG16 network in order to convert the input image to a multidimensional feature
representation. The output of the encoder is then fed into the deconvolutional network which generates
object segmentation probabilities from the convolution network’s feature. The deconvolutional network
contains multiple series of unpooling and deconvolution layers while its structure is a mirrored version
of the encoder network. Deconvolution networks, in contrast to convolution networks which lower the
size of feature activations by feed-forwarding, effectively increase the size of feature activations through
a mix of unpooling and deconvolution operations. The unpooling operator is done using max-pooling
indices, which are stored in the convolutional network during the convolution process. Deconvolution,
which is essentially the reverse operation of a convolutional layer, uses a set of learned filters to perform
the upsampling and provide output feature maps at a higher spatial resolution.

U-Net based architectures
U-Netisanotherencoder-decoderarchitectureoriginallyproposedforthetaskofimagesegmentation

the feature maps by downsampling. The expanding (upsampling) path, uses a series of upsampling and
convolutional layers in order to reduce the number of feature maps and also increase their spatial resolu-
tion. U-Net does not use pooling indices for the upsampling, but instead transfers the feature maps from
the contracting path to the corresponding decoders and concatenates them with the upsampled maps of

6.3.2.3 Multi-scale Methods
The Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) [98] explored the traditional image processing technique of an-
alyzing images at multiple scales in the context of deep learning architectures. As we have seen in the
previoussection,itwasinitiallyproposedforobjectdetectionbuthasalsobeenappliedtoimagesegmen-
tation. Similarly to the U-Net like architectures it has a bottom-up pathway and a top-down pathway that
are connected through lateral connections, which merge low and high-resolution features to produce the
final output. For image segmentation, the FPN uses two Multi-layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to generate the
masks.
The Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPN) [190] is another multi-scale network that was devel-
oped to better learn the global context representation of a scene. PSPN uses a pyramid pooling module
to aggregate context information on top of the features maps extracted using a CNN backbone. The fea-

6.3.2.5 Semantic segmentation with Transformers
After the Vision Transformers (ViT) [36] transformer networks have emerged as a powerful tool for var-
ious computer vision tasks, including semantic segmentation [183, 178, 151, 24]. The Segmenter model
[151]isbuiltontopofaViTbackboneandintroducesamaskdecoderinspiredbyDETR[ 14]. Asshown
in Fig.6.36, the image patches are first turned into a sequence of embeddings and then processed by a
transformer encoder. Then the decoder takes the encoder output and class embeddings as inputs and
uses a mask transformer to generate segmentation masks.
6.3.3 Action recognition
Action recognition, which involves automatically identifying and classifying human actions in videos, is
an important area of research in computer vision many potential applications, such as in video under-
standing, sports analysis, robotics, and human-computer interaction. Prior to 2015, the most common
approach in the field of action recognition was the use of hand-crafted features and the their classifica-
tion using classicalmachine learning algorithms. The most widely employedmethod in this category was
the improved Dense Trajectories (iDT) [169, 170] that achieved state-of-the-art results on video clas-
sification, but had heavy computational requirements making them challenging to deploy in real-world
applications. Recently, also following the general trends in computer vision, deep learning architectures

6.3.3.1 Early methods based on 2D CNNs
One of the first attempts to use CNN networks for human action recognition was made by the work of
[80] that explored several approaches for aggregating information along the temporal dimension. This
methodemploysasingle2DCNNpretrainedmodelforeachframeinavideo,independently. Afterwards,
several ways to fuse temporal information from consecutive frames are explored, such as late fusion, early
fusion, and slow fusion (see Fig6.37a). However, its transfer learning performance on standard evalua-
tion datasets, such as UCF101 [149], was notably inferior to hand-crafted iDT features, raised questions
about the ability of CNNs to surpass traditional hand-crafted methods in video action recognition. This
observationalsoemphasizedtheimportanceofcapturingmotioninformationeffectivelyinvideounder-
standing tasks and also understand why CNNs did not outperform traditional techniques, as they often
did in other computer vision tasks.
To address the limitations of early CNN-based approaches, many approaches started exploring the
integrationofLongShort-TermMemory(LSTM)networksintoactionrecognitionsystems[ 35,184]. In
theseLSTM-basedapproaches,thefeaturemapsgeneratedbyCNNswerefedintodeepLSTMnetworks
(Fig.6.37b). The goal was to aggregate frame-level CNN features into video-level predictions, leveraging
the temporal information captured by LSTMs. However, despite the introduction of LSTMs, there was
no clear improvement compared to the hand-crafted features baselines.
6.3.3.2 Two-Stream Networks
In a parallel attempt, Simonyan and Zisserman [145], inspired by the physical separation of video into
its spatial and temporal parts, proposed a two-stream convolutional neural network, consisting of a pre-
trained spatial network that models information about the appearance of people or objects and is applied
to static frames, and a temporal network that describes the motion within the video and is applied to
volumes of optical flow around the frame of interest (see Figure6.38).
The temporal network operates on a stack of10 optical flow images, which capture the pixel-wise
local motion between consecutive frames, both horizontally and vertically, and are scaled to the range
[0, 255] to match the intensity of the RGB images. Afterwards, the convolutional layers of the tempo-

6.3.3.3 Methods based on 3D convolutions
One alternative approach for action recognition and generally video understanding is to view the video
as a three-dimensional tensor with two spatial dimensions and one temporal dimension and employ 3D
Convolutional Neural Networks (3D-CNNs) to capture the temporal information. The first attempt to
use 3D-CNN for human action recognition was made by [77], which proposed the extension of existing
2DCNNsinto3Dspacebyapplying3Dconvolutionstoconsecutiveframesofavideoinordertoextract
spatiotemporal features. Later on, in [161], deeper 3D-CNNs based on the VGG16 architecture were
trained on large-scale datasets of human actions [80], which they were named C3D.
The use of 3D convolutions in the convolutional layers of CNNs allows for the extraction of features
from both the spatial and temporal dimensions. 3D convolution is achieved by convolving a 3D ker-
nel with the cube formed by stacking multiple consecutive frames of the video (see Fig6.40). This way,
the feature maps obtained at each convolutional layer are connected to multiple consecutive frames or
feature maps from the previous layers, thus modeling motion information. More specifically, the value

The I3D variant, which was introduced in [15], emerged as a significant development in deep learning
for video action recognition. I3D takes a video clip, typically consisting of16 or 32 frames, as input and
passes it through inflated 3D-CNNs. In this process, the filters and pooling kernels of popular and very
deep image classification architectures are expanded into 3D. Moreover, I3D inflates the 2D weights that
are trained on ImageNet to their 3D counterparts, avoiding the need to train 3D-CNNs from scratch.
Thisallowsfortheseamlessextractionofspatio-temporalfeaturesfromvideoswhileleveragingsuccessful
ImageNet architecture designs and parameters.
With pre-training on the large-scale Kinetics400 dataset [81], the I3D achieved impressive results:
95.6% accuracy on UCF101 and74.8% on HMDB51, outperforming the usage of hand-crafted iDT
by a significant margin and establishing Kinetics400 as the new baseline dataset for action recognition
evaluations. ThefinalI3Dmodel(Fig 6.42a)includesacombinationoftheI3Darchitectureandthetwo-
stream framework, which can achieve even better performance with98.0% accuracy on UCF101 and

There are also many efforts to improve the efficiency of 3D-CNNs in terms of speed and handling of
long-term dependencies. The SlowFast network [43] comprises two pathways: a slow one and a fast one.
The slow pathway operates at low frame rates to capture detailed semantic information, while the fast
pathway works at a high temporal resolution to capture fast movements and is lightweight by using only
a fraction of feature channels. V4D [187] extended 3D CNNs to video-level 4D CNNs by adding the
number of action units as the 4th dimension. This enables the modeling of long-range spatio-temporal
representations within videos that are not captured by the limited receptive fields of 3D kernels. X3D
[42] offers a family of efficient video networks to meet various complexity requirements. It does so by
expanding2Dimageclassificationarchitecturealongmultipledimensions: temporalduration,framerate,
spatial resolution, network width, bottleneck, and network depth.

of their feature channels along the temporal dimension, thereby facilitating the exchange of information
among adjacent frames.
6.3.3.4 Action Recognition with Transformers
Like other computer vision tasks, the spatio-temporal extensions of the transformer networks have also
proventobehighlyeffectiveatactionrecognitionandvideounderstandingproblemsingeneral. Theearly
workof[ 48]utilizesatransformer-stylearchitecturetoextractinformationfromthespatialandtemporal
surroundings of the person whose actions are being classified. TimeSformer [9] explores five distinct
variations of space-time attention mechanisms and proposes a factorized space-time attention approach
due to its balance between speed and accuracy. Meanwhile, ViViT [4] also investigates four factorized
configurations of spatial and temporal attention within the pretrained ViT model [36] (Fig.6.43). The
VideoSwinTransformer[ 107]extendstheSwinTransformer[ 106]architectureforvideounderstanding
and employs shifted windows and hierarchical feature maps to efficiently process video frames.

Summary: Manual gestures are intertwined with language and cognition, playing an im-
portant role in human communication. This has motivated the development of computer
vision algorithms that recognize gestures from visual data, usually acquired by color cam-
eras or depth sensors. The main goal is to design intuitive human-machine interfaces that
can be employed in various applications, including interaction with robots, touch-less driv-
ing, video gaming and virtual reality. Conceptually, gesture recognition is closely related
to action and sign language recognition, and many approaches that target these problems
sharealotincommon. Thischapterwillpresentacomprehensivereviewofthemostimpor-
tant approaches for visual gesture recognition from videos, focusing on dynamic gestures.
The content of the chapter covers methods from traditional machine learning that employ
handcrafted image features, as well as modern methods from deep learning that automati-
callyextractvisualgesturerepresentations. Boththeoreticalandpracticalconsiderationsare
highlightedwithspecialattentiongiventodatarelatedaspectsofgesturerecognitionsystem
design.
Prerequisite Knowledge: Introductory course on calculus, linear algebra, computer vision,
and machine learning.
7.1 Introduction
Human communication and interaction takes advantage of multiple sensory inputs. Among them hand
motionisgenerallyconsideredanintegralpartofcommunicationalongsidefacialexpressionsorlanguage,
as discussed later in this chapter. For instance, speakers pronounce words while executing hand gestures
thatmayhaveredundantorcomplementarynature,andevenblindspeakersgesturewhiletalkingtoblind

listeners [32]. It has even been proposed that both speech and gestures stem from a common initial unit
of thought and convey information about the underlying idea [56].
This human inclination towards gesturing has inspired the design of multi-modal human-machine in-
terfaces,wheregesturesaloneorincombinationwithspeechcanpotentiallyofferannaturalandintuitive
way of interacting with computers [71, 76]. Gestures can broadly be categorized into two classes:
• Static hand gestures (or hand shapes, hand postures, hand poses) are those in which the hand ap-
pearance does not change during the gesturing period. They can be discriminated based on the
relative position of the finger joints.
• Dynamic gestures, in which the hand position changes continuously with respect to time. Dy-
namic gestures generally have three temporally overlapping phases: preparation, nucleus, and re-
traction [26], of which the nucleus mainly conveys the intended message. The other phases are
typically similar for different gestures. Dynamic gestures are discriminated based on the hand tra-
jectories and orientations, relative position to the body and the hand appearance/posture.
Static gesture/hand-shape recognition is more closely related to image classification and hand pose esti-
mation in static images. In this chapter, we will explore the fundamental computer vision methods for
recognizingdynamic gesturesusing video input. In computer vision, dynamic gesture recognition is a spe-
cial case of the more broad problem ofaction recognition; in fact most gesture recognition methods in the
literature are adapted versions of action recognition methods. There are, however, some key differences
between the two problems:
• Background information is not informative in the case of gesture recognition, as is the case with
action recognition (e.g. a chair in the frame may hint towards a subset of actions, such as standing
up etc).
• The most discriminative body parts for gesture recognition are the arm and hand regions, which
may occupy a small portion of a video frame.
The most important application of automatic gesture recognition is the design of interactive human-
machine interfaces. There are numerous examples of such interfaces: communication with robots, com-
puters, phones, wearable devices using gestural commands, interactive video games, touchless driving,
etc. A closely related problem is sign language recognition. It is undoubtedly more complex, as gestures
areveryintricate,thevocabularyisalmostlimitlessandthelanguagefollowstherulesofsyntaxandgram-
mar. However, many developments in automatic sign language recognition are inspired by advances in
action and gesture recognition [43, 96].
Section 7.2 will provide evidence on the importance and role of manual gestures in our communica-
tion,whichhasmotivatedthedevelopmentofcomputervisionalgorithmsthataddressautomaticgesture
recognition from visual data. Many gesture recognition methods do not directly process RGB frames;
they, rather, extract higher-level information, such as the hand position or the body pose. These pre-
processing methods are briefly reviewed in Section7.3. Section 7.4 will present some of the first meth-
ods introduced for gesture recognition: Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Dynamic Time Warping
(DTW). They both consider gestures as temporal sequences of hand features. In the case of HMMs,
each gesture sequence is modeled as the output of a stochastic process and the problem amounts to find-
ing the process that most likely produced a given sequence. DTW compares each gesture sequence with
pre-defined gesture prototypes, by temporally aligning them using dynamic programming. The gesture
recognitionmethodspresentedinsection 7.5arebasedonspatio-temporalinterestpointdetection. These
approaches represent a video as a collection of salient spatio-temporal patches that characterize the per-
formed action. Appearance and motion features are extracted from these patches and their distribution
is encoded using Bag-of-Visual-Words or similar methods to produce a final video vector that is fed to a

7.2 Manual Gestures in Human Communication
In this section we will provide a brief survey on how gestures have been of great significance in human
communication. In particular, according to specific theories [3, 54, 93], they have supported the begin-
nings of language formation, after which gesture shapes and language can reinforce each other.
By gestures we mean visible actions involving shapes of manual and non-manual bodily motions and
postures; most of them are dynamic (i.e. time-varying for part of their duration) and use the hands.
Kendon [38] classifies human gestures in 1) Gesticulations, 2) speech-framed, 3) pantomimes, 4) em-
blems (quotable gestures), and 5) sign language. The above sequence has been calledKendon’s continuum
[55]. Asthenumericalindexofthegestureclassincreases,thedegreetowhichspeechshouldaccompany
a gesture decreases whereas the degree to which a gesture shows language-like properties increases.
The theory that gesture-based human communication evolved first whereas conventional languages
evolved later has had many supporters from the antiquity until it became more definite in the eighteenth
century; afterwards gesture and sign languages started being studied as natural languages. Wittgenstein
in his work [106] on the philosophy of language argued that “What we call meaning must be connected
with the primitive language of gestures”. In search of the origins of human communication, Tomasello
[93] has provided ample evidence about the critical importance of gestures, in particular of the pointing
and pantomiming types, for humans to develop i) social cognitive skills that create a common concep-
tual ground, including joint attention, shared experience and common cultural knowledge, and ii) so-
cial motives such as requesting, informing, helping and sharing with others. These developments of so-
cial cognition and motivation create ashared intentionality, as is called by some modern philosophers of
action, e.g. [83]. Quoting from [93], “pointing (deictic gestures) direct the attention of a recipient to
something in the immediate perceptual environment, whereas pantomiming (iconic gestures) direct the
imagination of a recipient to something that typically is not in the immediate perceptual environment
by simulating an action, relation, or object”. Interestingly, apes have also developed pointing (attention-
getters) and pantomiming (intention-movements) gestures for their communication. One big difference
between the gesture-based ape versus human communication is that for apes it serves individual inten-
tionality, whereas for humans it serves shared intentionality. This shared intentionality is at the heart of
the cooperative model for human communication[93].
Thus, according to the theory and evidence presented in [93], human social cognitive skills and social
motivationcreateacooperativepsychologicalinfrastructureofhumancommunicationbasedongestures,
which laid the foundations for the later development of conventional languages. By “conventional lan-
guage”wemeanasymboliccommunicativecode,whichassumessomepreexistingcodifiedformofcom-
munication like the gesture modality. Such a linguistic code is based on a non-linguistic infrastructure
of intentional understanding and common conceptual ground [93, 105]. From a computational view-
point, we may conjecture that, nowadays, if we are given a collection of gestures referring to a common
perceptual ground of objects, then by clustering and feature encodingwe could in theory map gestures to
some abstract language words which could be the cluster centroids. Of course, after their early develop-
ment, human conventional languages, mainly spoken languages, evolved into a very creative and versatile
form of communication which, despite its complexity, has fundamentally supported and propelled hu-

<!-- PDF_PAGE: 420 -->

418 GESTURE RECOGNITION
man civilization. In contrast to gestures, the vocal modality in nonhuman mammals remained inflexible
and has not created a language. Quoting from [93], “for all mammals, including nonhuman primates,vo-
cal displaysare mostly unlearned, genetically fixed, emotionally urgent, involuntary, inflexible responses
to evolutionarily important events that benefit the vocalizer. In stark contrast, a significant number of
nonhuman primategestures, especially those of great apes, are individually learned and flexibly produced
communicative acts, involving an understanding of important aspects of individual intentionality.”
Another supporter of the “gesture-first” conjecture is Arbib [3] who supports a theory that human
language evolved as a result of biological and cultural evolution starting from simple manual gestures we
share with apes, progressing to the imitation of manual skills and pantomime, and culminating to the
development of sign language and speech.
The potential role that gestures have in our communication from an evolutionary and physiological
perspective justifies the idea that intuitive human-machine interfaces need to consider gestures as part of
our interaction.
Inadditiontothegesture-firsttheorywhichadvocatesthathumanlanguagestartedasnon-spokenges-
tures and signs, there are also combined theories that advocate a fusion of the gesture and speech modal-
ity. This has inspired the design of multimodal approaches that process optical data depicting gestural
commands as well as acoustic data with the corresponding utterances [71, 76].
7.3 Gestures and Visual Shapes
Shapesaretraditionallyperceivedandunderstoodasobjectsofgeometry,two-dimensional(2D)orthree-
dimensional (3D). For a better understanding, perception attributes may be added to them, e.g. as in
Gestalt psychology. For automated shape recognition, the computer vision community further explores
broader appearance characteristics of shapes by viewing them (whenever possible) as gray intensity im-
ages that have both shape and texture. Thus, if 2D shapes are perceived from images, they obtain a third
dimension of brightness texture. Instead of brightness, we may also add color to a 2D shape. Temporal
dynamics are also important in recognizing moving shapes. Another way of adding a third dimension to
a 2D shape to be recognized as a projected silhouette of a 3D object is by using depth. For 3D shapes,
including brightness or time evolution will add a fourth dimension.
Thus, in addition to their 2D main projection or silhouette, shapes of world objects can have some
additional geometric attributes such as depth and region summary as exemplified by their skeleton axis
and its branch points, or evenoptical attributes, e.g. intensity, color, as well as motion (in case of moving
shapes) possibly represented by dynamics of the above attributes as time evolves. We shall call this aug-
mented shape information avisual shape, meaning that it contains attributes both from geometry (2D
or 3D) and optics (photometry and motion). A rich category of such visual shapes that include all the
aboveattributesandwillbethemainparadigmofthischapterare gestures. Bothfromahumanperception
andacomputerrepresentationperspective, gesturescompriseseveralinformationstreamswhichinclude
a main 2D shape information such as the projection of the handshapes and possibly the moving arms on
the image plane, color information, 3D shape, 3D motion, and by using appropriate sensors or computer
vision algorithms they can be supplemented with depth and skeleton information. This is illustrated in
Fig.7.1via an example showing a user performing the Italian gesture “basta” (“that’s enough!”). We sam-
pledthevideoofauserperformingthisgestureandselectednon-uniformlyfiveframestodepictthemost
importantstatesofthe“basta”gestureastimeevolves. WesupplementtheRGBframeswithskeletonand
depth information, as well as images of the right or both handshapes. In this example the RGB, depth
and skeleton data were provided by a Kinect sensor. The skeleton information of this sensor includes the
human skeleton axis and its branch points, such as the hands’ centers, elbows, shoulders, face, knees and
other critical points.

7.4 Older Methods: Hidden Markov Models and Dynamic Time Warping
7.4.1 Hidden Markov Models
Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are statistical tools that model sequential data and allow us to predict
a sequence of unknown (hidden) variables from a set of observed variables. They have numerous appli-
cations in different fields where temporal or sequential data analysis is required. This section serves as a
brief review of HMMs; an in-depth introduction can be found in [72].
In the context of HMMs, the observed data are assumed to be a time seriesO = (o 1, o2, ... oT ).
The HMM posits a set of discrete statesS = (s 1, s2, ... sN) that determines the observable data. The
hiddenstate stattimestep tgovernstheobservation otattimestep tbyselectingoneoutof N probability

while in the latter casebj(ot) is a continuous distribution, often a multivariate Gaussian:
bj(ot) = p(o t|S = j) = N(o t|μj, σj), (7.3)

2. Decoding: What is the sequence of hidden states, given our model, that best explains the given se-
quenceofobservations? Inotherwords,weseekthesequenceofhiddenstates S = (s 1, s2, ... sT )
with the highest probability of having a specific sequence of observationsO = (o 1, o2, ... oT ) as
its outcome, given our modelθ. This gives us valuable information about the underlying process
that produced our observations. For example, in speech recognition decoding can identify what
part of speech is each word in a sentence and in gesture recognition can help us analyze the differ-
ent phases of a dynamic gesture. The most widely used method of computing the optimal hidden
state sequence is a recursive algorithm, the so-called Viterbi algorithm.
3. Training: Given an observation sequenceO and a HMM, we can learn the best HMM parame-
ters θ = ( A, B, π). There is no analytical solution to this problem, so we have to approach it by
optimizing θ, such thatp(O|θ) is locally maximized. This is often accomplished using iterative
methods, such as the Baum-Welch (or equivalently Expectation Maximization) algorithm.
Features X = (x 1, x2, ... xT ) extracted from each framet = 1, 2, ... T in a given gesture clip corre-
spond to the observationsO = (o 1, o2, ... oT ) that an HMM emits. The most common features that
have been used for this task are:
• Handtrajectories[ 35]: Thesecanbe2Dor3Dhandcoordinatesnormalized,e.g.,bythemaximum
armspreadorthedistancebetweentheshoulders. Thecoordinatesofarelativelystablepointinthe
body (e.g. the face) should also be subtracted. Dynamic information can be encoded by comput-
ing the difference between the coordinates of each hand between two consecutive frames. These
features convey information about hand displacements during a sampling interval. The resulting
feature vector has dimension8 in the 2D case.
• Optical Flow: The histogram distribution of the magnitude and phase of the motion vector field
around the hand can be used to model hand movement [15]. The motion field represented by the
optical flow encodes motion information fingers, as well as global hand motion.
• FourierDescriptor[ 15]: ThecontourofthehandcanberepresentedbytheFourierseries c(n) =
a(n) + jb(n). Usually, the first coefficient is omitted and the second is used to normalize the rest,
resulting in a scale and rotation invariant descriptor. Thus the Fourier Descriptor is a vector with
elements:
S(n) = √[a(n)]2 + [b(n)]2
[a(1)]2 + [b(1)]2 , n = 2, 3 ... (7.9)
Assuming that the local variation of hand shape is smooth, higher order coefficients are not neces-
sary.
• Hand shape: This can be obtained by various methods, e.g. by measuring the variance of the con-
tourpointsfromthehandcentroid[ 73],thesurfaceandeccentricityofthehandblob[ 35]orother
shape descriptors.
Regardless of the choice of features, either continuous or discrete HMMs can be used. In the former
case,eachobservation ot isacontinuousvectoranditsdistributionistypicallymodeledbyasingleGaus-
sian or a Gaussian Mixture Model for each state. Ifot is discrete, an extra feature quantization step is
required. Each D-dimensional feature vector sequence is quantized into a finite symbol sequence for
HMMs, using a vector quantization algorithm, such as K-means. In this way, the feature space formed by
all D-dimensional training feature vectors is partitioned intoK clusters. Each cluster is represented by
a D-dimensional vector (the cluster’s centroid) and the set of all centroids forms theK-sized codebook.
Once the final codebook is obtained, it is used to quantize each training and testing feature vector into a

7.4.2 Dynamic Time Wrapping
Dynamic Time Wrapping (DTW) is an algorithm for measuring the dissimilarity between two temporal
sequencesofdifferentlength,originallyintroducedforautomaticspeechrecognition[ 62]. Itsuseforges-
turerecognitionfollowsatemplatematchingscheme[ 5,17]: eachgestureisrepresentedbyasequenceof
featurevectorsextractedfromagestureclip(e.g. relativehandposition,velocity). Oneormoretemplates
for each gesture category are constructed using training data, serving as gesture prototypes. An unknown
gesture is classified by comparing it to every gesture prototype. When we compare them, their difference
in duration should not influence their (dis)similarity metric. Intuitively, DTW addresses this problem by
warping the sequences in a nonlinear fashion to match each other.
Figure 7.5: Time alignment between two sequences of lengthTx = 30 and Ty = 35 using DTW (left).
Alignment can be seen as a path through a two-dimensional lattice structure (right).

p contains index pairs(i, j)that satisfy the following:
• The beginning and the end of the two series match:p(1) = (1, 1) and p(T ) = (T x, Ty).
• The alignment is monotonically increasing in bothi and j.
• All feature sequence indexes appear at least once.

the two feature sequences. A variety of local slope constraints can be applied on the warping function to
guarantee that excessive compression or expansion of the time scales is avoided. Some well-known sets
of constraints are the Rabiner-Myers (Figure 5 in [63]) and the Sakoe-Chiba (Table I in[79]) sets.
7.5 Recognition using Interest Points
The Bag-of-Visual-Words framework has received a lot of attention for various problems in the field of
imageandvideounderstanding, duetoitsrobustnessanddiscriminatepower. Bag-of-Wordswasinitially
introduced in the field of natural language processing and information retrieval [84, 103] to create text
embeddings. Its success inspired many researchers to repurpose it for various computer vision problems,
most notably image classification [25], object detection [90] and action recognition [67, 46], making it
one of the best performing approaches for visual classification problems.
The main idea is that a video can be described as a collection of local features, whose distribution is
used to discriminate between different video classes. The typical pipeline that is usually employed is the
following (see Fig.7.6):
• Interest points are extracted from the raw RGB or depth video.
• Appearance and motion features are computed in regions or spatio-temporal volumes around the
interest points.
• The distribution of all features in a video is encoded using a visual codebook.

<!-- PDF_PAGE: 428 -->
### Σελίδα 428

426 GESTURE RECOGNITION
• Encoded features are used as inputs to a classifier, such as a Support Vector Machine.
The training phase includes the construction of the visual codebook and classifier training. This pipeline
views the video as a whole, without focusing to specific regions in the video. This may be acceptable if
gesturesareperformedinastaticenvironmentwithlittleirrelevantmotion. However,inmorechallenging
environments, a pre-processing step may be necessary. For example, one can process only discriminative
spatial sub-regions of the image, such as the arms and the hands, use background subtraction methods or
use background models to ignore irrelevant movements.
7.5.1 Interest Points
Interest points are salient spatio-temporal points in a video with significant local variation of the pixel in-
tensity. They typically correspond to complex motion or abrupt changes and potentially characterize the
video in a unique way. Interest point detectors usually aim to balance between the need for: a) an ade-
quate number of interest points (maybe redundant) to deal well with irrelevant and possibly misleading
features generated by scene clutter and imperfect detection and b) a much sparser representation than
direct pixel representation. Various interest point detectors have been introduced in the past which differ
in the number of points they detect and their computational complexity.
Harris3D: This is a 3D extension of the famous Harris corner detector [45]. Following the same idea
asits2D counterpart, it detectspointswith largevariationsalongboththespatialandthetemporaldirec-
tions. These points are characterized by high information content. Given a videoI(x, y, t), the first step
is to calculate a3 × 3 structural tensor matrixM (x, y, t):
M (x, y, t; σ, τ ) = g(x, y, t ∣ sσ, sτ ) ∗ (∇L(x, y, t ∣ σ, τ )(∇L(x, y, t ∣ σ, τ ))T ),
where
g(x, y, t ∣ σ, τ ) = 1

σ and temporal scaleτ, and ∇L(x, y, t ∣ σ, τ ) are spatio-temporal gradients for these scales. Interest
points are obtained by maximizing a “cornerness” criterion:
H(x, y, t) = det(M (x, y, t)) − k ⋅trace3(M (x, y, t)). (7.10)
Hessian: Thisisalsoa3DextensionoftheHessianoperatororiginallyintroducedforblobdetection[ 104].
The determinant of the3 × 3 Hessian matrix that contains all second order partial derivatives serves as
a saliency measure and interest points are given by its local maxima. The Hessian detector eliminates the
need for scale selection and it can also be efficiently implemented using integral images.
Cuboids: Incontrasttothepreviousdetectors, theauthorsofCuboids[ 19]claimthatdirect3Dcoun-
terparts to commonly used 2D interest point detectors are inadequate. They propose to processes the
spatial and temporal dimensions differently, by introducing a 2D Gaussian smoothing kernel which is
applied only along the spatial dimensions and a quadrature pair of temporal Gabor filters:
hev(t ∣ τ , ω) = − cos(2πtω) exp(−t2/2τ 2) (7.11)
hod(t ∣ τ , ω) = − sin(2πtω) exp(−t2/2τ 2). (7.12)
Frequency ω of the spatial filter is related to the temporal scaleτ through ω = 4/τ . Interest points
correspond to the local maxima of the response function:

HOG: Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) was originally introduced for object detection [18],
but has been very successful in various image and video understanding problems. Its core idea is that the
shape and appearance of an image patch can be described in terms of the distribution of local gradients
(see Fig.7.9). For digital images this translates to calculating the image gradient and approximating their
distributionwithahistogram. Specifically,themainstepsforthecomputationofHOGarethefollowing:
• The image gradientIx, Iy is computed using the kernel[−1 0 1] and its transpose.
• Compute the gradient magnitude and angle of each pixel:
M (x, y) = √I 2x + I 2y and A(x, y) = arctan Iy
Ix
.
• The gradient matrices (magnitude and angle matrix) are divided into8 × 8 pixel cells (8 × 8 × 8
for videos) and for each cell a9-point histogram is computed. Each histogram bin corresponds to
a 20∘ angle. The image gradient in each pixel is quantized by ”voting” for its closest bin according
to its respective magnitude.
• Cellsaregroupedinto 2×2blocksandtheseparatehistogramsareconcatenatedandnormalizedby
theirL 2norm. Thisnormalizationisdoneperblocktoreducetheeffectofchangesinillumination
and contrast. If the input image consists of more than a block, the individual block descriptors are
concatenated and normalized.
The main advantage of HOG is that it is invariant to photometric and geometric changes, mostly due to
the fact that it is computed in small regions and due to the normalization scheme.
HOG3D: This descriptor is based on3-dimentional oriented gradients and it is a direct extension of
HOG [39]. 3D gradients inside a voxel are quantized into bins that are defined by convex regular poly-
hedrons. In this way, HOG3D encodes information about the appearance as well as the local movement.
HOF: Histograms of Optical Flow use the optical flow to encode the local movement in a small spatio-
temporal volume, following the same spirit as HOG. Specifically, the first step is to compute the optical
flow per pixel between two frames of an image patch and calculate its magnitude and orientation. The
orientationisquantizedinninebins,withtheninthbinreservedforpointswhoseopticalflowmagnitude
fallsbelowathreshold. Theopticalflowpatchisdividedintocellsand,foreachcell,ahistogramofoptical
flow orientations is made, in a similar way as HOG. HOF is constructed by concatenating the individual
cells’ histograms and normalizing the resulting vector.

MBH: Motion Boundary Histograms (MBH) aim to alleviate the effect of camera movement on other
descriptors [18]. Specifically, when the camera is moving, descriptors like HOF encode this movement,
minimizingthecontributionofmoresubtlemotion(e.g. handmovement)tothedescriptorcomputation.
MBHaddressesthisproblembycomputingthegradientoftheopticalflow,removingconstantmovement
fromthecomputation; therestisthesameasHOG.Thisresultsinadescriptorthathastwocomponents,
one for each optical flow direction. MBH encodes only changes in the optical flow field, making it more
robust in challenging environments.
7.5.3 Feature encoding
Features extracted from an action or gesture video characterize the action that is performed in it. Many
actions/gesturessharesimilarmovementsormayappearsimilar,whichimpliesthatsomeoftheirfeatures
should be “close” in the respective vector space. In addition, the duration of an action directly influences
the number of features extracted from it. Therefore, it is clear that thedistribution of the features, rather
than the features themselves offers a way to distinguish between different actions. Many methods have
been developed to represent the features’ distribution, the most popular beingBag-of-Visual-Words. This
familyofencodingmethodsrepresentvideosasacollectionofvisualwordsthatarisefromavisualvocab-
ulary (or visual codebook).
7.5.3.1 The Visual Codebook
The first step to encode the distribution of features in a video is to construct a visual codebook or vocab-
ulary, which is a set of vectors called “visual words”. Each visual word represents a set of “close” features.
Intuitively,aspecificmovementthatisfoundwithsomevariationinmanygesturesshouldberepresented
by a visual word that corresponds to the average of that movement.
Given a collection ofN trainingfeatures X = {x1, x2, ... , xN}, wherexi ∈ R D and Dis the features’
dimension, we can compute a representative subsetC = { c1, c2, ... ,cK} of X. C is the visual codebook
thatwillbeusedtoencodethedistributionoffeaturesfoundineachvideo. Thevisualcodebookisusually
constructedbyapplyingaclusteringalgorithmonourtrainingdata,suchasK-meansorGaussianMixture
Model (GMM) clustering, which are briefly reviewed here.
K-means clustering: This is the most widely used vector quantization algorithm. It divides the initial
feature spaceX into K clusters, each one represented by a vectorck ∈ C = { c1, ... , cK}, where C is
the set of centroids, that is the visual codebook. To find the centroids, K-means uses a set of auxiliary
binary variablesri,k ∈ {0, 1}, i = 1, ... , N , k = 1, ... K that indicate whether a vectorxi is assigned
totheclusterrepresentedby ck. Everyfeaturevectorbelongstooneclusteronly,i.e. ri,k = 1 impliesthat

7.5.3.2 Encoding methods
In the context of local methods for action/gesture recognition, encoding refers a single vector represen-
tation that aggregates the features extracted from a video. An encoding vector typically describes the
distribution of features extracted from a video, based on the visual codebook. Here, we will present the
most widely used encoding methods used.

7.5.4 Classification
Support Vector Machines (SVM) [95] are the most commonly used classification method from classical
machine learning employed in action recognition [82]. In its simplest form it is a linear binary classifier
that estimates a separating hyperplane by minimizing the data separation error with amaximal margin.
Theoptimalhyperplaneischaracterizedbyasubsetoftheinputvectorsthatlieclosesttoit,called support
vectors. Finding the optimal hyperplane is formulated as a constrained optimization problem where the

7.6 Deep Learning Methods
In recent years, deep learning methods have predominated in the field of image and video representation
and have become the standard approach for gesture classification and recognition. This can be attributed
totheavailabilityoflargedatasetsrequiredformodeltrainingaswellastheadventofhigh-endGPUsthat
make training and inference computationally tractable, even for real-time applications. In a similarl way
to previous hand-crafted approaches, gesture recognition follows the advances in action recognition in
terms of methodology.
The main idea of CNNs is to perform a sequence of simple operations (usually dot products followed
bynon-linearfunctions)ontheinputdatatoencodecomplexpatternsthatoccurinimages. Theexactop-
erationsperformedaredeterminedbythehiddenlayers’weights,whicharelearnableusinglargeamounts
of training data.
Inspiredbythesuccessof2DConvolutionalNeuralNetworks(CNNs)instill-imageanalysis,researchers
initially used pre-trained image models for action and gesture recognition. The advantage of these pre-
trained models is that they are trained on datasets (such as ImageNet) larger than any gesture dataset.
However,2DCNNsignoretemporalinformationandresultsfromindividualframeshavetobecombined
with a temporal pooling or feature aggregation scheme. To model temporal information, 3D CNNs were
introduced, that use 3D kernels to extract features based on the spatial and temporal dimensions. The in-
put to these networks can be RGB frames, depth frames, pre-computed optical flow or human pose. The
use of optical flow as the input indirectly integrates motion dynamics into 2D CNNs. These networks
typically have an RGB and an optical flow branch and are known as “two-stream” networks [88]. An-
otherwaytointegratetemporalinformationintothemodelarchitectureistouserecurrentnetworks,that
encode temporal relations between consecutive frames. In this section, we will review the most impor-
tantdeeplearningalgorithmsforgesturerecognition. Amoredetailedpresentationondeeplearningand
various image and video analysis architectures can be found in Chapter6.
7.6.1 2D Convolutional Neural Networks
Two-dimensional convolutional neural networks are the most common type of CNNs. They have rev-
olutionized the field of computer vision and are foundational in many state-of-the-art image processing
tasks. The most important elements in a CNN are (Fig.7.10):
• The input layer: the input data are typically represented as a multi-dimensional grid with shape

image.
• Convolutional (hidden) layers: the convolution operation applies a set of learnable filters (“con-
volutional kernels”) to this input grid. Each filter slides along the input matrix, performing a dot
product of the convolution kernel with the layer’s input matrix, followed by a non-linear “activa-
tion” function, usually ReLU. This results in an abstract representation of the input image, known
as a feature map or activation map. The activation map captures hierarchical features from simple
edges and textures to more complex patterns.
• Pooling (hidden) layers: the output of each convolutional layer is typically followed by a pooling
layertoreducethespatialdimensionsoffeaturemapswhileretainingthemostsalientinformation.
These layers combine the elements of a region of the activation map (or the whole map) with a
simple operation such as a max or an average. The activation maps’ size progressively diminish
until 1 × 1 maps are fed to a fully connected layer.
• Fully connected (hidden) layers: these connect every element (“neuron”) in one layer to every
element in the subsequent layer.
• An output layer: this is determined by the specific problem that the CNN addresses. For classi-
fication problems the output layer is a vector with size equal to the total number of classes. The
highest-scoring element in the output layer represents the neural network’s class prediction.
Some notable 2D CNN architectures include AlexNet [44], VGG [89], ResNet [30].
The use of 2D CNNs for gesture recognition requires the efficient motion representation of the arm
and/orthewholebody. Oneexampleis[ 7],whichproposestheconstructionofamotionrepresentation
imagebasedonframedifferences,bypre-processingsub-sequencesofRGBframes. ThreedifferentCNNs
are used for feature extraction: the first channel receives the original motion image, while the other two
channels receive the horizontal and vertical components of the motion image gradient, computed with
the Sobel operator. Late fusion is used to combine the features and classify gestures in a human-robot
interaction setting.

The depth modality has also been explored as an alternative for efficient motion representation. The
authors in [101, 100] extract three pairs of images from a sequence of depth maps: Dynamic Depth
Images (DDI), Dynamic Depth Normal Images (DDNI) and Dynamic Depth Motion Normal Images
(DDMNI).Thesedynamicimagesareconstructedusingbidirectional(forwardandbackward)rankpool-
ing. DDIs are computed using the raw depth maps to capture the pose dynamics, whereas DDNIs and
DDMNIsarecomputedusing3Dsurfacenormalstoencodespatio-temporalstructuralinformation. DDM-
NIsaresimilartoDDNIs,buttheyarecomputedonlyfortheforegroundmotion,whichisestimatedusing
GMMs. The resulting dynamic images are used to fine-tune a VGG16 [89] model pre-trained on RGB
data for classification.
A variant of 2D CNNs includes two separate neural networks (“brances” or “streams”), one for the
cameraframesandonefortheopticalflow,whoseoutputsarecombined(Fig. 7.11). Opticalflowiscom-
puted for each pair of consecutive images. These “two stream” methods can operate on RGB videos [88,
97], as well as depth maps [107].
In [41], the authors fuse motion information from static images, which are fed into a 2D CNN. First,
each video is divided into sub-clips and for each sub-clip optical flow frames are appended to selected
color frames to form the Motion Fused Frames (MFFs). A pre-trained BN-Inception [31] network is
used to extract features from each MFF, which are combined to create a final feature vector for classifying
the whole video. A similar concept is proposed in [81], where RGB frames in a video are fused together
to encode the temporal evolution of a gesture. The fusion process is based on frame differences and the
resulting representation is fed to two separate ResNets for classification.
Variousmethodsfocusoncombiningfeaturesfrommultiplecomplementaryopticaldatastreams,such
asRBG,depth,IR,opticalflowetc. In[ 64]amulti-modalmulti-scaleapproachcombinesRGB,depthand
opticalflowextractedfromeachframe,aswellasregionsaroundthehands. Thesestreamsareprocessedin
parallel 2D CNNs and a late sparse fusion scheme is employed. Similar ideas were previously introduced
in [66, 65].
Wang et al. [102] propose ACTION-Net, a modification to existing 2D CNNs that inserts an “AC-
TION” module consisting of three parallel branches or “paths”: aSpatio-Temporal Excitationpath that is
essentially a modified 3D convolutional block, aChannel Excitationpath that performs 1D convolutions
across channels to model their dependencies and theMotion Excitationpath that calculates feature-level
temporal differences between adjacent frames. The authors designed different ACTION-Nets based on
different backbone 2D CNNs and produced excellent results on action and gesture recognition datasets.

7.6.2 3D Convolutional Neural Networks
Three-dimensional convolutional neural networks (3D CNNs) extend convolution and pooling opera-
tions to the temporal dimension of video sequences. The primary building block is the 3D convolutional
layer usually followed by a 3D pooling layer, which works on 3D grids or volumes. The resulting 3D fea-
ture maps provide a better ability to model spatio-temporal information. The rest of the architecture is
essentially the same as in 2D CNNs and includes fully connected and softmax layers for classification or
regression.
The most notable 3D CNN architecture is C3D (Fig.7.12, which was introduced by Tran et al. for
action recognition [94]. It processes fixed length clips, so each video has to be divided into sub-clips
and features, or class prediction scores from each sub-clip have to be fused in some way. Originally, C3D
was used only as a feature extractor, coupled with SVMs for classification. This implies that the network’s
output layer can only be used for training and that the output of a fully connected (fc) layer serves as a
feature vector during inference.
However, C3D can also be used in an end-to-end fashion for gesture recognition as in [9]. In [52]
C3D is only used as a feature extractor from the hand and face regions of RGB and depth channel. In
this work, features are extracted from the fc6 layer and the fc6 outputs from RGB and depth channels
are concatenated. The resulting feature vector is fed into an SVM for classification. A similar pipeline is
followed by otherworks that alsouse C3D toextract features frompre-processed versions of RGB, depth
and optical flow streams [48, 49]. Feature vectors from different modalities are fused in various levels
and they are fed into an SVM for classification. An interesting modification in [47] uses C3D to extract
features from saliency maps of RGB videos. Saliency maps can serve as an extra modality that remove
gesture-irrelevant information in RGB data. In [114] a sub-sampled version of the input clip as well as
three sub-clips are used as inputs for a C3D network and the resulting features are fused. According to
the authors, this “pyramidal” input retains contextual information from multiple temporal scales. Class
predictions from RGB and depth streams are computed separately and fused.
Molchanov et al. [59] classify gesture clips by constructing spatio-temporal volumes consisting of in-
terleaved image gradients and depth frames. These volumes are fed into two separate 3D CNNs: a high
resolution and a low resolution network. The predictions of the two networks are fused by multiplying
their respective class-membership probabilities element-wise.
A different 3D CNN architecture which used for gesture classification is ResC3D [58], which adopts
residualblocksfromResNetalongwith3DconcolutionallayersfromC3D.Theauthorsfixtheinputvideo
length by sampling video segments based on their relative importance, which is measured using optical
flow. Finally, features from the RGB and depth modality are fused using Canonical Correlation Analysis.
3D CNNs can also be employed for skeleton-based gesture recognition. In [21] the authors use a pose
estimatortoextract2Dskeletonheatmaps. Thesearestackedtogethertoforma3Dvolume,whichserves
as input to a 3D CNN.
In [1] another popular 3D CNN architecture called I3D [11] as well as C3D are employed for mul-
timodal gesture recognition. In contrast to other methods that combine features or class membership
probabilitiesfromdifferentdatastreamsinasimplemanner,thisworkproposesmultimodaltraining. The

<!-- PDF_PAGE: 439 -->
### Σελίδα 439

TOPICS IN COMPUTER VISION AND MACHINE LEARNING 437
main idea is that feature maps in networks that processes different modalities in parallel should encode
similar higher-level semantics; in other words, they should be semantically aligned. To accomplish this,
the authors propose to maximize the correlation between the elements of corresponding feature maps
from separate networks by introducing a spatio-temporal semantic alignment loss function based on a
cross-modality feature map correlation matrix.
7.6.3 Recurrent Neural Networks
RecurrentNeuralNetworks(RNNs)areaclassofartificialneuralnetworksdesignedtohandlesequential
dataandcapturedependenciesovertime. Theyareparticularlyusefulfortasksinvolvingtimeseriesanal-
ysis, natural language processing, speech recognition and have been successfully used for gesture recog-
nition. RNNs have a unique architecture that allows them to maintain hidden states and update them
as they process each input element in a sequence. RNNs are a broad class of neural networks, but the
most common types used in computer vision are the Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs) and
Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs). The fundamental building block of an RNN is the recurrent neuron or
Figure 7.13: Architecture of an LSTM cell, the most widely used type of RNN. Information is stored in
the cell memoryCt. At each time stept the LSTM cell receives3 inputs: the cell stateCt−1 and the
hidden stateHt−1 from the previous time step, as well as the input vectorxt. The LSTM regulates, via
the gates, the internal flow of information and transforms the values of the cell memory and hidden state.
Thereare 3typesofgates: theforgetgate,theinputgate,andtheoutputgate. Allgatesreceivethe 3inputs
and compute selection vectors that eventually modulateCt−1 and Ht−1, producingCt and Ht.
cell (Fig.7.13 depicts an LSTM cell). Each cell maintains a hidden state vector, which serves as memory
to capture information from previous time steps. This hidden state is updated at each time step based on
thecurrentinputandtheprevioushiddenstate. RNNsprocesssequentialdataonetimestepatatime. At
eachtimestep,theRNNtakesaninputvector,updatesitshiddenstate,andproducesanoutput. Theout-
put can be used for various tasks, such as making predictions, classifying inputs, or generating sequences.
RNNs have weight matrices that are shared across all time steps. These weights determine how infor-
mation from the current input and previous hidden state is combined to update the current hidden state
and produce the output. Long Short-Term Memory networks are probably the most successful form of
RNNs(Fig. 7.13). Theyhavebeenintroducedtotackletheproblemofvanishingandexplodinggradients,
which is oftenseen in RNNs. Specifically, when trainingRNNs on long sequences, gradientscan become
too small (vanishing) or too large (exploding), making it difficult to learn meaningful representations.
LSTMs mitigate this problem by using “forget gates”, which prevent exponential decay of the cell state
derivative.
For gesture recognition, RNNs often process skeleton data, which is either readily available in many

layer. In[13]thehandsandfacearedetectedusinganobjectdetectionmodel(Faster-RCNN).Handpo-

global motion features from skeleton sequences. Finger motion features are extracted using a variational
autoencoder while global hand features are the angles, translation and rotation parameters of a kinematic
hand model. These features, along with the hand skeleton itself are processed by parallel LSTMs, whose
outputs are merged before they are fed to fully connected layers for classification.

7.6.4 Other Neural Network architectures
Some other approaches use neural networks that do not fall into the above categories or use hybrid ar-
chitectures. Theauthorsin[ 108]proposeacomputationallyefficientskeleton-basedapproachusingtwo
kinds of skeleton features: (a) Euclidean distances between all pairs of joints in a frame to make static
location and viewpoint invariant (b) temporal differences between joint coordinates in different frames
to encode motion information. These features are flattened to1D vectors and they are fed into a series of
1Dconvolutionlayerstocomputelowerdimensionembeddings. Thesearefinallyusedasinputsfora 1D
CNN for classification.
Another 1DCNNapproachisproposedin[ 75]. Afine-grainedgesturerepresentationiscomputedby
decomposinggesturesintostaticgestures,actionandmovementdirectionusingonlythehandpose. Static
gestures are encoded by computing geometric hand pose features, which are fed into a fully connected
layerforclassification. Handlandmarks’locationsandvelocitiesareusedtopredictactionsandmovement
direction using a1D CNN. The hand skeleton sequence is processed in15 frame segments and the1D
CNN outputs are combined with weighted average pooling, whose weights are estimated by a different
attention layer. An overview of this architecture is depicted in Fig.7.15. This approach is very useful
for datasets that contain both static and dynamic presents, as the static hand pose component of system
system is shared between them. In [50] dynamic gestures are decomposed into hand posture evolution
and hand movements and different skeleton-based representations are constructed for each one. These
are processed by a 3D and 2D CNN respectively and the output features are combined for classification.

7.7 Datasets
Many computer vision algorithms tend to employ some form of supervised learning, relying on large
amountsofdatafortrainingandevaluation. Dataisofgreatimportanceespeciallyforgesturerecognition,
as the choice of a gesture vocabulary is related to the specific application: for example different gestures

<!-- PDF_PAGE: 442 -->

440 GESTURE RECOGNITION
are used for touchless driving, human-computer interaction etc. This section will briefly review gesture
datasets that are widely used in the literature.
7.7.1 The ChaLearn Gesture Dataset
The ChaLearn Gesture Dataset (CGD) was built in the context of the 2012 ChaLearn Gesture Chal-
lenge [29], which addressed the problem of one-shot gesture learning and was the first in a series of Ges-
ture Challenges [28]. The dataset provided for the challenge was one of the first datasets that acquired
data using the Kinect sensor, including pairs of RGB and depth videos. Each video depicts a single user
facing a fixed Kinect camera.
The dataset includes62, 000 gestures in total and it is grouped into540 batches. Each batch corre-
sponds to a single user and includes47 RGB and depth video pairs (Fig.7.16) with1 − 5 gestures each,
for a total of100 gestures per batch. Batches are further grouped in development, validation and final
(testing) batches and the validation and final batches were provided with labels only for one example of
each gesture class in each batch, i.e. there is only one training sample per class in every batch. Gestures in
each batch are drawn from a small vocabulary of8 to 12 unique gestures, called a “lexicon”. In total there
are 289 gestures from30 lexicons. Each lexicon is related to one of nine categories of gesture classes cor-
responding to various settings or application domains. They include body language gestures (scratching
your head, crossing your arms), gesticulations performed to accompany speech, illustrators or descrip-
tive gestures (Italian gestures), emblems or symbolic gestures (Indian mudras), linguistic signs (sign lan-
guages for the deaf), signals (referee signals, diving signals, or marshalling signals to guide machinery
or vehicle), actions/activities (drinking or writing), pantomimes (gestures made to mimic actions), and
dancepostures. Gestureswereseparatedbyreturningtoarestingposition, makingthetemporalsegmen-
tation problem relatively easy.

7.7.2 The Chalearn Multi-modal Gesture Dataset 2013
The second installment of Chalearn gesture challenges was the 2013 Multi-modal Gesture Recognition
Challenge [23] which, in contrast to CGD, focused on multiple instance, user independent learning of
gestures from multi-modal data. The dataset built for the challenge includes13, 858gestures from a lex-
icon of20 Italian cultural-anthropological gesture classes of everyday life. They are recorded by27 users
withaKinectcamera,providingRGBanddepthimages,skeletalmodelandusermask(Fig. 7.17)accom-
panied with respective audio (in Italian). There are956 sequences grouped into training, validation and

7.7.3 Chalearn 2016 IsoGD and ConGD
The2016Chalearn“LookingatPeople”Challenge[ 98]introducedtwodatasetsforlarge-scaleuserinde-
pendent gesture recognition (Fig.7.16). Both are derived from CGD by integrating all batch classes and
samples:
• An Isolated Gesture Recognition dataset (IsoGD) that consists of 47,933 RGB-D gesture videos.
Each RGB-D video represents one gesture only, and there are 249 gestures labels performed by 21
different individuals.
• AContinuousGestureRecognitiondatasetthatconsistsof22,535RGB-Dvideoswithatotalnum-
ber of 47,933 gestures. Each RGB-D video may represent one or more gestures, and there are 249
gestures labels performed by 21 different individuals. The temporal segmentation is manually la-
beled (start and end frames for each gesture).
Forbothdatasetsavalidationprotocolisprovided, alongwithpre-definedtraining-testingandvalidation
splits, so that training samples from the same person do not appear in the validation and testing sets.
7.7.4 NVGesture
The NVGesture dataset [60] focuses on touchless driver controlling. It includes 1,050 training and 482
for testing that fall into25 gesture classes. The videos are recorded indoors in a car from multiple view-
pointswiththreemodalities: RGBanddepthfromaSoftKineticdepthcamera,stereoIRfromaDUO3D
camera (Fig.7.18). Gestures include moving either the hand or two fingers up, down, left or right; click-
ing with the index finger; beckoning; opening or shaking the hand; showing the index finger, or two or
three fingers; pushing the hand up, down, out or in; rotating two fingers clockwise or counterclockwise;
pushing two fingers forward; closing the hand twice; and showing “thumb up” or “OK”.

7.7.5 Briareo dataset
Similar to NVGesture, the Briareo dataset addresses the problem of hand gesture recognition in the con-
text of automotive control. It includes12 gesture classes related to touchless driving: Fist, Pinch, Flip-
over, Telephone, Right swipe, Left swipe, Top-down swipe, Bottom-up swipe, Thumb, Index, Clockwise
rotation, Counter-clockwise rotation. Every gesture is performed three times by each of the40 subjects,
leading to120gesture instances for each class. Data channels include RGB, Depth and infrared, acquired
using a traditional RGB camera, a Pico Flexx sensor and a Leap Motion sensor respectively. 3D hand
joints estimated by the Leap Motion SDK are also included.
7.7.6 EgoGesture Dataset
EgoGesture [113] is a multi-modal large scale dataset for egocentric hand gesture recognition that ad-
dresses the problem of human interaction with wearable devices. Videos are captured by50 subjects
wearing an RGB-D RealSense camera with a strap belt on their heads under six diverse conditions such
as indoors, outdoor, static, walking etc. (Fig.7.19). There are 83 classes of static or dynamic gestures
performed in continuous sequences of9 − 14gestures, with a total of2, 081RGB-D videos and24, 161
gesture samples, making it one of the largest gesture datasets. The temporal boundaries of each gesture in
each continuous sequence are annotated.
7.7.7 The Jester Dataset
The Jester [53] is one of the largest gesture datasets, including148, 092 3-second RGB clips of people
performing gestures in front of a camera. The videos were acquired by1, 376 actors, offering a wide di-
versity in background and recording conditions, in general. There are27 gesture classes that correspond
to commands for a human-computer interface, such as “Zooming In With Two Fingers” and “Zooming

Summary: This chapter serves as an introductory guide to emotion recognition within the
field of affective computing. It introduces the computational models of emotion and exam-
inesthevisualchannels,notablyfacialexpressionsandbodyposes,throughwhichemotions
are expressed. The chapter further discusses the application of deep learning techniques to
analyze these emotional indicators. Key experimental findings are presented, demonstrat-
ing the advantages of leveraging multiple channels for more accurate emotion recognition.
Overall, the chapter aims to provide foundational insights on automatic emotion recogni-
tion and its practical applications in enhancing human-computer interaction.
Prerequisite Knowledge: Introductory course on calculus, linear algebra, computer vision,
and machine learning.
8.1 Introduction
Emotions and the ability to express oneself is a fundamental aspect of human behavior. Across thou-
sands ofyears, emotionshavebeenevolvingalongwithhumanity andhavebothintra-andinter-personal
functions. They helpwith rapid decision-making, influencethoughts, andareinterwovenwith the cogni-
tive process. Inter-personally, emotions help us understand others better, building stronger social bonds
through empathy and emotional expressiveness.
Charles Darwin, in “The Expression of Emotion in Man and Animals” [21], highlighted the univer-
sality and evolutionary roots of emotions. Complementing this, Damasio’s “Descartes’ Error: Emotion,
Reason, and the Human Brain” [20] underscores the indispensable link between emotion and reason,
a vital concept in developing emotionally intelligent computational systems. This concept is further ex-

plored in recent studies, which delve into the nuanced interaction between emotional expressions and
their interpretation by artificial intelligence.
Rosalind Picard’s pioneering concept of “Affective Computing” [59] describes the potential for com-
puters and robots to express, recognize, and model emotions, and possibly even to “feel” them. While
feeling emotions remains a philosophical challenge, the first three aspects have pragmatic value, fostering
more natural interactions between humans and machines. Social robotics, a burgeoning field in affective
computing, demonstrates this via applications in therapy, daily living assistance, and education [9, 11,
10], enhancing trust and authenticity in human-machine interactions.
The objective of this chapter is to familiarize the reader with the concept of “automatic emotion recog-
nition” technology, one of the constituents of the broad field of affective computing. By the end of this
chapter, the reader will have gained a understanding of the computational modeling of emotions, the dif-
ferent channels through which emotions can be expressed or inferred, and how deep learning techniques
can be utilized to recognize emotions.
8.2 Theoretical and Computational Models of Emotion
8.2.1 Theories of Emotion
Thereisnoscientificconsensusoneitherthedefinitionnorthemodelingofhumanemotions. Mostworks
in literature approach the subject from two different perspectives. The first perspective sees emotions as
discrete entities which also manifest in specific, distinguishable ways. This study of “basic” emotions and
howtheymanifestcross-culturallywasthestudyofDarwin’spioneeringworkinhisbook“Theexpression
of the emotions in man and animals” [21]. A more systematic approach and an attempt at deriving a set
of “basic emotions” was presented decades later by Ekman and Friesen [24], with the initial derivation
of six basic emotions: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise. After discovering evidence of
cross-cultural[27,25]constantsinemotionandfacialexpressions,theyderivedthe“FacialActionCoding
System”(FACS)whichbreaksdownfacialexpressionsintoindividualcomponentsofmusclemovements
(ActionsUnits(AUs)-seeFigure 8.1dforexamplesofactionunits). TheFACSsystemhassubsequently
associateddifferentAUswithbasicemotions[ 31]. Asecondmorecomplexmodelofcategoricalemotions
isthewheelofPlutchik(Figure 8.1a)whereeightbasic(andbipolar)emotions(joyversussadness;anger
versusfear;trustversusdisgust;andsurpriseversusanticipation)cangetcombinedtoformmorecomplex
emotional states such as remorse (sadness plus disgust) or contempt (disgust plus anger). Furthermore,
the model includes different intensities of emotions.
The second viewpoint sees emotions not as discrete categories, but rather as a continuous spectrum
in one or more dimensions. The most famous model in this viewpoint is the VAD (Valence, Arousal,
Dominance) or PAD (where valence is called pleasure) model [54, 53]. Valence (or Pleasure) measures
the degree of “pleasantness” of the emotion, arousal measures the “energy” of the emotional expression,
anddominancethecontrolling/dominantnatureoftheemotion(e.g.,fearisasubmissiveemotion,while
anger is a dominant one). An example of the VAD model can be seen in Figure8.1b.
Thereisalsoacategoryofmodelsthatcombinestheabovetworepresentations,calledthe“circumplex”
models. Inthesemodels,discreteemotionslieonatwo-dimensionalbasisofvalenceandarousal. Models
of this type were popularized by Russell [62] (see Figure8.1c).

ofemotions. Themostcommonlyusedlabelingschemehoweveristheinitialsixbasicemotionsproposed
by Ekman, or an extended version of it with the addition of contempt. This is a reasonable consequence

8.3.1 Facial Expressions
The first pioneering works on automatic visual emotion recognition were almost exclusively focused on
thefaceandfacialexpressions[ 63,52]. ThiswaspossiblyduetotheworkofDarwin[ 21]andhisstudyof
facialexpressionofemotions,aswellaslaterstudiesonprototypicalemotionsbyEkmanandFriesen[ 26,
24] and the association of these with standard facial muscle movements/contractions [31]. It is also im-
portanttonotethatemotionrecognitionusingthefacegrewinparalleltoimprovementsinfacialdetection
and recognition methods, with each one borrowing research from the other.
The standard pipeline for automatic emotion recognition using facial expressions thus included face
detection, feature extraction, and then classification. Some of the first representations extracted included
the optical flow [52], as well as geometric (shape) features, using Active Shape Models (ASM). Then,
more sophisticated features have also been used such as Local Binary Patterns [39], Gabor filters [22], in
conjunction with traditional machine learning techniques such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs) or
Adaboost [51, 57].
More recently, with the breakthrough of deep learning [45] and the development of larger databases
(someexamplesincludeAffectNet[ 55]Aff-Wild2[ 42],andEmotioNet[ 28]),methodsnowcompletely
skipthefeatureextractionprocedure,anddesignend-to-endneuralnetworkarchitectureswhicharetrained
with gradient descent methods that can achieve high performance in datasets which include hundreds of
thousands of samples. As an example, some of the state-of-the-art methods for facial expression recogni-
tion include residual Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and 3D convolutional architectures.

8.3.2 Body Language and Emotions
Nevertheless, as we know from our personal experiences, emotion is not only displayed through the hu-
man face but also through body language. This was highlighted again by Ekman and Friesen in [26],
and has subsequently been the study of many works. These early works assumed that body posture was
only indicative of the intensity of the emotion, and that there existed no specific body configurations and
movements associated with specific emotions. However, more recent studies have discarded this, show-
ing that both posture and movement convey distinct information about the emotional state [18, 66, 1],
andobservingthebodyinfluenceshowweperceiveemotionalexpressionbythefaceorvocally[ 67,3,2].
In [19], the Body Action and Posture Coding System (BAP) was developed; an attempt at a systematic
approach to identifying specific body micro-movements and configurations that can be associated with
different categorical emotions. Figure8.3 illustrates various instances which showcase the importance of
body language as an indicator of the emotional state.
Figure 8.3: Body language is an important indicator of the emotional state. Source: [56].
8.3.3 Contextual Features
In a strict sense, the context (i.e., the surrounding environment/scene) differs from the two previous
channels of communication. Context includes a two-way channel, a person expressing their inner emo-
tion affects their environment (e.g., a person throwing or breaking something), but also is affected by
their environment (e.g., a graveyard elicits different emotions when compared to a theme park). In this
way, context is a more implicit stream of information, and for this reason, it has been largely ignored in
automatic emotion recognition.
Nevertheless, recent studies have underscored that emotional perception can be heavily affected by
the context/scene [17, 8]. The first attempt at introducing context as additional information for visual
emotion recognition was done by Kosti et al. [44, 43] in 2017, and following works also showed how to
leverage context for emotion recognition [60]. They introduced the large-scale dataset EMOTIC (Emo-
tions in Context), which contains annotated emotions of individuals in multiple scenes. Subsequently,
they introduced a two-way CNN architecture which fused information from both the human and the
scene, in order to recognize the depicted emotion.

8.4 Enabling Technologies
Emotion recognition and expression synthesis are higher-level problems; before attempting to estimate
the emotional state of a person, we need to be able to detect their face, mouth, and body posture. As a
result, the techniques presented in this chapter rely upon these technologies, in order to first localize and
extract landmarks of the person.
8.4.1 Body Pose Estimation
Body pose estimation refers to the act of localizing a human body, and then extracting key landmarks
from the body. The result of a body pose estimator, which can be either the 2D/3D points or the im-
age cropped around the body, can then be used to perform higher level tasks, such as action recognition,
intent recognition, and emotion recognition, among others. While there is a large amount of interest in
body estimation and techniques are improving at a rapid pace, there are some established methods in
the literature which already achieve remarkable results in this task. One such example is OpenPose [15]
(Figure 8.5a), which achieves realtime multi-person 2D pose estimation, using Part Affinity Fields and
bipartite matching, in order to correctly associate the parts of multiple persons in an image. Other meth-
odsincludeAlphaPose[ 47],MediaPipe[ 49],DensePose[ 33],ViTPose[ 69]. Inthischapter,wewilluse
these techniques as building blocks in order to move on and tackle higher level problems, i.e., emotion
recognition. In some cases we rely on the detected 2D landmarks to estimate emotion, while in other
cases we first obtain the cropped body image by calculating a bounding box from the landmarks and then
use the image as the input for CNNs.
8.4.2 Face Alignment
The second important building block of the techniques described in this chapter is Face Detection and
Alignment. Following the seminal work of Viola and Jones for face detection [68], such as with body
pose estimation, there has been a growing line of research focused around detecting the human face and
extracting 2D and 3D landmarks. The most widespread method for face alignment is probably FAN, the
work of Bulat and Tzimiropoulos [12], which is built by stacking four HourGlass networks. Another
notable work in this field is the lightweight 3DDFA [37], which jointly predicts not only 2D and 3D
landmarks but also the parameters of the 3D Basel Face Model [58].

8.5.1 Hierarchical Emotional Labels
A problem that arises when dealing with spontaneous (i.e., not acted) or in-the-wild data is the fact that
