8.5.2 Method
Based on the aforementioned analysis, in Figure8.7 we present a Deep Neural Network (DNN) archi-
tecture for automatic multi-cue affect recognition using Hierarchical Multi-Label training (HMT)[29].
We assume that we have both the whole body labely, as well as the hierarchical labelsyf for the face and
yb for the body.The network initially consists of two different branches, with one branch focusing on
facial expressions, and one branch focusing on body posture. The two branches are then combined at a
later stage to form the whole body expression recognition branch that takes into account both sources
of information. This design allows setting up different losses on different stages of the network based
on the hierarchical labels, offering stricter supervision during training. The output of the network is the
recognized emotional state of the person detected in the input video.
Facial Expression Recognition Branch The facial expression recognition branch of the network is
responsible for recognizing emotions by decoding facial expressions. Considering a sequence of frames
Ii|i=1,..,N, we first apply at each one a head detection and alignment algorithm in order to obtain the
cropped face image (see Section8.7.1). Subsequently, the image is fed into a Residual CNN [38] to get
a 2048-long feature vector description of each frameHf
i |i=1,..,N. Then, we apply temporal max-pooling
over the video frames to obtain the representation of the facial frame sequence.By assuming that the
feature map obtains its maximum values in frames where the facial expression is at peak intensity, max-
poolingselectsonlytheinformationregardingthefacialexpressionsattheirpeakovertheframesequence.
Then, we apply a Fully Connected (FC) layer onHf to obtain the facial emotion scores,sf.

8.6 The BabyRobot Emotion Database
In order to evaluate the previous method, we have collected a database that includes multimodal record-
ings of children interacting with two different robots (Zeno [61], Furhat [32]), in a laboratory setting
that has been decorated in order to resemble a child’s room (Figure8.8).
We call this dataset the BabyRobot Emotion Database (BRED)[29,23]. BRED includes two different
kindsofrecordings: Pre-Game Recordingsduringwhichchildrenwereasked byahuman toexpressoneof
sixemotions,and GameRecordings duringwhichchildrenwereplayingagamecalled“Expressthefeeling”
withtheZenoandFurhatrobots. Thegamewastouchscreen-based,andthroughoutitsdurationchildren
selected face-down cards, each of which represented a different emotion. After seeing the cards, the chil-
dren were asked to express the emotion, and then one of the robots followed up with a facial gesture that
expressedtheemotionaswell. Atotalof30childrenofagesbetween6to12tookpartin bothrecordings.
It is important to note that we didnot give any guidelines or any information to the children on how to
expresstheiremotions. TheexperimentalprocedurewasapprovedbyanIndependentEthicsCommittee
from the Athena Research and Innovation Center in Athens, Greece.
The emotions included in the database are:Anger, Happiness, Fear, Sadness, Disgust, andSurprise, the
six basic emotions included in Ekman and Freisen’s initial studies [25]. This categorical representation of
emotionisthemostcommonlyusedinresearchstudiesofautomaticemotionrecognition[ 34],andistyp-
ically adopted across different databases of emotional depictions [48]. When compared to dimensional
approaches (e.g., valence/arousal space), the categorical emotional approach is less flexible in expressing
more complex emotions, however, it is easier to annotate [36].
Hierarchical Database Annotations Intotal, the initialrecordingsincluded 180samplesof emotional
expressions from the “Pre-Game” session and180 samples from the “Game” session (30 children × 6
emotionsforbothsessions). Theannotationprocedureincludedthreedifferentphases. Inthefirstphase,
six different annotators filtered out recordings where the children did not perform any emotion (due to
shyness, lack of attention, or other reasons), and identified the temporal segments during which the ex-
pressionofemotionstakesplace(startingwiththeonsetoftheemotionandendingjustbeforetheoffset).
In the second phase, two annotators validated the annotations of the previous phase.Finally in the third
phase, threedifferent annotators labeled the videos hierarchically, by indicating for each video whether
the child was using the face, body, or both, to express the emotion.The final hierarchical labels were ob-
tained using majority voting over the three annotations. Inter-annotator agreement was also measured
using Fleiss’ kappa coefficient [30], with a value0.48 for the face labels and0.84 for the body labels.

include facial landmarks (although we do not use them in any way in our method) in order to protect
privacy.
ThenewlycollectedBREDdatasetisverychallengingasitfeaturesmanyintra-classvariations,multiple
poses, and in many cases similar body expressions for different classes.These include the similar pattern
of hand crossing in anger and fear, and lowering of the head pose in fear and sadness. The BRED dataset
is available athttps://zenodo.org/record/3233060.

8.7 Experiments
Inthissectionwewillpresentourexperimentalprocedureandresults 2. Wefirstperformedanexploratory
analysis of the different branches and pathways of the HMT architecture of Figure8.7 on the GEMEP
(GEneva Multimodal Emotion Portrayals) database [6]. As far as we are aware, this is the only publicly
available video database that includes annotated whole body expressions of emotions. We believe that
databases of upper body depictions, such as FABO [35] where the subjects are sitting, restrict body pos-
tureexpressionandforcethesubjectstofocusmostlyonusingtheirhands. Ourmainevaluationwasthen
conducted on BRED where we experimented with variations of the HMT network.
8.7.1 Network Setup and Initialization
In order to avoid overfitting due to the small number of sequences in both GEMEP and BRED, and es-
pecially in the facial branch which includes a large number of parameters, we pretrained the branch on
the AffectNet Database [55]. The AffectNet Database contains more than 1 million images of faces col-
lected from the internet and annotated with one of the following labels: Neutral, Happiness, Anger, Sad-
ness,Disgust,Contempt,Fear,Surprise,None,Uncertain,andNon-face. Themanuallyannotatedimages
amount to440k, with about295k falling into one of the emotion categories (neutral plus 7 emotions).
The database also includes a validation set of 500 images for each class, while the test set has not yet been
released.
Topreparethefacialbranchforthesubsequentfeatureextractionforourtask,westartedwithaResNet-
50CNNwhichhadbeentrainedusingtheImageNetDatabase 3. Next,inordertolearnfeaturesthatwere
pertinent to our task, we train the network again, this time on AffectNet by replacing the final FC layer of
thenetworkwithanewFClayerwitheightoutputclasses(thesevenemotionsofAffectNetplusneutral).
The network was trained for 20 epochs using a batch size of 128 and the Adam optimizer [41], achieving
the best accuracy on the AffectNet validation set at the 13th epoch (52.2%). The weights of the body
branch were initialized as in [46].
For detecting, cropping, and aligning the face for each frame, we used the OpenFace 2 toolkit [5].
We then used our pretrained facial branch to extract a2048-dimensional feature vector which is used
during training. This means that during training the parameters of the feature extraction layers of the
facial branch remain fixed. Similarly, we extracted the 2D pose of the subjects ineach database (GEMEP
and BRED)using OpenPose [16] along with the 2D hand keypoints [64]. In order to filter out badly
detected keypoints, we set all keypoints with a confidence score lower than0.1 as 0 for BRED and lower
than 0.3 for the GEMEP database.These thresholds resulted in a percentage of approximately 70% valid
joints in each database.The total size of the input vector for the body expression recognition branch was
134: 25 2D keypoints of the skeleton and 21 2D keypoints for each hand.
8.7.2 Results on the GEMEP Database
The GEMEP database includes videos of 10 adult actors performing 17 different emotions: Admiration,
Amusement, Anger, Anxiety, Contempt, Despair, Disgust, Fear, Interest, Irritation, Joy, Pleasure, Pride,
Relief, Sadness, Surprise, and Tenderness. In this work we used the core set of the database that includes
the first 12 of the aforementioned emotions.
We used 10-fold leave-one-subject-out cross-validation and then repeated the process 10 times, aver-
aging the scores in the end. For all different evaluation setups, we trained for 200 epochs, reducing the
learning rate by a factor of 10 at 150 epochs. We report Top-1 accuracy for several experimental setups

in Table8.3. For the body expression recognition branch we compared three different implementations:
a) the implementation with Global Temporal Average Pooling (GTAP) using a hidden FC layer of 256
neurons with ReLU activation, b) a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) [4] with eight temporal
convolutional residual blocks, 128 channels and kernel size 2, and c) a bidirectional Long Short-Term
Memory network (LSTM) [40] with 100 hidden units and two layers preceded by an FC layer of 128
neurons with activation.For both TCN and LSTM we averaged the outputs over all time steps. In the
first part of the table, we observe that GTAP (shown in bold) achieves the highest accuracy (0.34), even
though it is a much simpler method. We believe that due to the small amount of data the methods focus
only on certain representative postures that occur during the expression of emotions and ignore sequen-
tial information. As a result, the LSTM and TCN cannot outperform the DNN combined with GTAP,
and would require a larger database in order to accurately capture temporal information. The face branch
achieves a higher accuracy score (0.43) than the body branch (0.34), which is an expected result. Our
mainobservationisthefactthatthewholebodyemotionrecognitionbranch(withtheGTAPimplemen-
tation, shown in bold) achieves a significant improvement over the face branch baseline (an absolute 8%
improvement, from 0.43 to 0.51).
In Table8.3 we also include experiments at the frame level, where we only took the middle frame of
each video sequence and skipped the temporal pooling structures in each branch.We can see that, again,
the whole body emotion recognition branch (in bold) yields a large performance boost over the facial
branch (from 0.21 to 0.33), as well as the significance of applying temporal pooling over all video frames.
Emotion specific details can be seen in the confusion matrices of Figure8.9. We show the confusion
matrices for the separately trained body, face, and whole-body branches.We can see that in cases such as
pride, the body branch is much more efficient in recognizing the emotion, as opposed to the face branch,
a result which is also in line with [66]. In other emotions such as joy and anger, a combination of face
and body posture results in higher accuracy. There were also emotions for which the body branch failed
to learn any patterns, such as anxiety or pleasure. In these cases, the whole body branch achieved a lower
accuracy than the face branch.

report results in balanced and unbalanced F1-score and accuracy. Due to this imbalance we also used a

model that can reliably recognize all emotions.

Summary: Inthischapter,wewillpresentthefieldofThree-Dimensional(3D)Modelingof
Deformable Objects, with a particular focus on 3D Morphable Models (3DMMs). These
models represent a significant advancement in the fields of computer vision and graphics,
offering us the ability to reliably model complex deformable objects. One of the primary
strengths of 3DMMs lies in their ability to comprehensively capture the intricate variations
inshapeandappearance,providingaholisticrepresentationofdeformableobjects. Another
remarkable feature is their adaptability and versatility, which has become apparent by their
wide adoption by state-of-the-art deep learning techniques for 3D Vision and Graphics.
We will discuss the mathematical foundations as well as the most important frameworks
and pioneering methods of the field. We will also conduct a review of the multifaceted ap-
plications that 3DMMs have engendered. From enhancing facial animation to serving as
essential tools for modeling anatomical structures in medical applications, the influence of
3DMMs is pervasive.
Prerequisite Knowledge: Introductory course on calculus, linear algebra, computer vision,
and machine learning.
9.1 Introduction
Modeling deformable objects is of paramount importance for three-dimensional (3D) Computer Vision
and 3D Computer Graphics. Representing and estimating the detailed 3D shape, appearance and dy-

472 THREE-DIMENSIONAL MODELING OF DEFORMABLE OBJECTS
namics of a class of deformable objects such as human faces has numerous applications, for example
augmented reality, performance capture, computer games, visual effects, human-computer interaction,
computer-aided craniofacial surgery and facial expression recognition, to name a few.
3D Morphable Models (3DMMs) are by far the most popular choice for such modeling. They were
introduced in 1999 as a general representation for faces and other deformable objects, not just for aim-
ing at one specific task. By harnessing a combination of statistical techniques, shape deformations, and
texture variations, 3DMMs provide a powerful framework for representing and synthesizing 3D objects
with unprecedented precision and realism. They are unique in their generality across different tasks and
applications. 3DMMs have been shaping the fields of 3D Computer Vision and Graphics way before the
so-called “deep learning revolution”; however, during the last years they have also been used with great
success in the context of deep learning and have been incorporated into many state-of-the-art computer
vision systems.
Undoubtedly, the most pronounced class where 3DMMs have been used is the class of human faces.
It is, however, worth mentioning that, as will be discussed later in this chapter, 3DMMs have also proven
particularlybeneficialinmodelingothertypesofobjects,suchasthewholehumanhead,thehumanbody,
other specific parts of the body like ears and hands, human skulls, animals, and even cars.
In this chapter, we will review the main theory, most important advances and applications related to
the 3D modeling of deformable objects, focusing on 3D morphable models. From face recognition and
animation to medical applications and beyond, 3D Modeling of Deformable Objects has found its way
into a diverse range of fields, revolutionizing the way we perceive and interact with the digital world.
9.2 3D mesh representation
A prerequisite for the vast majority of 3D Computer Vision and Graphics applications is the adoption
of a 3D representation of deformable objects and other types of objects. The most popular choice for
that is the usage of3D polygon meshes, which offer several advantages. First of all, their 3D rendering
and visualization by modern graphics cards can be very efficient. In addition, they can be easily defined
and manipulated, having the ability to achieve a high level of accuracy in terms of geometry, color and
interaction with light sources. Furthermore, they can also be easily deformed and animated.
A 3D polygon mesh consists of a set of vertices that are linked with polygons (usually triangles), form-
ing a piece-wise flat surface, see e.g.9.1(a). In more detail, thegeometry of a 3D mesh is defined by the
following shape vector, containing the 3D coordinates of its vertices:
s = [x 1, y1, z1, x 2, y2, z2, ... , x N, yN, zN]

In conclusion, a triangle mesh can be formally defined as the setM = {s, T}, representing the collec-

It is worth mentioning that several mesh formats include color information via an alternative, more
complicated representation based on the so-calledUV space. The UV space is a separate 2D representa-
tion of the mesh “unfolded” on a plane that defines which parts of a 2D texture map should be applied
to different polygons of the mesh. This gives texture the ability to have much higher resolution than the
shape,resultinginmoreplausiblerenderedshapeswithfinedetailsinthetexture,whileavoidingtheneed
foracomputationallyexpensiveincreaseinthenumberofvertices. Itisalsopossibleformeshestocontain
other per-vertex information such as normal vectors and weight maps that control animation.
9.3 3D Morphable Models
This section will present the definition and main concepts which relate to 3DMMs. A 3DMM typically
models the variations of the 3D meshes that represent a specific type of objects. For the sake of presenta-
tion, we will assume that the type of object being modeled is the human face, but a very similar modeling
is used for other types of objects (see Sec.9.6).
A 3DMM usually considers three types of variations captured by three different sub-models:
1. 3Dshapevariationsacrossdifferentidentitiesarecapturedina shape identity model,asoutlinedin
Sec. 9.3.1. Frequently employed models include global models, which represent variations of the
entire face surface, and local models, which represent variations of facial parts.
2. 3D shape variations across different facial expressions are captured in ashape expression model,
as will be outlined in Sec.9.3.2. The two main categories of expression models are additive and
multiplicative models. Additionally, during recent years, there has been a growing exploration of
non-linear expression models.
3. Finally, variations in appearance and illumination are captured in a separatecolor modelas will be

outlined in Sec.9.3.3.
Details about each one of these models follow.
9.3.1 Shape identity model
Theshapemodelofa3DMMconsidersthatthetopology Tofthe3Dmeshremainsfixedandmodelsthe

As in the seminal work of Blanz and Vetter [11], the mapping (9.4) is usually considered linear and

sid(p) = ̄ s + Up (9.5)
where ̄s ∈ R 3N is the mean shape andU ∈ R 3N×n id is the matrix withnid identity basis shapes, see

Non-linear extensions have been explored in the context of modern deep learning. Since learning a
latent space can be seen as the goal of anautoencoder, recent methods have proposed training a 3DMM
in an encoder-decoder framework, starting with the work of Abrevaya et al. [26] and continuing with
several other works, e.g. [99, 18].
Theshapeidentitymodelofa3DMM(eitherlinearornon-linear)isessentiallyagenerativemodeland

mapping (9.4), see, for example, Fig.9.2(b). For example, it is often assumed that the coefficientsp are
independent, zero-mean Gaussian random variables.

9.4 Construction of 3DMMs
Intheprevioussection,wedefined3DMMsanddiscussedhowtheycanbeusedtosynthesizenovelshape
instances. Let us now discuss how they can be constructed, choosing again the human faces as our case
study.
Theconstructionofa3DMMrequiresasetoftraining3Dmesheswithalargevariety. Itinvolvesthree
main steps:
1. First, the training objects are captured and 3D meshes are generated.
2. Then, dense correspondences are computed between each of the 3D meshes and a reference tem-
plate. This allows the training meshes to be brought into a shared representation and a common
reference frame.
3. Finally, some form of statistical analysis (e.g. PCA) is applied on the shape and color information
of the 3D meshes
More details for each one of these steps are given below.
9.4.1 3D Object Capture
Thefirststepis3Dobjectcapture,inthesenseofacquiringraw3Ddataofthetrainingobjectinstances. It
is important to have a high level of accuracy in this object capture process. It is also important to acquire
data which is sufficiently diverse and that capture the variability in the object class, as present in the real
world, for example faces of individuals of different ages, genders and ethnic origins.

<!-- PDF_PAGE: 479 -->
### Σελίδα 479

TOPICS IN COMPUTER VISION AND MACHINE LEARNING 477
The object capture typically requires a controlled environment with high-end equipment and is done
via a method belonging to one of the following categories:
• Geometric methods aim to directly deduce the 3D coordinates of a shape [110, 56, 17]. This can
be achieved through either the observation of the same surface point from multiple viewpoints,
which poses the challenge of matching corresponding points across these images, or by observing
a projected pattern, which presents the challenge of establishing a correspondence between the
known pattern and an image capturing its projection. This category includes passive multi-view
stereo depth sensors, active sensors like laser scanners, structured light, time-of-flight sensors, as
well as hybrid active/passive approaches such as active multi-view photogrammetry.
• Photometric methodsusually focus on determining surface orientation, from which the 3D shape
can be reconstructed through integration [22, 65, 108]. The main challenge in this context lies
in selecting appropriate models that accurately describe the surface’s reflectance properties and
ensuring an adequate number of measurements to make the inversion of these models well-posed.
In comparison to geometric methods, photometric methods typically provide finer shape details
anddonotrelyonthepresenceofmatchablefeatures,makingthemsuitableforsmooth,featureless
surfaces. However, they often introduce low-frequency bias in the reconstructed positions due to
errors in modeling reflectance and illumination.
• Hybrid methods harness the advantages of both geometric and photometric methods [69, 112,
33]. In particular, they aim to mitigate the inherent low-frequency bias commonly associated with
photometric methods while enhancing the level of high-frequency details as compared to purely
geometric methods.
The technology of 3D shape capturing has already progressed to a point where very accurate high-
frequencydetailsintheobject’sgeometryandappearancearecaptured. Severalcommercialsystemshave
been developed and are used for the capture of 3D datasets of faces or other objects, see for example the
systems by 3dMD1, Di4D2 and Artec3D3.
9.4.2 Establishing Dense Correspondences
Afterthestepofdatacapturing,thetrainingdatasettypicallyconsistsofasetof Nd3Dmeshes {M1, M2, ... , MNd
}.
Each input mesh has its own number of vertices and triangles, and a particular ordering to its topol-
ogy. In order to combine the acquired shapes and construct a 3DMM, each mesh needs first to be re-
parameterized into a consistent form where the number of vertices, the triangulation, and the semantic
meaning of each vertex are made consistent across all meshes. For example, if the vertex with indexi in
onefacialmeshcorrespondstothenosetipitisrequiredthatthevertexwiththesameindexineverymesh
correspond to the nose tip too. Meshes satisfying the above properties are said to be indense correspon-
dencewithoneanother. Thisisacrucialstepin3DMMconstruction,sincethequalityoftheconstructed
modeldependsonit. Atthesametimehowever,solvingthisstepaccuratelyandrobustlybetweenhighly-
variable meshes is especially challenging.
The dense correspondences among the 3D meshesM1, ... , MNd
are typically found through the reg-
istration of every mesh with a template. Landmark annotations are used as additional priors that guide
theregistrationprocessinthecorrespondingsparselocations, seeFig. 9.4(a). Densecorrespondencecan
be seen as a generalization of non-rigid image registration to triangular meshes.
All dense correspondence algorithms typically take as inputs a template mesh and a target mesh that
havebeenlandmarkedwithsparseannotations. Establishingadensecorrespondencecanthusbethought

recent 3DMM construction pipelines, such as [13, 61]. See Fig.9.4(b) for an example.

Even though the linear PCA models have been very effective in 3DMMs, recent years have seen non-
linear extensions, aiming at further improving the quality of results. The component where non-linear
modeling seems to be most important and helping in improving the results is the color variation. Non-
linear models for 3DMMs include, for example, works such as [64, 6, 62, 94, 68, 30, 101, 99].
9.5 Fitting 3DMM parameters to images and videos
Once a 3DMM is constructed, its parameters for a specific object instance (e.g. the face of a specific real
person) can be estimated from several different types of input. The input modality can, for example, be
a single RGB image (as shown, for example, in the top row of Fig.9.6), an RGB-Depth image, RGB im-
ages from multiple cameras observing the scene, an RGB video or a 3D scan. A large variety of different
methods have been built to solve these problems and can be classified into two broad categories:energy
minimization approaches and deep learning approaches. More details about each category are given
below.
9.5.1 Energy minimization approaches
These approaches fall back on the principle of the so-calledanalysis-by-synthesis approach where the
model is adapted in an iterative manner until the synthesized shape matches the input data. The analysis-
by-synthesistechniquetypicallyadoptsenergyminimizationtoestimatetheoptimalparametersthatmin-
imize the difference between the synthetic and the observed image. To demonstrate the general idea, let
us assume the special case where the input is an RGB or RGB-Depth image of a face.

Given an image as an input, parameter estimation is conventionally framed as a general non-linear op-
timization problem (see e.g. [60, 16, 29, 96, 97, 98]). In this context, all unknowns are initially grouped
intoaparametervector P. Contemporarystate-of-the-artmethodologiestypicallyinvolveoptimizingfor
all or a subset of the following parameters: shape identity coefficientsp, shape expression coefficientsq,
color coefficientsλ, illumination parametersl, global head rotationR, and translationt.
The optimal parametersP are found by minimizing a reconstruction objective functionE:
P ∗ = argmin
P
E(P ) (9.13)
This optimization problem is typically non-linear and non-convex and the adopted objective function
consists of all or some of the following different terms:
E(P ) = w 1Esparse(P ) + w2Edense(P ) + w3Ereg(P ) (9.14)
where the first two components aredata terms that measure the similarity of the current synthesized
face and the input data and the third component is aprior term. More specifically, Esparse is a sparse
feature alignment term,Edense consists of one or more dense alignment terms andEreg is a term with
regularizers that help in better constraining the solution and resolve ambiguities. These components are
linearly combined together based on a set of tunable weightsw1, w2, w3. More details about each term
are given below:
• Sparse feature alignment term (Esparse ): Thisisoneofthemostcommonlyusedandmostimpor-
tant data terms, since several object types such as faces contain many visually-salient structures. It
forcesthatasmallsetoflandmarkpointsonthemodel(afterprojectionontheimageplane)which
align well with corresponding detected 2D features by penalizing their 2D distances.
Given the fact that the second data term (dense alignment termEdense) is typically non-convex
and includes many local minima,Esparse is a very important term that compensates for that. In
more detail, the landmark points bring the optimization close to the basin of convergence of the
dense alignment constraints. Without this data term, fast motion and strong deformation can not
be tracked reliably.
Thesuccessofthistermheavilydependsonthereliabledetectionandtrackingoflandmarks. There
is a rich body of literature on such methods, with recent deep learning approaches achieving es-
pecially robust and efficient performance, even under uncontrolled acquisition conditions, see
e.g. [15, 23].
• Dense alignment term (Edense): This term forces dense, pixel-level matching between the synthe-
sizedobjectandtheobserveddata. Often,itconsistsofadensephotometricalignmentterm,which
measures densely how well the input data is explained by a rendered version of the current model
fit.
WhentheinputcomesfromanRGB-Depthcamera,theterm EdensealsoincludesaDenseGeomet-
ric Alignment term that exploits the available depth stream, better constraining the reconstruction
problem and resolving the depth ambiguity. This is based on the idea that the reconstructed ge-
ometryoftheshapemodelshouldtightlyaligntothecaptureddepthstream. Tothisend,multiple
surface-to-depth distance measures can be employed. The most commonly used alignment term
measures the point-to-point distance between model surface points and the input depth.
• Regularization term (Ereg): This term uses the statistical information available in the face prior
and further constrains the reconstruction problem to resolve ambiguities. It typically forces the
model parameters (shape, expression, color) to be statistically close to their mean. It prevents de-
generation of the shape geometry andcolor. Underthe typical assumption that the parameters are
independent Gaussian distributed, this corresponds to a simple weighted sum of squares.

9.5.2 Deep Learning approaches
While energy minimization approaches have the ability to estimate a lot of parameters (shape, appear-
ance, illumination) simultaneously, they require solving an optimization problem for every new image.
Therefore, they are quite sensitive to the quality of the given RGB data, and, more importantly, can be
slowenoughtobecomethebottleneckforapplicationsthatareintendedtooperateinrealtime. Recently,
many approaches have tried to harness the power of deep neural networks for fast and efficient estima-
tion of 3DMM parameters. For example, Fig.9.6 shows results from a recent deep learning method that
achieves accurate, high-detailed 3D face reconstructions.
Themajorityofworksrelyon superviseddata,inthesenseofhavingimagedatapairedwiththeground
truth 3DMM parameters. However, even fullyunsupervised training has been demonstrated by mixing
model-based anddeep learningtechniques. The followingparagraphs discuss, in moredetail, eachone of
these two approaches:
• Inthe supervisedapproaches,thetasksimplifiestotrainingaregressor(orencoder)network. This
network takes an image as input and predicts the 3DMM parameters. During inference, no op-
timization is required, only a straightforward forward pass which yields the estimated coefficients
quickly. Theprimarychallengehereliesinobtainingaccurategroundtruthannotationsfortraining
such a network. One straightforward solution is manual annotation by experts, as demonstrated
in the work of Olszewski et al. [71]. However, this approach is not scalable for large datasets, and
annotation quality is subject to subjective judgment. Another option is to use a multi-view setup
that captures the true 3D shape of the face while recording RGB footage, as exemplified in [53].
Nevertheless,thismethodsuffersfromlimitedvariabilityduetothelaboratoryconditionsadopted
during capturing, which contrasts with real-world data. To address these limitations, various ap-
proaches (e.g., [52]) generate pseudo-annotations through analysis-by-synthesis reconstruction
and employ these estimations as ground truth data for regressor training. Alternatively, synthetic
paired data can be generated by creating novel 3D faces from a trained 3DMM and then rendering
2D images with random illumination and camera poses. Synthetic data incur no cost and are per-
fectly annotated by design, but a significant domain gap often exists between synthetic and real-
world images, impacting generalization to real images. A suitable compromise involves using a
combined dataset containing both real and synthetic data, as demonstrated in [47].
• Unsupervised training approaches have also been explored, as demonstrated in recent work by
Tewarietal.[ 95]. Intheirapproach,atrainableencoderandamodel-baseddecoderareemployed.
The encoder takes an image as input and is trained to produce shape coefficients, camera parame-
ters,andilluminationparametersthatcorrespondtotheinputimage. Subsequently,amodel-based
decoder(see,forexample,Eqn. 9.6)mapstheseparameterstoa3Dmesh,andadifferentiableren-
derer generates a synthetic image of the 3D face. The entire model is trained in an end-to-end
manner, eliminatingthe needfor groundtruth data. Traininginvolves minimizingthe discrepancy
betweentherealimageandthesynthesizedimage,followingtheprinciplesofstandardanalysis-by-
synthesis. Essentially, this approach extends analysis-by-synthesis to operate over a large dataset
rather than a single image. This concept, often in conjunction with supervised synthetic data, has
beenfurtherexploredintheliterature,incorporatinghigher-levellossfunctions. Forinstance,Gen-
ova et al. [31] enforce identity similarity between input and output, while Deng et al. [24] com-
bine image-consistency and perceptual loss to achieve enhanced results. Moreover, the decoder

itself can be made trainable, enabling joint learning of the model and reconstruction from 2D im-
ages. This opens the door to tasks such as refining an existing 3DMM using large image datasets,
as demonstrated by Tran and Liu [100]. More recently, Tewari et al. [83] introduced a pioneering
method for learning all three dimensions of a 3DMM, encompassing identity geometry, expres-
sion, and color, from unlabeled videos, without the need for a pre-defined 3DMM as an initial
reference.
9.6 Types of objects modeled with 3DMMs
Until now, we have focused our attention on the 3D modeling of human faces, since this is the most pro-
nounced object class where 3DMMs have been used. However, over the past years 3DMMs have also
been applied beyond faces, with especially promising results. Successful models have been built for the
surface of the whole human head [20, 80], human body [1, 63, 76, 49] and for other specific parts of the
body like ears [19] and hands [44, 85, 82, 81]. Furthermore, 3DMMs have been constructed for human
skulls [34, 70], animals [113, 91] and even cars [90].
Broadly speaking, we can argue that 3DMMs offer a particularly reliable framework to model any class
of 3D objects, provided that sufficient 3D data can be obtained (see Sec.9.4.1) and that consistent dense
correspondences across different objects of the class can be defined and estimated (see Sec.9.4.2).
9.7 Applications of 3DMMs
Deformable modeling with 3DMMs enables many impressive applications. In the following paragraphs,
wewilldiscussapplicationsinthedomainsoffacerecognition,entertainment,medicalapplications,foren-
sics, archaeology, cognitive science, neuroscience, and psychology.
9.7.1 Face recognition
3DMMs can be particularly beneficial for face recognition, since the identity as well as the color coeffi-
cients offer a compact representation of a person’s facial anatomy and appearance. For example, Blanz et
al. [10] proposed to perform face recognition using the cosine angle on the shape and color coefficients
estimated from a pair of 2D images as a distance metric for identification and recognition. This distance
metricexploitsthenaturaldisentanglementof3DMMsseparatingidentity(shapeandcolor)fromcamera
and illumination variation. It was shown that this 3DMM-based distance metric enables us to recognize
faces across large pose and illumination variations [10, 12, 77], while being robust to use with facial ex-
pressions[32],aswellasbeingabletodorecognitionfromfeaturesinthefacialtexture[ 79]. Whilstmost
workfocusesonfacerecognitionfrom2Dimages,the3DMMwasalsoappliedtothe3Dfacerecognition
task focusing on the shape coefficients and robust recognition with respect to facial expressions [2, 77,
35].
It is worth mentioning that purely data-driven approaches have remained the dominant approach to
face recognition, in particular since the advancement of deep learning technology [74, 87]. However,
data-drivenapproacheshavefundamentalproblemssuchastheirdependenceonlarge-scaletrainingdata
and their lack of generalization to out-of-distribution samples, such as with misaligned face images [48].
Thereissoundexperimentalevidencethat3DMMscansignificantlyhelptheseapproachesimprovetheir
performance, e.g., by performing reliable face frontalization [9, 37], augmenting real-world data in 3D
[67], generatingreliablesyntheticdatafortraining[ 51,89], aswellasanalyzingtheeffectsofdatasetbias
on face recognition systems [50].

9.7.2 Entertainment, visual arts and fashion
3DMMs also have various notable applications in the domains of entertainment, visual arts and fashion.
One such application is the so-calledfacial puppetry or cloning, which is a form of video-driven facial
animation that is employed in the movie and game industry as well as teleconferencing to animate virtual
characters. Itsgoalistotransferexpressionsandfacialmotionsofauserinaninputvideostreamtoatarget
character rig generated with computer graphics, see for example Fig.9.7(a). In such scenarios, 3DMMs
helpreconstructthemovingfaceintheinputvideo,reliablyextractitsmotionandexpression,andtransfer
them to the target character in a faithful manner, achieving even real-time performance [60, 96, 105, 14,
98]. Besides vision-based animation, recent works have advanced facial puppetry to such an extent that
theinputcanbejustanaudiosignalandtheanimationisdrivensolelybythespeechofasourceactor[ 42,
93].
Aclosely-relatedapplicationis face reenactment, wherethefacialactionsofapersoninadrivingvideo
areagaincapturedbutthistimearetransferredtoanotherrealperson,ratherthantoacomputer-generated
character, see Fig.9.7(b). It allows making a target subject say the words someone else says in a driving
videoandfollowitsexpressions[ 97,96,4]. Thisopensupthewayformanyintriguingapplicationsinthe
entertainment industry, ranging from visual effects and Computer-Generated Imagery (CGI) in movies
(e.g. reenactment of historical, long-deceased identities), to the realistic animation of people for Virtual
Reality and tele-presence applications. Recently, with the advent of deep generative models it has been
possible to copy not only the inner facial expressions, but also the head and upper body motion from
the driving person [46, 25]. Even more recently, using similar deep generative frameworks, it has been
even possible to alter the expressions of actors in movie scenes in order to display specific emotions spec-
ified by the user, while at the same time preserving the photo-realism of the scene and the actors’ mouth
movements that are related to the uttered speech [73].
A special case of face reenactment that is of particular interest to the movie industry isvisual dubbing,
wherethemouthmotionofanactorisalteredsothatitalignswithaforeignlanguagevoicespokenbythe
dubbing actor. In this way, the actor’s mouth motions become consistent with the voice of the dubbing
actor. In visual dubbing techniques, the facial deformations are only transferred in the mouth region,
using the source video sometimes coupled with the source audio to enforce speech-related constraints in
the mouth motion [21, 28, 45].
Anotherpopularapplicationistheso-called face replacement or face swapping,inwhichthefaceofan

actor in a target video is replaced with the face of a source actor, in a photo-realistic manner, as done for

novelsequencethatlooksrealisticandmaintainstemporalconsistencyunderdifferentacquisitioncondi-

3D representation of the face in the scene and an effective decoupling of identity, expression and head
motion parameters [43, 21, 27].
Face reconstruction and tracking based on 3DMMs has also been very successful in building virtual
mirrors that enable thevirtual try-on of accessories or virtual make-up. To this end, a personalized 3D
model of the user’s face is recovered and tracked across the video resulting in a dense set of correspon-
dences. These enable spatio-temporal re-texturing, e.g. to virtually apply facial make-up [86]. The latter
can be achieved via, for example, a reflectance/shading decomposition [58, 59]. Similar techniques en-
able accessories, such as eyeglasses, to be tried on [5].
9.7.3 Medical applications
3D Morphable Models (3DMMs) also offer significant benefits in the field of medicine. These models
find prominent applications in 3D shape analysis, enabling the identification of diseases based on facial
shape. An illustrative example is the classification and early diagnosis of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder
[92]. Similarly,Hammondetal. [36]demonstratedtheadoptionof3DMMsinvisualizingandrecogniz-
ing congenital craniofacial growth disorders. Moreover, 3DMM-based face synthesis plays a pivotal role
inmedicalapplications. 3DMMshavebeenleveragedforreconstructingmissingfacialcomponentsusing
model statistics [7]. Such reconstructions can be applied in personalized implant design. Additionally,
researchers have explored the synthesis capabilities of 3DMMs for analytical purposes, generating con-
trolledstimuliforstudyingresponsesinthefusiformfaceareaandtheircorrelationwithautismspectrum
disorder [41]. In the realm of medical imaging, 3DMMs are used as standard frameworks for segmenta-
tion and serve as prior models for capturing the shape variations of anatomical structures [111]. Many
of these applications focus on pathologies in young or elderly populations, which are often underrepre-
sented even in the largest face models [80].
9.7.4 Archaeology and forensics sciences
Another interesting application of 3DMMs is their usage in the problem of face reconstruction from dry
skulls, having impact to the fields of archaeology, through the visualization of the faces of past people
fromskeletalremains[ 106]aswellasforensicsciences,viatheproductionoffacialreconstructionswhich
sufficientlyresemblethedeceasedsoastoallowtheiridentification[ 107]. Thepredictionofthefacegiven
a dry skull is an ill-posed problem since, due to genetic and environmental factors, there can be several
possible different faces corresponding to a given skull. 3DMMs facilitate the control of attributes for this
reconstruction [78] so as to explicitly estimate the posterior solution of possible faces per skull [66] or
model soft tissue thickness directly grounded by a 3DMM [34].
9.7.5 Applications in cognitive science, neuroscience, and psychology
The capability to generate controllable facial images has gained significant popularity in the study of how
both human and non-human primate brains process faces. 3DMMs have been instrumental in creating
stimuli for such studies. One of the pioneering studies revealed high-level after-effects that suggested the

APPENDIX A
MA
THEMATICAL ELEMENTS OF IMAGE SETS AND
FUNCTIONS
Pe
tros Maragos
School of ECE, National Technical University of Athens
This appendix contains some elements from intuitive set theory focusing on basic definitions and prop-
erties of (i) sets, functions, relations and equivalences like cardinalities; (ii) level sets and their variants;
(iii) partially-ordered sets (posets). The goal is to provide mathematical elements in the above areas to
support the analytical chapters of this book on image and shape analysis.
SettheoryasamathematicaldisciplineoriginatedwithCantor. Someofhisrelatedpaperscanbefound
in [3]. Introductions to set theory can be found in [2],[4],[5],[8]. Level sets are used throughout cal-
culus and real analysis. However, their usage as a representation for image functions and the study of
their properties under several image analysis operations were systematically introduced in [7] for mor-
phological image analysis and in [6] for embedding active contours into functions and propagating them
via partial differential equations to solve various problems in computer vision. Posets are necessary for
understanding lattices which serve as nonlinear spaces for several classes of image operations; a classic
reference for poset and lattice theory is [1].
A.1 Sets, Functions, Relations
A.1.1 Sets
Cantor defined aset as a collection (or class, or aggregate) of definite, distinguishable objects which are
conceived by our intuition or intellect. These, generally abstract, objects are calledmembers, orelements,
or pointsof the set. We shall denote sets with capital Latin letters and their points with lowercase letters.
Writing x ∈ S means thatx is a member of the setS, whereas we writex ∉ S if x is not a member
of S. We assume that there is a unique set that has no elements, denoted by∅ and called theempty set.
A set will be either explicitly described by alist of its points or implicitly via apredicate, i.e. a property,

satisfied by all of its points. For instance, the setS = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4} can also be described asS = {x ∶
−1 < x < 6 and x = integer}. In general, ifP (x)is a sentence which asserts something aboutx, then
{x ∶ P (x)} denotes the “set of allxsuch thatP (x)”; thus,a ∈ {x ∶ P (x)} iff P (a)is a true statement.
A third alternative way to describe a set is viarecursive rules; e.g., the above setS can be generated by the
following rule: a)0 ∈ S , (b) Ifx ∈ S and x is less than 5, thenx + 1 ∈ S , and c) nothing else belongs
to S.
Accordingtoafundamentalprincipleofordinarysettheory,givenasetandanobject,eithertheobject
is a member of the set or it is not. There is no use of halfway, multiple, or gradual membership. (Gradual
membership exists infuzzy sets[9].) Thus, in the list notation of a set, writing a member more than once
does not change its membership status. For example, writing{a, a, b, c, c, c}describes exactly the same
set as{a, b, c}. Further, the order of listing the set members plays no role. In short, a set is a collection of
distinct unordered objects.
In set-theoretic or more general mathematical discussions, we often use declarative sentences formed
by using sentential connectives such asnot and, or, if...then (or implies), andif and only if(in short,iff)
to modify and/or combine atomic statements. The truth value of such composite sentences follows the
rules of statement calculus. Note: the conditional “P implies Q”, denoted by “P⟹ Q”, is equivalently
expressedas“PisasufficientconditionforQ”or“QisanecessaryconditionforP”.Similarly,thebicondi-
tional “P iff Q”, denoted by “P⟺ Q”, can also be expressed as “Q is a necessary and sufficient condition
for P”. Indefinitions, we shall use “if” to mean “iff”.
Two setsA and B are calledequalif they contain exactly the same members; thus,
A = B iff [ x ∈ A ⟺ x ∈ B ]
We shall say that a setA is asubset of a setB, or thatA is included inB (written asA ⊆ B ), iff each
member ofA is a member ofB. We may also express the same fact by saying thatB includes A, or that
B is a superset ofA, and writeB ⊇ A . A is called aproper subsetof B (written asA ⊂ B ) ifA ⊆ B
and A ≠ B. Obviously, set equality can be proven by showing inclusion in both directions:
A = B ⟺ [ A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A ]
Some elementary set operations are the following:
Set Union: X ∪ Y ∶= {x ∶ x ∈ X or x ∈ Y }
Set Intersection: X ∩ Y ∶= {x ∶ x ∈ X and x ∈ Y }
Set Difference: X \ Y ∶= {x ∶ x ∈ X and x ∉ Y }
Symmetric Set Difference: X△Y ∶= (X \ Y ) ∪ (Y \ X)
X \ Y isalsocalledthe relativecomplement of Y w.r.t. X. Henceforth,ifallsetsinadiscussionaresubsets
of a universal setE, instead of referring to a setE \ S as the ‘complement ofS w.r.t. E’, we shall simply
say the ‘complement ofS’ and denote it as
Sc ∶= {x ∶ x ∉ S} = U \ S, U is a universal set.
Two setsA, Bare calleddisjoint if A ∩ B = ∅ . Theyintersect if A ∩ B ≠ ∅ .
We reserve a specific notation for some number sets of particular interest:
N ∶= set of natural numbers= {0, 1, 2, 3, ...}
Z ∶= set of all integers= {0, ±1, ±2, ±3, ...}
Z>0 ∶= set of positive integers= {1, 2, 3, ...}
Q ∶= set of rational numbers
R ∶= set of real numbers
R>0 ∶= set of positive real numbers
C ∶= set of complex numbers

Examples A.1 (Sets and Collections).
(a) Given any setE, thepower set of E, denoted as
P(E) ∶= {X ∶ X ⊆ E}

nent aandthesecondcomponent bplaydistinctroles. Wecanexpressthisbywritingitasasetcollection:

If A is a set andn = 2, 3,..., the notationAn means then-fold Cartesian product ofA with itself. 2
A.1.2 Functions
A function f is a collection of ordered pairs such that if(x, y1) ∈ f and (x, y2) ∈ f , then y1 = y 2.
With each function we associate two sets: thedomainof f and therangeof f defined as
Dom(f) ∶= {x ∶ (x, y) ∈ f}, Ran(f) ∶= {y ∶ (x, y) ∈ f}
Thus, f ⊆ Dom(f) × Ran(f). For eachx ∈ Dom(f), f(x) denotes the unique element in Ran(f)
such that(x, f(x)) ∈ f and is called thevalue that f assumes at theargument x. Transformation, map
or mapping, andcorrespondence are often used as synonyms for the word ‘function’. The very common
notation
f ∶ X → Y
denotes a functionf with Dom(f) = X and Ran(f) ⊆ Y , and is read as ‘f is a functionfrom X to (or
into) Y ’oras‘ f isafunctionthat maps X into Y ’. IfX = Y , f iscalleda‘function on X’. IfRan(f) = Y ,
f is called asurjection or onto Y . If for allx, y ∈ Dom(f), f(x) = f(y) implies thatx = y , thenf
is called aninjection or one-to-one. If f is both an injection and a surjection, it is called abijection. For
example, letf(x) = x 2 and g(x) = x 3. Then f ∶ R → R + ∪ {0} is a surjection but not an injection,
whereas g ∶ R → R is a bijection.
If X ⊆ Y let id be the function defined byid(x) = x for eachx ∈ X . Thenid ∶ X → X is called
the identity mapon X, whereasid ∶ X → Y is called theinclusion mapof X into Y .
Considertwofunctions f and g suchthatRan (f) ⊆ Dom(g). Thenthe compositionof f and g isthe
function g ∘ f defined byg ∘ f(x) = g(f(x)) for eachx ∈ Dom(f).

A partition of a nonempty setS is a nonempty collectionK ⊆ P(S) of nonempty and pairwise

A.1.5 Cardinality and Infinite Sets
How big is the ‘size’ of a set regarding the number of its members? IsR larger thanZ? Does the set of
all points of the plane have more members than the collection of all subsets of the plane? To answer such
questions intuitively, we could measure the size of a set bycounting its members. This process would ter-
minateifthenumberofsetmemberswereapositiveinteger; suchsetsarefinite. However,therearesome
sets,e.g. Z,whosecountingofelementscouldneverstop;theseareinfinitesets. Tomeasureandcompare
the size of infinite sets we need a more general concept that would apply both to finite and infinite sets.
Thus, we call two setsA and B cardinally equivalent (with respect to the number of their members),
denoted as A ∼ B , iff there is a bijection fromA onto B. In a nonempty collection of sets,∼ is an
equivalence relationbecause it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. To each equivalence class there cor-
responds an abstract number, called acardinal numberor cardinality, which denotes the size of all sets
intheclass. Thus, givenaset A, itscardinality, denotedbycard(S) or #(S) or |S|, isanumbercommon
for all sets that can be put into a one-to-one correspondence withA.
Cantor’ s definition of cardinal number:“The strength or cardinal number of a set is this general concept
which,bytheaidofouractivecapacityforthought,arisesfromthesetwhenwemakeabstractionsfromthenature
of its various elements and the ordering of their presentation.
Cardinalities can be compared via set domination and equivalence. We say that a setAis dominatedby
a setB, denoted asA ⪯ B , iffA is equivalent to a subset ofB. For strict domination we writeA ≺ B
and mean thatA ⪯ B but B ⪯̸ A. The following theorem relates set domination with equivalence.
Theorem A.1 (Shroeder & Berstein).If A ⪯ B and B ⪯ A , thenA ∼ B .
By using these concepts we can compare cardinalities as follows:
card(A) = card(B) ⟺ A ∼ B
card(A) ≤ card(B) ⟺ A ⪯ B
card(A) < card(B) ⟺ A ≺ B
A setS is called:
• Finiteiff it is equivalent to{1, 2, 3, ... , n}for some fixed positive integern; thencard(S) = n .
By convention, the empty set is finite and card(∅) = 0.
• Infiniteiff it is not finite.
• Countableiff it is either finite or equivalent toN.
• Countably infinite(ordenumerable) iff it is infinite and countable.
• Uncountableiff it is not countable.

Thus, the countability of a set implies the ability toenumerateits members; this enumeration will exhaust
all the points of the set either by counting them and reaching a nonnegative integer when the set is finite,
or by putting them into a one-to-one correspondence with the elements ofN when the set is infinite.
Any infinite set contains a countable subset, since in any infinite set we can find an infinite sequence of
elements.
Wemaybeaccustomedtothinkingofasetasbeing‘larger’thananyofitspropersubsets. Thisisalways
true for finite sets, but often false for infinite sets. For example, the setN = {0, 1, 2, ...} of natural
numbers and the setE = {0, 2, 4, ...} of even nonnegative integers are equivalent because the function
f ∶ N → E with f(n) = 2n is a bijection. Hence, they have the same cardinality butE is a proper
subset ofN. Actually, Dedekind defined a set as infinite iff it is cardinally equivalent to a proper subset of
itself.
The cardinality of all countably infinite sets is denoted byא0. The next examples show that the union
or the Cartesian product ofN with other countably infinite sets yields again sets with cardinalityא0.

A.2 Level Set Representation of Image Signals
Image signals are usually represented by functionsf ∶ E → G , where the setE is thedomain of their
definition, whereas the setG is therange inside which they take values. The class of all such signalsf is
denoted by Fun(E, G).
The domain E is usually either the continuous Euclidean spaceRm or the discrete spaceZm, m =
1, 2, 3. Occasionally,E may also be the set of vertices of a graph on which the image is defined. Accord-
ing to whether the argument of the function is continuous or discrete, we call the signal a continuous-
domain or discrete-domain signal, respectively. If a discrete-domain signal has resulted from sampling a
continuous-domain signal, then the integer coordinates of each point inZm represent the integer multi-
ples of the sampling period along the corresponding direction.
For notational simplicity we shall often writef(x) for anm-dimensional signal. Wherever needed, its
independent variablex will be written explicitly as anm-dimensional vectorx = (x 1, x2, ..., xm). The
notation f(x, y) will be used for 2D spatial images whenever we need to emphasize the Cartesian coor-
dinates of the image plane. One-dimensional signals whose independent variable is time may be denoted
by f(t). Althoughmostof our discussionandthe notation f(x) willrefertocontinuous-domainsignals,
we may also occasionally use the notationf(x) for discrete-domain signals. However, when signals are
defined on a discrete domain and there is a need to emphasize their discrete argument, then they will be

denoted byf[⋅]. For example, we may writef[n] for discrete-time signals, andf[i, j] for discrete-space
images defined onZ2.
Thesignalrange Gisusually scalarandmainlyinteger-orreal-valued,asinthecaseofgraylevelimages.
(Color images are vector-valued.) Rarely, the scalar range is complex-valued, e.g., as in the cases of image
spectra or image-related functions in optical systems. For performing linear filtering operations on real
scalar signals, the signal is finite-valued and hence its range is a subset ofR. However, several nonlinear
operations (e.g. morphological filtering based on max-plus convolutions [7]) allowextended-real-valued
signals whose range is a subset of the setR = R ∪ {−∞, +∞} of extended real numbers. Allowing
signals to take infinite values(±∞) is a formalism very convenient for the nonlinear signal operations
examined in this book.
For the rest of this section, we shall deal with scalar extended-real-valued multidimensional signals
f ∶ E → R. We can extend various set transformations to signals by representing signals with sets and
transforming these set representations. The most important type of sets associated with a signalf is its
upper level sets
Xv(f) ∶= {x ∈ E ∶ f(x) ≥ v}, −∞ < v < +∞
obtained by thresholdingf at level v. Thus, the sets Xv(f) are also called upperthreshold sets. Each
Xv(f) is subset of the signal domain that contains exactly the points at which the signal has values≥ v.
SeeFig. A.5 foranillustrationwheretheactionofthresholdingisalsointerpretedastakingthehorizontal
cross-section of the function at heightv and projecting this section onto the domain.

By thresholding at all different signal amplitude levelsv we can associate a signalf with the collection
of its upper level sets which decrease monotonically asv increases. Examples are shown in Fig.A.5 and
Fig.A.6. If we know all the level sets, we can uniquely reconstruct the signal via a supremum operation.This is
illustrated in Fig.A.5(b) which shows a one-dimensional signalf and two of its upper level sets at levels
v1 < v 2. We observe that a given pointx belongs to Xv1
(f) if and only iff(x) ≥ v 1. By contrast,
x ∉ X v2
(f) because f(x) < v 2. Thus, the value off at x is equal to the largest (supremum) of signal
values v such thatf(x) ≥ v , or equivalentlyx ∈ X v(f).
In addition to the upper level sets, there also exist alternative families of threshold sets with which we
can associate a signal. Thus, we can also consider the sets

A.3 Ordered Sets, Posets
A binary relation≤ in a setP that is reflexive, anti-symmetric and transitive is called anpartial ordering
in P. A partially-ordered set, briefly poset, (P , ≤)is a nonempty setP in which a relation≤ is defined
that is a partial ordering, i.e. satisfies the following three properties for allx, y, z ∈ P :
(P1). x ≤ x ( reflexive)
(P2). x ≤ y and y ≤ x imply x = y ( antisymmetric)
(P3). x ≤ y and y ≤ z imply x ≤ z ( transitive)
A poset(P , ≤)is called atotally-ordered setor chainif ≤ has the additional following property:
(P4) x ≤ y or y ≤ x for any distinctx, y ∈ P ( connected).
Examples A.5 (Posets).
(a)In Rthenaturalordering ≤betweenrealnumbersisatotalordering; (R, ≤)isthearchetypalexample
of a chain.
(b)Inthepowerset P(E) ofanyset E,setinclusion ⊆ isapartialordering; (P(E), ⊆ )isthearchetypal
example of a poset.
(c) The set Fun(R, R) of all functionsf ∶ R → R equipped with the partial orderingf ≤ g , which
means f(x) ≤ g(x) for allx, becomes a poset. 2
The relationx ≤ y is usually read ‘x is less than or equal toy’, ‘x is contained iny’, or ‘x preceeds y’. It
is also writteny ≥ x and read ‘y is greater than or equal tox’, ‘y contains x’, or ‘y succeeds x’. The strict
ordering x < y , which meansx ≤ x and x ≠ y , is read ‘x is less thany’ or ‘x is properly contained
in y’. We say that ‘b is animmediate successorof a’ (or ‘b covers a’) iff a < b and there is noc such that
a < c < b .
A poset is calledfinite (resp. infinite) if its underlying set has finite (resp. infinite) cardinality. Finite
posets can be represented graphically byposet diagrams(also called ‘Hasse diagrams’) that are graphs

Proposition A.3 (a) Any finite nonempty subset of a poset has maximal and minimal elements. (b) In chains
the concepts of least and minimal element, as well as greatest and maximal element, are equivalent. Every finite
chain has a least and a greatest element.
According to (P1), (P2) and (P3) it follows that, to every partial ordering≤ in a setP there corre-
sponds aconverse partial ordering ≤′ defined by the converse relation ‘x ≤ ′ y iff x ≥ y ’. For example,
in the poset formed by the power set(P(E), ⊆ ) of a setE, where the partial ordering≤ is the ‘sub-
set’ relation A ⊆ B , the converse ordering≤′ becomes the ‘superset’ relationA ⊇ B . This simple
observation leads to an important principle.
Theorem A.6 (Duality Principle in Posets).If (P , ≤)is a poset, then(P , ≥)is also a poset, called
the dual poset. Further, to every definition or true theorem in(P , ≤)there corresponds a dual one in(P , ≥)
which results from replacing≤ with ≥.
Note that this is a theorem about theorems and belongs to the field of ‘metamathematics’. For brevity,
if ≤ is understood from the context, we refer to the poset(P , ≤)and its dual poset(P , ≤′) as simply
P and P ′ respectively. As an application of duality, note that elements of a posetP that are a lower
bound,maximal,orinfimumforasubset S ⊆ P canbedefinedasupperbound,maximal,orsupremum,
respectively,foritsdualposet P ′. Whilethisprincipleeliminatestheneedforadditionalproofsregarding
dual concepts, it should be used with caution. As a counterexample, ifP has a greatest element, then its
dual P ′ has a least element, but this does not necessarily imply thatP has a least element. For a finite
poset P, itsdualposet P ′ canbevisualizedviaitsdiagramwhichisobtainedbyturningthediagramof P
upside down.
A transformation φ ∶ P → Q from a poset(P , ≤P ) to a poset(Q, ≤Q) is called increasing (or
isotone) if it isorder-preserving), i.e.∀x, y ∈ P
x ≤ P y ⟹ φ(x) ≤ Q φ(y)
The mappingφ is called aposet isomorphismiff it is a bijection such that
x ≤ P y ⟺ φ(x) ≤ Q φ(y)
Namely, φ is an isomorphism iff (i)φ is a bijection, (ii)φ is increasing, and (iii)φ−1 is increasing. A
counterexample illustrating the need for the third requirement is the mappingf ∶ B4 → C4 between
the 4-element posets B4 and C4 of Fig.A.7 defined byf(O) = O, f(a) = a, f(b) = b, f(I) = I .
Then f is a bijection and increasing, butf −1 is not increasing; clearly, the two posets are not isomor-
phic. Isomorphic finite posets have the same diagram modulo a different labeling of their elements. An
isomorphism fromP to itself is called a posetautomorphism.

Theorem A.7 Any poset(P , ≤)is isomorphic to a collection of sets partially ordered by set inclusion. Such
an isomorphism is the mappingφ that maps each poset elementx ∈ P to the subset{a ∈ P ∶ a ≤ x} .
Proof: Let K = {{a ∈ P ∶ a ≤ x} ∶ x ∈ P } . Then φ ∶ P → K is a bijection, and the inverse
mapping isφ−1(X) = sup X, X ∈ K . Both φ and φ−1 are increasing. Henceφ is an isomorphism.
Q.E.D.
A poset mappingψ ∶ P → Q is calleddecreasing (orantitoneif it isorder-inverting), i.e.
x ≤ P y ⟹ ψ(x) ≥ Q ψ(y)
If ψ is a bijection where bothψ and ψ−1 are decreasing, then it is called a posetdual isomorphismor
anti-isomorphism. A dual isomorphism fromP to itself is called adual automorphism. A posetP is called
self-dual if there exists a dual automorphism on it that makes it anti-isomorphic with its dual posetP ′.
For example, for any setE, the poset(P(E), ⊆ ) is self-dual since the set complementation mapping
X ↦ X c is an anti-automorphism on it.
A poset is calledwell-orderedif it is a chain such that each of its nonempty subsets contains a least ele-
ment;suchanorderingiscalleda well-ordering. Thearchetypalexampleofawell-orderedsetistheset Z+
of positive integers with its natural ordering.
Well-ordering Principle: For every nonempty set, there exists a well-ordering.
Applying this principle to the set of positive integers yields the principle of induction.
Principle of Finite Induction: Assume thatS is a subset ofZ+ such that1 ∈ S , andn ∈ S implies that
n + 1 ∈ S . ThenS = Z +.
Thewell-orderingprincipleisequivalenttothefollowingstatementwhosevaliditycanneitherbeproved
nor refuted.
Axiom of Choice: Let K be a nonempty collection of nonempty sets. Then there exists a functionσ defined
on K that selects one element from each setS ∈ Kk .
Equivalent to the axiom of choice is also each one of the following two principles.
Zorn’ s Lemma: Assume that(P , ≤)is a poset where every chainC has an upper (resp. lower) bound inP.
Then P has a maximal (resp. minimal) element.
Hausdorff ’ s Maximality Principle: Every poset contains a maximal chain.

In this appendix we will review basic concepts first from i) topological spaces and ii) metric spaces, and
then we will focus briefly on iii) topologies and metrics for spaces of sets modeling shapes. These topics
provide mathematical background for the analytical chapters of this book on image and shape analysis.
There are many good books on parts (i) and (ii), i.e. on introductory ideas from topology and metric
spaces; in these areas our exposition is based mainly on Kasriel [7], Naylor and Sell [10], Dugundji [3],
and Rudin [13]. We will emphasize concepts that are useful for spaces of shapes, images and signals. In
part (iii) our coverage summarizes results from Hausdorff [5], Matheron [8], Serra [14], Heijmans [6],
and Barnsley [1].
B.1 Topological Spaces
Supposewestudyasetofmathematicalobjectsandmappingsdefinedonitandweneedtoanalyzeissues
such as limit points, interior, boundary, convergence, continuity, compactness and connectedness, but
there is no metric available. We are still able to define such concepts if we can define the family of ‘open’
subsets, which play the role of ‘neighborhoods’.
Givenanonemptyset E,a topologyfor E isanycollection Tofsubsetsof E thatsatisfiesthefollowing
three properties1:
(T1) ∅ and E belong toT;
(T2) the union of every subcollection ofT is a member ofT;
(T3) the intersection of every finite subcollection ofT is a member ofT.
The pair(E, T) is called atopological space; ifT can be inferred from the discussion, we may refer only
to E as the topological space. The members ofE are calledpoints, whereas the members ofT are called

the open sets of this space. Thus,∅ and E are open; further, every union and every finite intersection of
open sets is open. A subsetF of E is calledclosed if its complementF c = E \ F is open. Obviously,
∅ and E are closed; further, every finite union and every intersection of closed sets is closed. Open sets
allow us to define neighborhoods and express ‘nearness’ around a point; simply put, aneighborhoodof a
point x is any open set that containsx.
A subcollection B ⊆ T of open sets is called abasis for the topologyT if every open set can be
expressed as a union of some basis members. This implies that the basis is an open covering of the space.
Each topology may have more than one basis, and the topology itself is a basis. Each basisB generates a
unique topology
T(B) = { ⋃ G ∶ G ⊆ B}
by collecting the unions of all subcollections of the basis;T(B) is the smallest topology containingB.
Twobasesarecalled equivalentiftheygeneratethesametopology. However, noteverycollectionofopen
sets that covers the space can serve as a basis, becauseB is a basis for the topology iff for each open setG
and eachx ∈ G , there is aV ∈ B such thatx ∈ V ⊆ G . To avoid this limitation with the basis, it is
possible to create a topology in a set from an arbitrary collection of its subsets as the following procedure
explains.
Theorem B.1 ([3, 7]). Consider a nonempty collectionS of subsets ofE such that ⋃ S = E . This can
always create a unique smallest topology whose basis consists of the finite intersections of members ofS:
B(S) = { ⋂ F ∶ F is a nonempty finite subcollection ofS}
The collectionS is called asubbasisfor this topology.
The topology T(B(S)) created by a subbasisS contains ∅, E, all finite intersections of members ofS
(which are the basis members), and all arbitrary unions of these finite intersections. Obviously,S ⊆
B ⊆ T .
Examples B.1 (Topological Spaces).
(a)Foranarbitraryset E,itspowerset P(E) definesatopologywhereeverysetisbothopenandclosed;
this is called thediscrete topology. The collection of all singletons{{x} ∶ x ∈ E} is a basis for this
topology. This is the usual topology for the setZ of integers. (E, P(E)) is called adiscrete (topological)

B.1.1 Closure, Interior, Boundary, Continuity, Convergence
Let (E, T) be a topological space and consider a subsetS ⊆ E . A pointx ∈ S is called:
(i)accumulation point(orlimit point) ofS if for each open setG containing x, G intersects S in at least
one point different thanx.
(ii)interior pointof S if there is an open setG such thatx ∈ G ⊆ S .
(iii)boundary pointof S if every open set containingx intersects bothS and its complementSc.
These types of points define three important sets related toS, its closure S, interior S∘, and boundary
∂S:
S ∶= S ∪ { accumulation points ofS}
S∘ ∶= set of interior points ofS
∂S ∶= set of boundary points ofS
In general,S∘ ⊆ S ⊆ S. Obviously, a set is open iff it equals its interior. Similarly, a set is closed iff it
equals its closure. A closed set is calledperfect if it is equal with the set of its accumulation points.
A subsetD of E is calleddense if D = E . For example, the setQ of rationals is dense inR. In general,
D is dense iff every nonempty open subset of the space intersectsD. Note that the only closed subset
of E that can be dense isE itself. A point x ∈ E is called anisolated pointif it is not an accumulation
point of E, or, equivalently, if{x} is a open set. A dense subset must contain all isolated points of the
space. Thus, spaces with a discrete topology, like(Z, P(Z)), cannot have a proper dense subset. Namely,
discrete spaces contain only isolated points; they do not contain any accumulation points.
A mappingf ∶ (X, T X) → (Y , T Y ) between two topological spaces is calledcontinuous at a point
xo ∈ X if for each neighborhoodU of f(x o) in Y there is a neighborhoodV of xo in X such that
f(V ) ⊆ U , where f(V ) is the image ofV under f. f is called continuous if it is continuous at each
point. Equivalently,f is continuous iff the inverse imagef −1(U )of each open subsetU of Y is an open
subset ofX.

B.1.2 Topological Countability
A topological spaceE is calledfirst-countable(or satisfies the first axiom of countability) if its topology
admits a countable local basis for each point’s neighborhood collection. Namely, for each pointx ∈ E
there is a countable collection(Vn) of some of its neighborhoods, which plays the role of a local basis in
the sense that every other neighborhoodU of xcontains at least one member of this collection; i.e. there
is somen such thatx ∈ V n ⊆ U .
A stronger case is for the whole topological space to admit a countable basis; this is called asecond-
countablespace. Obviously, a second countable space is also first countable. For example, consider the
basis B = {(x − r, x + r) ∶ x ∈ R, r > 0} for the Euclidean topologyT of R. Focusing at each
point xand keeping only its symmetric neighborhood intervals(x − 1/n, x + 1/n)with inverse radius
n = 1, 2, 3, ...,createsacountablebasisforthecollectionofallitsneighborhoods,whichmakesthespace
first countable. Further,T can be created from a countable subcollection ofB that consists only of those
intervalswhosecentersandradiiarerationalnumbers. Thus, Rissecond-countable. Asanotherexample,
every discrete space is first-countable; furthermore, it is second-countable iff it is countable. Thus,Z is
second-countable; its basis is the collection of all its singletons.
In first-countable spaces, all topological concepts, e.g. limits, closure and continuity, can be expressed
and analyzed simply by using sequential convergence, as the following indicates.
Proposition B.1 On a first-countable topological spaceX the following hold:
(a) A pointx is an accumulation point of a subsetS iff there is a sequence inS \ {x} that converges tox.
(b) A sequence(xn) has a cluster pointp iff there is a subsequence(xnk
) that converges top.
(c) A subsetS is closed iff every convergent sequence inS converges to a point inS.
(d)Amapping f from X toatopologicalspace Y iscontinuousiffforeachpoint xandeachsequence (xn) → x
in X f(x n) converges tof(x).
A more general concept than second countability is separability. A topological spaceE is called sep-
arable if it contains a countable dense subsetD. For example,R is separable since it contains the set of
rationals. If a topological spaceE is second-countable, then it is separable. To see this, let a countable
basis B = {V i ∶ i ∈ N} contain only nonempty sets; then, by picking one point from each basis set,
we formD = {c i ∶ c i ∈ V i} which is a countable dense subset ofE since every nonempty open sub-
set ofE contains some basis set and hence intersectsD. For metric spaces, the converse is also true; i.e.
separability implies second countability.

B.1.3 Topological Separation
Wehavelistedbelowsomepropertiesoftopologicalspacesthatspecifywhetherpairsconsistingofpoints
orclosedsubsetsaretopologicallydistinguishable,i.e. canbeseparatedbydisjointneighborhoods. These
arecalledseparation propertiesorseparation axiomsandtheirprecisedefinitionsmayvaryslightlyin the
literature; we follow the definitions in [7]. Metric spaces satisfy all of the separation axioms. However,
studyingweakertopologicalspacesthatsatisfyonlysomeoftheseaxiomshelpstoclarifywhichadditional
properties are needed for a topological space to be given the structure of a metric space.
A topological space is called:
• T 1-space orweakly separatedif for each pair of distinct pointsx and y in the space, there is an open
set V that containsx but not y and an open setU that containsy but not x. (This is equivalent to all
singletons being closed subsets of the space.)
• Hausdorff spaceor T2-space orstrongly separatedif for each pair of distinct pointsx and y, there exist
two disjoint open setsV and U containing x and y, respectively.
• Regular spaceif for each closed setA and pointx ∉ A there exist two disjoint open setsV and U that
contain A and x, respectively.
• T 3-space if it is is bothT1 and regular.
• Normal spaceif for each pair of disjoint closed setsA and B there exist two disjoint open setsV and
U that containA and B, respectively.
• T 4-space if it is bothT1 and normal.
Obviously, T4 ⟹ T 3 ⟹ T 2 ⟹ T 1.
The above separation properties can simplify the types of limit points of sets and sequences. First, in a
T1-spaceanaccumulationpoint pofaset X hastheadditionalpropertythateveryopenneighborhoodof
p contains aninfinitesubset ofX. Second, in a general topological space, a sequence(xn) may converge
to more than one point. However, if the space is Hausdorff, then a convergent sequence converges to a
unique point called thelimit of the sequence and denoted by limxn. In this bookall topological spaces
will have at least the separation structure of Hausdorff spaces. Thus, henceforth the neighborhoods of an
accumulation point of a set will intersect the set at infinitely many points, and all sequences will converge
to, at most, one point.
B.1.4 Topological Compactness
Given a topological space(E, T), a subcollectionK ⊆ T of the topology is called anopen coveringof
E if E = ⋃ K. If H is a subcollection ofK that coversE, thenH is called a subcovering. The space
E is calledcompact if every open covering ofE contains a finite subcovering. For example, the spaceR
is not compact, because the covering{(−r, r) ∶ r > 0} does not contain a finite subcovering. A subset
S ⊆ E is called acompact setif S is a compact space under the relative topology. Obviously, all finite
subsets are compact. A discrete space is compact iff it is finite.
Some properties closely related to compactness are the following. A topological spaceX is called:
Sequentially compactif every sequence inX has a subsequence that converges to a point inX.
Bolzano-Weierstrass (B.W.) compact: A spaceX has the B.W. property if every infinite subset ofX has an
accumulation point inX.
Theorem B.2 ([7]). (a) If a topological space isT1 and first-countable, then sequential compactness and
B.W. compactness are equivalent and both are implied by compactness.
(b) If a topological space is aT1 second-countable space or a metric space, then compactness, sequential com-
pactness and B.W. compactness are all equivalent.
AsubsetofaEuclideanspace Rm iscompactiffitisclosedandbounded. However, thisclassicresultis

B.1.5 Topological Connectedness
A topological space(E, T) is called connected if it is not the union of two disjoint open subsets ofE.
A subset X ⊆ E is called connected ifX is a connected space under the relative topologyT|X. All
real normed linear spaces are connected; examples includeRm, C([a, b], R) and l2(Z, R). If a set is not
connected,itiscalled disconnected. Anymaximalconnectedsubsetof X iscalleda connectedcomponent of
X. Obviously,aspaceorasubset X isconnectediffitconsistsofasingleconnectedcomponent, X itself.
At the other extreme, a topological space is calledtotally disconnectedif every subset with a single point is
a connected component. For example, all spaces with the discrete topology are totally disconnected and
so are countable subsets of a metric space like the set of rationals inR. A space that is both compact and
connectediscalleda continuum. Forexample, theinterval [0, 1]ofrealnumbersisacontinuumandsois
any closed ball inRm.
Aconnectedset X canbecomedisconnectedbyremovingasubset S. Namely,ifX\S isdisconnected,
then S separates X. As a special case, ifS = {x} for somex ∈ X , thenx is called acut pointof X. For
example, in the Euclidean spaceR every point is a cut point, whereas a circle inR2 has no cut points.
A stronger form of connectedness is based on paths. Apath in a subsetS of a topological space is a
continuous mappingf ∶ [0, 1] → S . If for each two pointsa, bin S there is a path inS that joinsa to b,
then S is calledpath-connected. Path-connectedness implies that the space is also connected.

f −1 are continuous, thenf is called ahomeomorphism(ortopological mapping) and the two topological

B.2 Metric Spaces
A metric spaceis a pair(E, d) of a nonempty setE and a real-valued functiond, defined onE × E, that
satisfies the following four properties for allx, y, z ∈ E :
(M1) d(x, y) ≥ 0 and d(x, x) = 0 (Positivity)
(M2) d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) (Triangle inequality).
(M3) d(x, y) = d(y, x) (Symmetry)
(M4) Ifd(x, y) = 0, thenx = y (Strict positivity).
The functiond is called ametric for E or adistance3. If it satisfies only (M1), (M2) and (M3), it is called
a semimetric(orpseudometric).
For any subsetS of E, the restrictiondS = d| S×S is a metric forS. The corresponding metric space
(S, dS) called a metricsubspaceof (E, d).
B.2.1 Metric Topologies and Metric Equivalence
In metric spaces it is simple to createlocal neighborhoodsaround a pointx by defining the closedball
B(x, r) and open ballB∘(x, r)centered atx and with radiusr > 0:
B(x, r) = {y ∈ E ∶ d(x, y) ≤ r}, B ∘(x, r) = {y ∈ E ∶ d(x, y) < r}
Thenasubset G ⊆ E is calledopenifaroundeachpoint x ∈ G thereisanopenball B∘(x, r)contained
in G. The collection of all such open subsets forms a topology for the metric spaceE. Thus, every metric
space is a topological space. A basis for this topology is the collectionB = {B ∘(x, r) ∶ x ∈ E, r > 0}
of all open balls centered at all points. Conversely, if the topology is induced by a metric, the topological
spaceiscalled metrizable. Foragivenset E,theremayexistmanypossiblemetrics,andeachmetric dcan
generateatopology T(d)for E. Twometrics d1 and d2 on E arecalled equivalentiftheycreatethesame
topology, i.e.T(d1) = T(d 2). Then, the spaces(E, d1) and (E, d2) are calledtopologically equivalent.
Proposition B.2 Two metrics d1 and d2 on a spaceE are equivalent if and only if there exist two positive
constants c1, c2 such that for allx, y ∈ E
c1d2(x, y) ≤ d 1(x, y) ≤ c 2d2(x, y)

Let (E, d) be a metric space. A sequence(xn) converges to a pointx, called thesequence limitand

there is a subsequence converging to this point.
