B.2.3 Compactness and Boundedness in Metric Spaces
The general concept of a topological spaceE being compact iff each open covering ofE contains a finite
subcovering becomes equivalent (see TheoremB.2) to each one of the following two more useful prop-
erties when the space is metric and separable:
Sequential compactness: Every sequence inE has a subsequence converging inE.
Bolzano-Weierstrass compactness: Every infinite subset ofE has at least one accumulation point inE.
However, general metric spaces are not separable (equivalently second-countable); they are always first-
countable. Thus,weshallexplorenextanadditionalstructureformetricspacestomakethemcompactor
relax the concept of compactness and work with finitely compact spaces.
Compactness in metric spaces is related to the topological concept of closedness and to the metric
concept of boundedness. Given a subsetS of a metric space(E, d), itsdiameter is defined by
diam(S) ∶= sup{d(x, y) ∶ x, y ∈ S}
S is calledboundedif its diameter is finite; otherwise it is unbounded. For exampleRm is not bounded,
but any (open or closed) ball in it is bounded. The space is said to havebounded metricif the choice ofd
yields diam(E) < ∞ .
Boundednessisnotatopologicalproperty. Tooseethis,consideraboundedmetric d′ relatedto d;two
such examples ared′(x, y) = min(k, d(x, y)) or d′(x, y) = kd(x, y)/(1 + d(x, y)) , wherek > 0 .
Both choices ofd′ are equivalent tod and hence give homeomorphic spaces. But a subsetS ⊆ E may
be unbounded in(E, d) whereas it is always bounded in(E, d′).
Proposition B.3 ([2]). Compact subsets of metric spaces are closed, bounded and separable.
The converse of the above proposition is not always true. In Euclidean spaces we have the following
classic and useful theorem to fully characterize compact sets.
Theorem B.4 (Heine-Borel).A subset of the Euclidean spaceRm is compact iff it is closed and bounded.
However, this theorem does not always apply to general metric spaces. One approach is to pair closed-
ness with a stronger version of boundedness. Specifically, it can be shown that a metric space(E, d) is
separable iff for eachε > 0 we can find a countable setFε ⊆ E such thatE can be represented as a
countable union
E = ⋃{B∘(x, ε) ∶ x ∈ F ε}
of open balls whose centers comprise the setFε and whose radiusε controls the scale of this covering.
Namely,eachpointof E iswithin εdistance(measuredvia d)fromsomepointin Fε. Iftheset Fε (called
ε-net)isfiniteforeach ε > 0,thenthespace E iscalled totally bounded. Thisisastrongerpropertythan
separability or simple boundedness, since a totally bounded space is both separable and bounded.
Theorem B.5 ([7]). (a) A metric space is compact iff it is complete and totally bounded. (b) In a complete
metric space, a subset is compact iff it is closed and totally bounded.

B.2.4 Finitely Compact Metric Spaces
Generalmetricspacesdonotpossessarichgeometricstructure. Onesufficientlygeneralcategoryofmet-
ricspacesendowedwitharichstructureandusefulinavarietyofproblemsinimageanalysisandcomputer
vision abstracts the main idea in Heine-Borel’s theorem as well as in the following classic theorem from
Euclidean spaces.
Theorem B.6 (Bolzano-Weierstrass).Every bounded infinite subset of the Euclidean spaceRm has at least
one accumulation point inRm.
Inspired by the above theorem, we shall find the following weaker concept of compactness analyzed in
detailbyBusemann[ 2]andRinow[ 12]useful. Ametricspace (E, d) iscalled finitely compactprovided
that every bounded infinite subset of the space has at least one accumulation point. For example,Rm is
finitely compact. Some properties of finitely compact metric spaces and sets include the following:
Proposition B.4 ([2, 12]).
(a) For a metric space to be finitely compact is equivalent to the condition that a subset of the space is compact iff
it is closed and bounded.
(b) A finitely compact set is closed and separable.
(c) Compact metric spaces are finitely compact.
(d) Finitely compact metric spaces are complete, locally compact and separable.
B.3 Topologies and Metrics on Spaces of Sets
Sets are useful models in image analysis and computer vision for representing shapes and image signals
via their level sets or graphs. Thus, to study topological aspects of spaces of shapes and images as well as
oftheirtransformations,weneedtoequipsetcollectionswithappropriatetopologiesandifpossiblewith
metrics. Given a topological spaceE whose subsets are potential image models, we are mainly interested
in four types of subsets: its power setP(E), the collectionF(E) of its closed subsets, the collection of
its open subsetsG(E), and the collectionK(E) of its compact subsets. The two most frequent cases for
E is the Euclidean spaceRm and the discrete spaceZm. Another general case is forE to be a finitely
compact metric space. We will begin with some fundamental concepts on the convergence of a sequence
of subsets of a spaceE, for which we shall examine two cases.
Case 1. LetE be an arbitrary set. Given a set sequence(Xn) in P(E), itsset-theoretic upper limit(or
limit superior), denoted as Limsup(Xn), is defined as the set of allx ∈ E that belong to infinitely many
Xn. Theset-theoretic lower limit(orlimit inferior) of the set sequence, denoted as Liminf(Xn), is defined
asthesetofall x ∈ E thatbelongtoalmostallthe Xn. Ifthesetwolimitsareequal,thenthesetsequence
(Xn) is said to converge toX, written as LimXn = X , which is called theset-theoretic limitof (Xn).
Note that, for the above set-theoretic limits there is no topology involved. It can be shown that

B.3.4 Semi-continuity of Set Mappings
The corresponding concepts of convergence and continuity in topological spaces with a countable basis
arenotfineenoughtodescribewhathappensinsomecaseswhereasequencemaynotconvergetoalimit
but it may still have an upper or lower limit. Thus, similarly to the concepts of upper and lower limit, we
can also define upper or lower semi-continuity.
Consider the spaceF = F(E) of closed subsets ofE, whereE is a locally compact Hausdorff space
with a countable basis, and an arbitrary topological spaceS. According to the general definition of a
continuous mapping between topological spaces based on preserving open neighborhoods, a mapping
ψ ∶ S → F is called upper semi-continuous (u.s.c.) if ψ−1(FK) is open inS for each compact set
K ⊆ E , where ψ−1(FK) is the inverse image ofFK = {X ∈ F ∶ X ∩ K = ∅} under ψ.
ψ is called lower semi-continuous (l.s.c.) if ψ−1(FG) is open inS for each open setG ⊆ E , where
FG = {X ∈ F ∶ X ∩ G ≠ ∅} . Ifψ is both u.s.c. and l.s.c., then it iscontinuous, and conversely.
If S is a second-countable topological space, we can relate and analyze the above definitions of semi-
continuity by using upper and lower limits of set sequences.
Proposition B.8 ([8]).Let ψ be a mapping from a second-countable topological spaceS into F. Then: (a)ψ
isu.s.c. iff sn → s impliesthat lim ψ(sn) ⊆ ψ(s) . (b)ψisl.s.c. iff sn → s impliesthat ψ(s) ⊆ lim ψ(sn).
If S = F , then u.s.c. becomes equivalent to a type of monotone convergence which is much simpler
to analyze. Specifically, a set sequence(Xn) in P(E) is said to↓-converge toX, written asXn ↓ X , if
Xn+1 ⊆ X n for each n and X = ⋂n Xn. Then, a set operatorψ is called ↓-continuous if Xn ↓ X
implies ψ(Xn) ↓ ψ(X) .
Proposition B.9 ([8]). An increasing operatorψ ∶ F → F is u.s.c iff it is↓-continuous.

### Σελίδα 534

Summary: This book is a postgraduate-level textbook that bridges theory and applications on selected topics
in computer vision and machine learning. The first part (Chapters 1–5) develops the theoretical foundations,
covering linear operators and Hilbert spaces, least-squares met h o d s  a n d  S V D  f o r  i l l - p o s e d  p r o b l e m s ,
r e g r e s s i o n  a n d  P C A ,  e l e m e n t s  o f  a b s t r a c t  a l g e b r a  f o r  v i s i o n  a n d robotics, nonlinear operators from
mathematical morphology and tropical algebra on lattice spaces, and theoretical analysis of fractals for vision
and signal processing. The second part (Chapters 6–9), co-autho red with collaborators, focuses on modern
deep learning applications, including  deep neural networks for  object detection and image segmentation,
action and gesture recognition for human–machine interaction, v isual emotion recognition, and 3D models
for deformable objects. Appendices provide supporting mathemati cal tools, making the book a
comprehensive resource for students with prior background in linear algebra, image processing, and machine
learning.

Short Bio: Petros Maragos received the M.Eng.Ε.Ε. Diploma from the National Technical University of Athens
(NTUA), Greece, in 1980, and the M.Sc. and Ph.D. degrees from G eorgia Tech, Atlanta, in 1982 and 1985. In
1985 he joined the faculty of the Division of Applied Sciences at Harvard University, where he worked for
eight years as professor of electrical engineering, affiliated with the interdisciplinary Harvard Robotics Lab. In
1993 he joined the ECE faculty at Georgia Tech and its Center f or Signal and Image Processing. During 1996-
98 he had a joint appointment as director of research at the Institute for Language and Speech Processing in
Athens. In 1998 he joined the faculty at NTUA ECE School, where  he founded the Computer Vision, Speech
Communication & Signal Processing Lab and also served as the di rector of the Intelligent Robotics and
Automation Lab. During 2023-25 he co-founded the Robotics Insti tute at the Athena Research Center and
served as its acting director. Since 2025, he has been the co-f ounder, Director, and Scientific Coordinator of
HERON – the European Center of Excellence in Robotics in the AI  era. His research and teaching interests
include computer vision and image processing, audio-speech and language processing, machine learning, and
robotics. He is the recipient of several distinctions for his a cademic work, including an NSF PYIA, best paper
awards for publications in IEEE journals and computer vision co n f e r e n c e s ,  a n d  t h e  E U R A S I P  t e c h n i c a l
achievement award. He is a Fellow of IEEE and EURASIP.
